News.title: Football regulator chair vows to quit if there is political interference in Man City case
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The head of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has declared he will resign if political interference compromises any potential probe into Manchester City.

An independent commission previously ruled that the club deliberately set out to bypass Premier League financial regulations over a nine-season period.

While City have lodged an appeal against that decision, an upheld verdict could trigger action from the IFR, which holds the authority to mandate that owners sell their stakes in severe instances.

Comments from Prime Minister Andy Burnham sparked discussion after he admitted he would be "really concerned" should the Abu Dhabi owners depart following the ruling, highlighting the potential knock-on effects for diplomatic and commercial relations between the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates.

However, IFR chair David Kogan maintained a firm stance that his organisation would refuse to tolerate outside influence if they decide to proceed with measures against City’s ownership.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has previously said he would be ‘really concerned’ if Man City’s Abu Dhabi owners leave the English game (Sean Gallup/PA)

Speaking at the launch of the regulator's ‘State of the Game’ publication in Manchester on Tuesday, he said: "We are absolutely bound by one thing, and that one thing is regulating football and regulating football clubs."

He added: "Our independence is absolute, and my independence personally is absolute. I made it very clear in an interview last year that if we (experience) any form of political interference on the way we operate it is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely.

"Just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic, and I don’t expect to in the future."

A provision in an earlier draft of the Football Governance Bill had instructed the regulator to evaluate the UK Government’s trade and foreign policy priorities when determining suitability, though that requirement was subsequently removed.

Kogan’s own appointment as chair recently faced scrutiny from the Commissioner for Public Appointments due to his past ties to the Labour Party.

The investigation established that Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy had violated procedural rules by failing to register donations received from Kogan, yet it determined he was unaware of the breach and raised no concerns regarding his fitness for office.

Shadow Culture Minister Louie French subsequently remarked that a "Labour donor and key crony cannot lead an Independent Football Regulator".

Addressing the criticism, Kogan stated: "I’ve been doing the job properly, and the idea that you would associate that (his history of donations to the Labour Party) with anything to do with the politics of what’s going on at the moment around Manchester City is just frankly ludicrous.

open image in gallery Man City have continued to deny any wrongdoing ( Reuters )

"I’m not in the slightest bit concerned about accusations about my probity. I think it stands up to scrutiny, and you’re more than welcome to scrutinise it."

The ‘State of the Game’ document revealed that Premier League expenditure on legal disputes surged from £45million in 2015-16 to £212m in 2024-25, driven largely by its primary case against Manchester City alongside separate challenges concerning associated party transaction (APT) regulations.

Kogan explained that the financial burden of any future legal battles brought by the IFR against City would ultimately be funded by the football clubs themselves.

"We wouldn’t go into legal action unless we thought we were going to win," he added.

"Whereas the Government will be cash-flowing us to do stuff – and they absolutely have to do that because we’re not going to go into legal action unless we know we can afford to pay for it – then ultimately, that will be charged back to football as part of the levy mechanism.

"I don’t expect a problem with the Treasury or with DCMS if we’re suddenly facing a substantive legal challenge, assuming we believe that legal challenge is one that we’re prepared to fight and prepared to win."

News.title: Why Saudi Arabia has struggled to defend itself against the Houthis' recent attacks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology.

But in recent days it has appeared helpless in the face of barrages of missiles and drones fired by the Houthi rebel group from neighboring Yemen. The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors and work from home.

The Iran-backed Houthis, once seen as little more than a ragtag militia, have grown into a formidable fighting force. They have inflicted damage on the region’s top oil producer, threatened critical supply routes in the Red Sea and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands.

The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defenses failed to stop the Houthis' attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next.

Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict:

Saudi Arabia has a vast arsenal of US weapons

Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12% of all U.S. arms exports from 2021-2025.

Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defense systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers.

Saudi Arabia's annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles.

But it has a huge area to defend

The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia's large size.

Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country's sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) through rugged desert areas.

“Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday.

At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help.

Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support.

President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision.

Houthi weapons and tactics are battle-tested

Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting.

The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defenses.

The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year.

Andreas Krieg, a professor at King’s College London, said this experience in challenging Israel’s cutting-edge air defenses has given the Houthis confidence and expertise as they now strike Saudi Arabia.

“They’ve learned how to over-saturate the radars,” he said.

The Houthis, working with allied militias in Iraq, have also targeted Saudi oil installations, including a vital pipeline used to export oil through the Red Sea while movement through the Strait of Hormuz is limited. The Houthis have also seized territory in Yemen near the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea waterway, putting additional pressure on Saudi oil exports.

Saudi Arabia appears to have miscalculated

Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, says the kingdom assumed the Houthis wouldn’t strike civilian targets like airports. Doing so marked “a paradigm shift,” he said.

Ratney, now an adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Saudis now find themselves in a position where they have to respond while also trying to prevent the fighting from spinning out of control.

“They can’t not strike back — they were attacked in a very brutal way by their archenemies,” he said. “They need to exert military pressure on the Houthis and then find a way to kind of deescalate.”

Rather than sending troops into Yemen, the Saudis will likely launch airstrikes against the Houthis and ramp up support of nationalist forces, several analysts said.

“It will be surrogate warfare,” Krieg said.

The Houthis are now a formidable force

While the Houthis don't have the firepower of Saudi Arabia, they have grown into a fearsome force controlling roughly one-third of Yemen thanks to help from Iran.

The United Nations estimates that the Houthis by 2024 had recruited up to 350,000 fighters. That's up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in the internationally recognized Yemeni government's civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade.

Ratney says the Houthis now have a “symbiotic relationship” with Iran and should not be seen as an Iranian puppet.

The strikes on Saudi airports and economic assets symbolize a sharing of lessons in asymmetric warfare between the Houthis and the Iranians: how to not just puncture expensive air defenses, but also damage vulnerable energy installations and threaten global maritime routes.

“Over the course of the past few years, the Iranians have been innovating and sharing that with the Houthis and it’s gone both ways. The Houthis have been innovating, and sharing it with the Iranians,” Ratney said. “It’s no coincidence that they’ve ended up with a similar approach.”

Their recent military successes have made the Houthis feel “untouchable,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a fellow at Chatham House focused on Yemen.

“It’s very hard to convince a man he’s going on the wrong side if he just moved forward and he has a gun in his hand,” he said. But the Houthis are now likely to suffer a brutal Saudi counterattack, he said.

___

Associated Press writers Samy Magdy in Cairo, Sam Metz in Jerusalem, and Melanie Lidman in Tel Aviv, Israel, contributed reporting.

News.title: Supreme Court will review asylum case of Nigerian man who cooked meals for terrorist leaders
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to consider if a Nigerian man is ineligible for asylum because he cooked meals at a camp for leaders of a group that the U.S. government considers to be a terrorist organization.

The high court, granting a request by President Donald Trump's administration, will hear arguments on whether Izuchukwu Ozurumba's cooking job for leaders of the Unknown Gunmen qualifies as providing “material support” for a terrorist group.

The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to review a decision by the Richmond, Virginia-based 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to vacate Ozurumba's removal order. The Republican administration says the 4th Circuit decision conflicts with rulings by at least three other circuits and, if upheld, will hamper the government's ability to deport immigrants with terrorism ties in many other cases.

“Providing meals to a terrorist organization's members is no less a material form of support than providing gasoline for its vehicles,” they wrote.

Ozurumba testified that he didn’t know the true purpose of the camp until after he started working there. The Unknown Gunmen is believed to be a group of separatists operating in southern Nigeria. Ozurumba's lawyers say the group's leaders forced him to work without pay and repeatedly threatened him after he escaped from the camp.

His attorneys further argued that there is no circuit split for the Supreme Court to resolve. “No federal court has adopted the government's rule, under which any interaction with a terrorist organization, no matter how attenuated or inconsequential, qualifies as ‘material’ support,” they wrote.

Ozurumba fled the camp near his home in Lagos, Nigeria, and traveled to Venezuela before entering the U.S. illegally in July 2023 and surrendered to Border Patrol. Several months later, an immigration judge ordered Ozurumba to be deported to Nigeria.

A divided 4th Circuit panel decided that Ozurumba's work at the camp didn't constitute material support of terrorism. The majority opinion says it appears that he was “simply a captive laborer” whose work had nothing to do with terrorist activities.

News.title: The secret to the perfect holiday in Somerset
News.content:
Somerset’s landscapes are steeped in legend, from the lush fields of “Avalon” to Cheddar Gorge and the wilds of Exmoor. Its winding, country lanes lead to secrets and natural splendour. The local food scene is flourishing, too, involving everyone from Michelin-starred chefs to foragers on the Mendip Hills and farmers selling cheddar and cider from the barn door.

Glastonbury Festival shines as the centre of the musical universe in June – but the region is becoming known for much more than this. Quiet, agrarian villages are now fashionable places to spend time – I’m often found dawdling over a lazy brunch, browsing designer ceramics and paddleboarding down river. Bruton has an internationally renowned art gallery and the county’s hip, country house hotels – from Soho House-owned Babington House to The Newt – are some of the UK’s most desirable.

What makes Somerset so exciting is that it preserves a bucolic way of life while keeping its finger firmly on the pulse.

News.title: Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle
News.content:
You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. There was a half-hearted attempt to close Cherif down from Yoane Wissa and then a shot that somehow went through a crowd of three Newcastle defenders, including the legs of Botman, and nestled in the bottom corner.

News.title: AI cuts diagnosis for eye disease from 23 days to just 30 seconds
News.content:
Patients whose eye scans were read by an AI programme got results in 30 seconds, compared to facing an average waiting time of 23 days for results from a doctor, a study in Tanzania has shown.

Millions of people around the world have diabetic retinopathy, a condition where high blood sugar levels damage the tiny blood vessels in the retina.

It can lead to irreversible blindness if left untreated. Around a third of the 23 million people with diabetes in Africa have the complication.

In its early stages, diabetic retinopathy can have no symptoms, and the World Health Organization recommends that people living with diabetes undergo regular screening to check their eye health, so that they can be treated if necessary.

For the new study, published in the Lancet Global Health, researchers randomly assigned over 2,000 patients with diabetes visiting clinics in Tanzania’s Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions to either receive usual screening care, or to have a new type of AI-assisted screening.

Two fifths of the participants had changes in their eyes that needed referral to specialist care. In the half screened using AI, 36 per cent attended the central ophthalmology clinic within eight weeks, compared to 18 per cent in the standard care group.

Most of the people working in the regions where the study was based are farmers, said Dr Justus Rwiza of the Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre, co-author on the paper. “They depend on vision.”

The economic effects of blindness are felt by the whole family, he said, recalling how the daughter of one patient “had to stop schooling to help the mother”.

News.title: WHO probes ‘unanswered questions’ over Russian plague worker
News.content:
The World Health Organization has said it still does not have enough information to rule out a lab accident after the death of a worker in a Russian plague lab.

Last week reports emerged that Darya Shipilova, a lab worker in Irkutsk, Siberia, had died of pneumonic plague after dropping a test tube containing samples of the pathogen Yersinia pestis, which causes the disease.

Some 200 people were quarantined and there were reports of a further case. Shipilova was working at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk.

Russian authorities have insisted that there was no lab accident and Shipilova’s mother, Svetlana, has also disputed that her daughter dropped a test tube.

“It’s impossible to break a test tube like that,” she said. “Even if you fling it at the wall. Only an amateur could say something like that,” she said.

News.title: El Nino, hunger and fuel threaten ‘perfect storm’, says UN
News.content:
A triple shock of rising energy prices, spiralling borrowing costs and a turbocharged El Niño could push “tens if not hundreds of millions of people” into poverty, the UN has warned.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) said the three “compounding crises” are hitting developing economies especially hard, with governments running out of resources to shield people from the fallout, in a new report.

“We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty,” said Alexander De Croo, the UNDP administrator, warning that surging oil and food prices mean families across the world have “no safety margin”.

“Governments of developing countries are left with impossible choices: cut support to their poorest citizens or risk their entire development agenda,” he added.

The report was published ahead of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, which kicked off in Bangkok on Monday. Debt pressures, energy prices and geopolitical tensions are high on the agenda.

But UNDP stressed that the meetings were taking place as three shocks converge, and the crisis morphs from a regional to a global one that’s affecting roughly 100 countries.

Seven months ago, when the war in Iran broke out, the UN agency warned that the conflict had triggered the “most severe oil supply shock in history”. That continues today – after a brief respite, oil prices have been pushed back beyond $100 a barrel, as hostilities have resumed in the Middle East.

But two more threats now “challenge the capacity of developing countries to manage the energy shock”, meaning developing economies “will have trouble funding their policy responses in the months ahead”.

News.title: Max Verstappen is back and Mercedes are already worried
News.content:
Kimi Antonelli, third: “It was a very tough race out there but really happy with a podium at the end, I managed to take advantage of the fight between Lewis and Lando. To take P3 is a great result from the team, very happy with that.”

He is told that he can clinch the title at the next race:

“Can I, really? Let’s not worry about that. Let’s try to do the best weekend possible and finish the job.”

Charles Leclerc, second: “We were quite strong at the beginning of the race and then we started degrading at the end of the first stint. I pushed a lot at the beginning of the last stint and then degraded a bit more than the others. I gave it all and I don’t regret anything.

“I don’t think there’s anything more we could do but be a bit more aggressive at the start. It’s true that we brought some small new parts to the car which maybe helped us to do a little step forward but it’s enough. Today I think we had a good pace overall.”

Max Verstappen, winner: “It’s taken a while but I think this race was very good. We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre and the medium. Very happy to win here. You always try to do your best and luckily [the start] it was just good enough.

“I think the last few races have been really positive for us. It’s great to see and we have a lot of motivation in the team to try to deliver even more results... hopefully we can have a bit more fun until the end of the year.”

News.title: The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool
News.content:
Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Sports.title: English football warned it faces ‘collapse’ as staggering new report reveals 32 clubs are just 30 days from going bust
Sports.content:
Next

ENGLISH football must fix its financial issues “while the sun is shining” – rather than risk “collapse”.

That was the stark warning from the new body set up to oversee the entire pyramid.



In its 245-page draft “State of the Game” report, the Government-backed Independent Football Regulator outlined the scale of the looming crisis if football does not heed the danger signs.

While Premier League clubs, led by the Big Six, have enjoyed unprecedented growth in a “virtuous circle of success”, the rest of the food chain has risked its very survival trying to catch up.



In its landmark findings, the IFR found FOUR Prem clubs and “60 per cent” of EFL and National League outfits are “technically insolvent”.

Some 32 clubs in the top five leagues “would not survive 30 days without owner funding”, while clubs collectively owe £3.4bn transfer fees.

Remarkably, 17 clubs – 11 in the EFL and six in the National League – would be in the red each week even if their players played for free.

Despite revenues of more than £9bn this year, and a total estimated Prem player squad valuation of £12.5bn, 94 per cent of English clubs are losing money.

Regulator chiefs gave the clearest signal yet that the EFL should accept the new £320m per-season package on the table from the Prem or face missing out on two years worth of cash.

Yet Richard Monks, chief executive of the new body, warned: “We have the most popular league in the world, the deepest pyramid in the world and Premier League club revenues have grown 10 times more than the UK economy since 1992, truly spectacular growth.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

“But the report describes a game which is loaded with financial risk. That risk is increasing.

“We’re not saying football is a house of cards and about to collapse but that financial risk is increasing and there needs to be action taken.

“When things go wrong, when a club is on the brink or when a club goes into administration or is docked points, it’s the fans that suffer. We are here to protect and support those fans.

“We’re absolutely not doomsayers. There’s a chance that the sun continues to shine. But let’s not take that chance. Let’s fix the financial holes in football when the sun is still shining.”

The launch of the report comes with Prem and EFL bosses still to agree a new long-term funding deal.



While regulator chairman and report co-author David Kogan spoke of his willingness to use his “back stop powers” and impose a settlement, he signalled the latest Prem offer is one the EFL should be looking to ratify.

That will see an increase from the current £138m per season solidarity fund to around £320m each year, with Prem clubs overseeing a reduction in the value of parachute payments, currently worth £55m in the campaign after relegation.

Kogan said: “Both the Premier League clubs and the EFL clubs have got to the point where they are recognising that it is better to strike an agreement than not.

“Having a regulator come in and impose a deal on football, frankly, would be a real failure on the part of the football authorities to do what they should have done five years ago.



“They’re at the point where they wish to actually reach agreement. So their number is their number, and who am I to argue with them?

“The Premier League is not wrong about parachute payments because the impact of relegation is colossal, but as Rick Parry and the EFL have said, they do have a massive distortive effect.

“The leagues are pretty much agreed on the need to reduce the level of parachute payments over the three years that they’re paid, so there’ll be less money going to relegated clubs.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But as you’re giving more money to the rest of the pyramid, and it is much more money, then how that is distributed within the Championship changes, a merit rake, so the top 10 in the Championship receive more.

“That does not achieve everything that the EFL might have wanted three or four years ago but it actually goes a long way towards addressing the issue.”

Sports.title: Head of Football Regulator vows to QUIT if there is political interference in Man City verdict after Burnham’s comments
Sports.content:
Next

THE head of the new Football Regulator pledged to QUIT if there is any “political interference” over the future of Manchester City.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s supportive comments about City’s Abu Dhabi ownership raised questions over whether the Government might lean on Premier League chiefs after the club were found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules.



David Kogan, the chairman of the new body, which has the power to strip unfit owners from clubs, has also been in the firing line after revealing he was a Labour Party donor before his appointment.

But in a public vow, Kogan said: “We are absolutely bound by one thing – regulating football and regulating football clubs.



“I made it very clear that any form of political interference in the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role. And I stand by that completely.

“Just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic. And I don’t expect to in the future.”

City have appealed against the independent commission verdict that they were responsible for substantive rule breaches over contracts and payments, including booking £830million in “sham” sponsorship deals.

Burnham’s previous role as Mayor of Manchester, where UAE investment has totalled more than £1billion, fuelled fears of a possible stitch-up soft punishment.

Kogan was speaking at the National Football Museum, barely two miles from the Etihad Stadium where City play their first home game since the commission findings against PSG in the Champions League tomorrow night.

He added: “The original legislation had a reference to us having to take regard of some British trade relationships – but that was removed.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“We have a serious job to do and I’m very proud to be doing it. I’m not in the slightest bit concerned about accusations about my probity. It stands up to scrutiny.”

While Kogan insisted he could “not make any judgements” while City’s appeal was being considered, he did warn: “Once we know the outcome, we will sit and apply the legislation as we need to.

“We have powers to review not only owners and directors and senior executives but also whether those owners are the proper people to run clubs going forward.

“That process is reliant on us having very detailed knowledge and information which requires a certain amount of investigation.



“Then we would take judgements based on the legal advice that we then receive.”

City, who fielded £5,000-per hour Lord Pannick KC at the original 42-day hearing, have now added more legal recruitment in the form of another “super silk”, Mark Howard KC, who has previously represented both Roman Abramovich and Sir Elton John.

Sir Elton lost the financial advice case against accountants PricewaterhouseCoopers, and was landed with an £8m bill, after admitting in evidence he had spent £293,000 on flowers.

City vehemently insist a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” was ignored by the commission, arguing it had bought the “Premier League’s conspiracy theories.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

But Richard Monks, the chief executive of the new regulator, added: “After any investigation, if we determine an owner is unsuitable, we would require them to sell the club within a particular time frame.

“If they can’t do that we would appoint a third party to sell the club on their behalf – and they would lose the choice element in terms of a price.”

Sports.title: I experienced biggest football rivalry you’ve never heard of – I was confronted by fans who threatened to rip me apart
Sports.content:
Next

DEATH threats, sexist abuse, 50,000 fans, and a desperate plea for equality in football.

Last week I experienced the biggest footballing rivalry you have never heard of: Mohun Bagan Super Giants vs East Bengal – the Kolkata derby.



Carlo Ancelotti claimed that India had ‘no football culture’ ahead of his Brazil side facing off against the Blue Tigers in Kolkata, so I travelled there to challenge his view on that.

Attending the national team matches was one thing, seeing how the nation came together to support their side at the stunning VBYK stadium – but as in any country, to REALLY get a taste of the football culture, you have to go local.



Fortunately for me, and my pal Davina who was by my side for most of the trip, we had Mohun Bagan Super Giants on our doorstep, who are widely considered the best and most successful football club in India, also being one of Asia’s oldest football clubs.

MBSG’s semi-final against Punjab FC in the IFA shield semi-final was our destination, with a matchday feeling unlike any I have experienced anywhere else in the world.

Flags, shirts, headbands, scarfs and flags were a blanket over the city of Kolkata.

They painted West Bengal red and green for the day as we strolled through busy streets decorated with colourful houses and overhanging trees towards the Kishore Bharati Krirangan stadium.

With both of us fully immersed in the experience – our faces were painted to match our £25 player-edition shirts, purchased from the local Sketchers store.

There was no pre-match burger van, sweets, or programmes being shipped off for £5 a pop – instead you can pick up samosa’s cooked in front of you, or pani puri if you’re lucky – for less than £1 each.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Fans showed up in numbers, and speaking to them was really the start of our story into the culture of football in India, and sport in India more generally – particularly when it came to women’s football.

When kick-off took place, the lack of goals on the pitch was made up for by the atmosphere off of it.

Mohun Bagan ultras, or Mariners as they are known, welcomed us with open arms and even allowed us to lead their ultras as we sang chants and played their drums to try and gee up the team.

It was, though, a young girl in red and green who took our hearts with her story, one we needed to tell.

She is one of MBSG’s biggest supporters, describing the club as her mother, with football being a safe place for her amid struggles in her personal life.



Her dream? To become the goalkeeper for the women’s Mohun Bagan team.

The problem? There is no women’s team…

Mohun Bagan’s chairman is a man by the name of Sanjiv Goenka – though I use the term ‘man’ loosely – if he was a man of honour then MBSG would have a women’s side.



He is not alone at fault though, with fans also campaigning for a women’s team to be made, it is those at the top of the club who have issues with women in sport, and with women in a wider scope.

So much so that former club president Swapan Sadhan “Tutu” Bose once described his team’s CFL win in the following light: “Had daughters for seven consecutive years, suddenly a son is born. How would you feel then, brother? That’s how I’m feeling now,”.

Disgusting.

Davina and I, after attending the game, stayed up into the early hours of the morning editing our video, with the purpose being to tell the story of this young fan, and campaign for a women’s team to be formed.

So after pouring our efforts into this video, we were left shocked and furious at what happened next.



The video was incredibly well received, so much so that the club’s official accounts decided to share it.

Excellent, right? Wrong.

They had remixed our content and cut out ANY mention of their lack of a women’s team, without asking for our permission, and without any form of payment or compensation.

Comments from myself and Davina saw the post swiftly deleted, but without anything in the way of an apology.

Conveniently, Mohun Bagan’s fierce rivals, East Bengal, were playing the very next day in their IFA shield semi-final.



So we committed football’s ultimate sin.

We went from Barcelona to Real Madrid, from Arsenal to Tottenham, from River Plate to Boca Juniors.

We embodied Luis Figo, Sol Campbell and Mo Johnston, to switch allegiances and support East Bengal instead – a helping hand being that they are the reigning men’s AND women’s champions of India.

East Bengal gave us an equally warm welcome for their 7-2 win against NorthEast United.

The Ultras were louder, the team was better, and the fans’ pride in their women’s team was so welcome.



One fan told us: “We are the women’s league champions of India, they are as important as our men’s team because in today’s society women play such a crucial role.

“We are so proud of having a women’s team, a champions team who have made us proud and made India proud.”

It was a repeat that night of the one prior, a late night spent editing a video of us embracing Indian football culture, sending a message to those in charge of Mohun Bagan.



It was a message that sparked conversation, as intended.

Unfortunately we couldn’t do that without also receiving some criticism that turned to abuse.

I was told to go back to my own country, but the abuse towards Davina, as a woman with brown skin, was far worse – despite us existing in the same capacity and creating the same content.

An ironic and damning endictment of the system we were fighting against.

A wider system in which women are ogled at in the streets and intrinsically taught to believe they are inferior to men.



We in fact upset the fans so much that we were confronted outside the VBYK stadium the next day, while received empty threats about being “ripped apart” and beaten up.

Davina is a Spurs fan, and me Chelsea, so we know a thing or two about fierce football rivalries – not many people are more well versed in trolling each other online than we are.

We also know when the line is crossed, and any kind of abuse or threats in football should never be tolerated, no matter where you are.



With fans recognising us all over Kolkata, either as Mohun Bagan traitors or East Bengal heroes, and the derby taking place a matter of days later, the pair of us were told it wouldn’t necessarily be safe of us to attend.

Though I was assured that “I will always be protected by the East Bengal mafia” – which was reassuring.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In the final, Mohun Bagan won the IFA shield final and the latest rendition of the Kolkata derby 1-0 in front of 52,000 supporters while we flew back to London.

But this trip had a far more important message than anything that took place on the pitch, a message for equality and the uprising of women, and women’s football in India.

Sports.title: Man City add £9m ‘super silk’ lawyer who worked for Roman Abramovich and Elton John in bid to fight guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER CITY have added one of the UK’s top lawyers to their legal team in its fight against their guilty verdict.

The club was found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial regulations last month.



But the ownership has maintained its innocence, and has already launched an appeal against the decision.

And that defence will now benefit from the expertise of Mark Howard KC, one of the UK’s top barristers.



The Lawyer reports that the vastly experienced lawyer is advising the club on their case.

Howard’s profile on the website of Brick Court Chamber, which he jointly-heads, claims: “He is widely regarded as one of the leading commercial silks at the bar.”



He passed the bar in 1980 and was made King’s Counsel (KC) in 1996.

His seniority and expertise have led to him being colloquially referred to as a ‘super silk,’ a name for a top-level KC – a status given to senior barristers who wear their silk gowns in court.

His previous employers include Sir Elton John, who secured his services in 2002 for an appeal against an earlier decision in a case brought against his former manager over touring costs.

The court ruled against Howard and John, with the latter incurring estimated legal costs of around £8m, per the BBC.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

He also represented Roman Abramovich in a 2008 case brought against the former Chelsea owner by oil company Yugraneft.

Howard’s wealth of experience and expertise does not come cheaply.

In 2023 he reportedly made £9million in appearance fees while representing the Federal Republic of Nigeria against Process & Industrial Developments – a record for a barrister in a UK case.

City are currently in the middle of an appeal, but there have been no indications as to how long the process could take to complete.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney urges Michael Carrick to DROP Man Utd captain Bruno Fernandes or risk an ‘explosion’
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED legend Wayne Rooney has urged under-fire gaffer Michael Carrick to DROP star man Bruno Fernandes.

He feels there is an “explosion” brewing in the dressing room if he continues to start, as he’s “not scared to come out and voice his opinion”.



Carrick said no one is “undroppable” after being questioned on his captain’s form over the past weeks.

And Rooney offered his take on the situation on Stick to United, saying: “He’s fed up. I genuinely do think he looks ‘oh here we go again’.



“There are only so many times. He has carried the team, but sometimes you need taking out of that position, of that role, to breathe again. I feel like now you can see it building up and there’s going to be an explosion with him if this carries on.

“He’s not scared to come out and voice his opinion. So there is going to be that explosion if this carries on the way it’s going.



“For me you need that three in midfield at the minute because they’re getting outrun, they’re getting outplayed.

“All of a sudden then you’ve got [Kobbie] Mainoo and [Youri] Tielemans, who are not the quickest and not the most mobile, to cover the full width of the pitch as two midfield players, and they can’t do it.”

Fernandes has been carrying an injury over the past month but has clocked up 90 minutes in seven of United’s eight games.

The 32-year-old played in three of Portugal‘s four Nations League games during the recent internationals but was rested for the 2-1 win away to Norway.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Fernandes is the reigning Professional Footballers’ Association and Football Writers’ Association Player of the Year but he has underperformed regularly so far this term.

But perhaps we could see the United skipper dropped for the first time this season in tonight’s clash with Spanish giants Atletico Madrid.

Sports.title: Former England keeper Alex McCarthy reveals doctors told him to retire after discovering heart problem caused by Covid
Sports.content:
Next

EX-ENGLAND goalkeeper Alex McCarthy was told to retire by doctors due to a heart problem caused by Covid-19.

McCarthy, 36, currently plays for Leicester in League One but came close to having to hang up his gloves at the back end of the coronavirus pandemic.



The exact date of the keeper’s diagnosis is not fully known but he didn’t compete between December 2021 and May 2022 while playing for Southampton.

The former England international, who only played once for the Three Lions in a friendly victory over USA back in 2018, underwent a series of tests during the pandemic.



The doctors discovered an issue with his heart and thus the ex-Premier League ace was told he couldn’t play football anymore, even though he never had any symptoms.

McCarthy told the Fozcast podcast: “I don’t think I’ve spoken about it before. It was coming out the back end of Covid when I missed a year because I had a heart condition from Covid.



“Not many people know this. I think it was during Covid, when you had to have all the tests. I had to wear a heart patch. I think a few of the lads in football who had Covid had to.

“They picked up some formalities with my heart. I had no symptoms or anything. So they monitored it for a while but I couldn’t get signed off to play.

“I ended up getting called in by the doc at Southampton to see a specialist down in Southampton. He was like, ‘Bring your agent and your wife’. I was like, ‘This can’t be good’.

“Turned up there and the guy basically said, ‘You can’t play football anymore, you need a defib fitted like Christian Eriksen and that’. This was out of nowhere. I felt fine.”



But McCarthy decided to have a second opinion from another doctor in London.

And the ex-Crystal Palace keeper managed to prolong his career following a heart procedure and returned to football a few months later.

McCarthy added: “Long story short, I had to have a think about what I wanted to do. I said to Southampton that I wanted a second opinion. [I] go up to this guy in London and he said, ‘I think I can sort this’.

“A month or two later I had to go back to London. They cut my groin open, I had to be awake for this because they needed the heartbeat to be normal. They put a tube up to my heart and did an ablation where they burn a part of your heart.



“They found that when I was exercising, my heart would skip quite a few beats. They then put a chip in my chest, which is linked to my phone to them to always monitor it.

“I missed a good few months, and I had to go through all that to get signed off to play again. [I’ve] gone from nearly having to retire to still playing. It’s mental.”

Sports.title: PSG ‘lining up Man Utd star Leny Yoro’ in shock transfer two years after £52m move to Old Trafford
Sports.content:
Next

PARIS SAINT-GERMAIN are lining up a shock move for Manchester United star Leny Yoro just two years after his £52million switch to Old Trafford, according to reports.

The French giants are keeping close tabs on the defender, 20, with scouts watching him make his France debut in the 4-1 Nations League win over Belgium earlier this month, claim talkSPORT.



With Yoro’s long-term future at United still uncertain, PSG could look to tempt the Red Devils into cashing in on one of their most highly-rated young talents.

United remain hopeful that Yoro can develop into a key figure at the heart of their defence.



But PSG are said to be huge admirers of Yoro and are assessing the possibility of bringing him back to his homeland, according to TEAMtalk.

There is a growing feeling in France that a big offer could test the Premier League side’s resolve, with Bayern Munich also understood to be monitoring the situation.

The defender has made 55 Premier League appearances since joining United from Lille in the summer of 2024.

However, regular game time has not always been easy to come by, and United are understood to be weighing up their options after investing heavily in the youngster.

The club could consider recouping their initial outlay if they decide his future lies elsewhere, although they have not given up hope of seeing him fulfil his potential in Manchester.

Yoro has shown his versatility during his time in England, featuring at centre-back, on the right of a back three and at right-back.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

He impressed in the latter role against Tottenham on Saturday, having also performed well there during pre-season.

Speaking after his display at right-back against Spurs, Yoro said: “It’s a position I can play. If I play centre back or right back, I’m happy to play. Different things to do, of course, but you have to adapt.

“Whatever the position, I’m ready and happy to play.”

But centre-back remains his preferred position, and he made a solid start to life with the senior France team in that role.

Yoro lined up alongside Chelsea defender Maxence Lacroix in their recent win over Belgium, helping keep Romelu Lukaku quiet in a convincing performance.



The youngster’s international breakthrough came amid growing attention around his development, with footage also emerging of him in dialogue with Zinedine Zidane during the recent break and taking part in training with the French football icon.

The chance to learn directly from Zidane will only add to the excitement around Yoro’s potential, with his talent continuing to attract attention despite his efforts to nail down a regular starting spot at United.

PSG’s reported interest could also be shaped by their longer-term plans at the back.



Captain and club legend Marquinhos is now 32 and has a contract running until 2028, meaning the European champions will need to consider their options for the future.

Willian Pacho, 24, has established himself as a key figure in the PSG defence alongside Marquinhos.

A partnership between Pacho and Yoro could therefore appeal as a potential long-term solution.

Sports.title: 'State of the Game' report finds most English clubs living on financial brink
Sports.content:
The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has produced a 'State of the Game' report, which has taken a forensic look at English football over the past 18 months, concluding that the game's finances are dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster.

The IFR added that interest and investment from around the world continues to grow within English football, but the underlying foundations of the pyramid are under intense strain and require urgent reform.

Despite over £9bn generated in revenue, 94 per cent of clubs are loss-making, with long-term security being put at risk through excessive short-term spending to keep up with rivals. This, the IFR says, has led to a "dangerous cocktail of rising debt and an over-reliance on owner funding, leaving clubs and their fans at risk".

The report acknowledges that the success of the Premier League has driven economic success, making English football the "richest, best and most deeply competitive in the world".

However, it points to "financial cliff-edges between and within leagues", with the average Premier League club making more than eight times the revenues of an average Championship club, and the system of parachute payments paid by the Premier League to Championship clubs relegated contributing to significant overspend by clubs in the Championship.

Indeed, the report highlights player wage inflation leading clubs to take big risks chasing a place in the Premier League.

The State of the Game report found that lower down the pyramid the pressure from operating costs was also on the rise, with 17 EFL and National League clubs incurring costs exceeding revenues. These clubs would be loss-making even if they did not pay their players.

It uncovered too that more than 60 per cent of EFL and National League clubs are technically insolvent, with their liabilities exceeding the book value of their assets.

And it found that more than a quarter of clubs would be unable to survive for more than one month if owner funding was withdrawn, with the majority lacking a basic contingency plan to mitigate their risk.

'We're trying to take an interventionist approach'

Chair of the IFR David Kogan told Sky: "I think what we see in English football is two completely different positions.

"The first is £9bn comes in every year, yet we have 94 per cent of the clubs of the 160 we regulate are trading unprofitably.

"We have 32 clubs that have got less than 30 days' cash cover in their accounts. So if the owner walks away or drops dead, they're insolvent and go bust.

"So what we see in football is rising debt. It's a problem of cash cover and liquidity within clubs, and it's a lack of management, and what financial management? And now we're in a position to help those clubs achieve a more stable future."

Kogan added: "What we're implying is today there's enough money going through into the Premier League and the EFL and into their individual clubs for the sun to shine. This is exactly the moment when we need to address structural issues because once that sun stops shining, those clubs will be in real trouble.

"So what we are trying to do is get ahead of the problem and take an interventionist approach with individual clubs that need it to help them get to the point of being stable and secure because too many clubs get close to the edge and depend on one thing and one thing only, which is a new owner coming down the track.

"That supply of owners may dry up, and supply of media money may dry out so we have to now get ahead of the game and give them levels of security and stability that allow them to go into the future."

The IFR's six-point plan...

The IFR report offered solutions, issuing a six-point plan to address some of the issues it has identified.

The plan includes measures for clubs to improve how they manage financial risk, including holding more cash and putting robust contingency plans in place in case owner funding is withdrawn; it also outlines how revenue distribution should be reformed to ease cliff-edges throughout the pyramid, urges action on rising losses and calls on clubs to show how they take fans' views into account, and the steps they are taking to improve diversity and governance in the boardroom.

It also highlighted yet again that the current distribution arrangements in English football create risk and should be reformed.

For several years the Premier League and EFL have been discussing and negotiating a new financial distribution model, but no agreement has yet been finalised. The IFR has consistently said, and has said once again in this report, that it is preferable that the Premier League and EFL come to an agreement themselves, but again mentioned that the IFR could apply a "back-stop" power to intervene if the Premier League and EFL do not come to an agreement.

The IFR said its goals on reform of the current distribution model were to:

Maintain the Premier League as the leading football league in the world and the Championship as the leading second-tier competition.

Maintain vital funding for the wider game.

Mitigate the financial impact of relegation from the Premier League.

Reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship.

Protect clubs by giving clubs the opportunity to rebuild their balance sheets and reduce risk.

Consider short-term support to clubs that face severe financial distress.

Kogan said: "There are three moves that are taking place that we think will help on this.

"First is that the Premier League and the EFL are currently discussing a new distribution deal with the game, which will radically change the amount of money going from the Premier League down to the lower leagues. And that will have associated with it controls on how that money is spent, which actually will go to the stability of those lower leagues, but we're going to see more money flowing down, assuming the deal is done, and we're going to see cost controls involved in that.

"The second is that from November onwards we're going to be licensing clubs, and by licensing those clubs we're going to intervene directly in individual clubs where we think they've got exposures that we can help them resolve and that includes things like having a business plan that involves having cash cover more than 30 days; it involves having genuine provision for the debts that they've raised.

"And the third thing we're doing is working with leagues to actually look at cost controls over a longer-term basis to actually build in financial stability as we go forward."

Sports.title: 'What do you want us to do?' - Maresca defends Anfield celebrations
Sports.content:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has defended the post-match celebrations of his squad following their 3-0 win at Liverpool on Sunday.

The trip to Merseyside was City's first game after an independent commission found them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The club have since appealed the verdict and continue to deny any wrongdoing.

City players were pictured celebrating with the travelling away fans following full-time at Anfield - after goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki secured the victory - which sparked criticism across social media.

When asked about the celebrations and the comments that followed ahead of facing Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday, Maresca said: "Criticised for what? We won 0-3 at Anfield. What do you want us to do?

"I am here today; the players are here today to win tomorrow. We work every day to win games.

"It is the only thing that we can think and focus on. The rest is just things from outside which we need to deal [with]. We were so, so happy from inside the pitch and the dressing room."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Man City take to the pitch for the first time since being found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission. City have lodged their appeal against the verdict and deny wrongdoing

'I don't stress about things I can't control,' says Maresca

The City boss then reiterated that he remains calm regarding the situation with the process ongoing.

City submitted their appeal on Thursday October 1 and the Premier League has new rules this season which state an appeal has to be heard within 12 weeks of it being lodged. The appeal can last a maximum of five days - held over a block of days, so Monday to Friday.

However, City may try to delay the appeal process by arguing that the new rules should not apply in this case as City were charged in 2023 - three years before the new rules were introduced.

But, as it stands, the five-day appeal, to be heard by a new three-person panel, has to be finished by mid-December.

"I said many times, I am completely calm and relaxed. I promise you that I stress a lot about game plan and how we train," Maresca added.

"I don't stress about things I don't control. The message with players will be the same.

"As I said, we know how serious the situation is. It is not something we can do something [about]. Where we can do something is inside the pitch.

"The noise around the team is a big noise but we need to try to deal with that and try and make our noise, to win games."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Liverpool's match against Manchester City in the Premier League

Dias: I stand by Maresca's words

City captain Ruben Dias, who played the full 90 minutes in the victory, echoed the statement from his manager, as he added: "I very much stand by the manager's words. It's a win at Anfield.

"In whatever circumstance, be it early in the season or late in the season, we will enjoy it just as much and celebrate however we feel in the moment. It's a show of how much it means to us.

"If there's more or less noise, for whatever reason, it's all the same. Same as before because people don't love us winning and we love to win.

"It's a normal scenario where whenever you win, there are people that are not happy with it because they have the same ambition to win.

"It all mixes together a little bit but mainly we know it's not easy to get three points at Anfield. That is definitely the main reason. We're here for the points and to win competitions; that's the main thing on our minds."

Dias also revealed the City players held a meeting after news of the guilty verdict broke on September 29.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ruben Dias has revealed how the Manchester City players responded after they found out the club were given a guilty verdict regarding serious financial breaches; City have appealed and deny all wrongdoing

"When it broke, we felt we should have a conversation as soon as we got back," he said, regarding their return from the international break.

"We did, for everyone to be on the same page and be clear about our peace of mind. We moved on from there.

"It happened in a moment when we were not together but quickly we reached out to each other, found calm and progressed forward."

'City players sent message with celebrations'

Sky Sports News' Ben Ransom at Maresca's press conference:

"We all saw those scenes at Anfield. The City fans wanted to show their support throughout the game to the club and the players, and the players reciprocated when they scored each of the three goals in front of them, and again at the end of the game when the result was confirmed.

"That was all set against the backdrop of the intense goading from the Liverpool fans who wanted to have their say about how they felt about the findings of that independent commission.

"For the players, I think it was as much about sending a message back to the fans at the end that they valued their support, but also a little bit of them wanting to send a message to the wider football world, to other clubs in the Premier League as well.

"They are defiant in the face of that verdict, certainly while the appeal is ongoing."

Sports.title: Hazlewood fires Australia to convincing first-Test win over South Africa
Sports.content:
Australia clinched a convincing 214-run win over South Africa in the first Test of their three-match series to take a 1-0 lead.

Australia went into the final day in Durban requiring six more wickets for victory, and South Africa a hugely unlikely 319 further runs to win, and though the visitors encountered some resistance from Aiden Markram (75) in particular, they eventually wrapped things up shortly after lunch.

Score summary - South Africa vs Australia, first Test, Durban Australia 390 all out in 137.2 overs in first innings (elected to bat): Matt Renshaw (190), Pat Cummins (43); Wiaan Mulder (4-68), Marco Jansen (3-68), Anrich Nortje (2-88) South Africa 284 all out in 74 overs in first innings: David Bedingham (49), Aiden Markram (37), Pat Cummins (3-54), Josh Hazlewood (2-54), Nathan Lyon (2-58), Mitchell Starc (2-63) Australia 314-6 declared in 58 overs in second innings: Matt Renshaw (82), Nic Maddinson (48); Anrich Nortje (2-56), Keshav Maharaj (2-56) South Africa 206 all out in 86.5 overs in second innings: Aiden Markram (75), David Bedingham (46), Marco Jansen (35); Josh Hazlewood (6-49), Matt Renshaw (2-30)

Josh Hazlewood (6-49) took four of the wickets to fall to finish with career-best figures, including the opening breakthrough of Wiaan Mulder (29) - caught down the legside - to end his and Markram's 69-run stand that offered South Africa some brief hope of clinging on for a draw.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nathan Lyon keeps the Australia superstition alive as he switches the bails - and South Africa lose two quick wickets on day five of the first Test in Durban

Kyle Verreynne would depart just three balls later, out to Player of the Match and part-time spinner Matt Renshaw (2-30), but the collapse was delayed until the other side of lunch as Markram found further support in Marco Jansen (35).

The pair put on 45 for the seventh wicket until Hazlewood's return, with the second new ball in hand, signalled the end of South Africa's resistance as he removed Jansen and Simon Harmer, for a duck, in the same over.

Jansen was bowled through the gate by a devastating nip-backer, a delivery that was bettered only by the vicious bouncer that did for Harmer third ball - gloved to Alex Carey.

Image: Marco Jansen was bowled by Josh Hazlewood as Australia closed in on victory in Durban

Markram's 237-ball stay at the crease would then be ended by Mitchell Starc (1-33) - out on review, inside-edging behind - as South Africa lost their final four wickets for five runs in litte more than two overs, Hazlewood fittingly wrapping things up with the dismissal of Anrich Nortje.

Renshaw claimed Player of the Match honours due to his magnificent 190 that rescued Australia from 124-6 on day one, as they were eventually bowled out for 390 and secured a 106-run first innings lead. He'd add 82 in the second innings.

Image: Matt Renshaw (left) added two second-innings wickets to his 190 and 82 with the bat in Australia's impressive first-Test win in Durban

South Africa will hope to have pace attack spearhead Kagiso Rabada back for the second Test in Gqeberha, which starts on Sunday live on Sky Sports, after he missed the series opener due to his ongoing recovery from a hamstring injury suffered in June.

Cummins: Win was built on Renshaw hundred

Australia captain Pat Cummins:

"It was a great win. A lot of it was built on what Matt Renshaw did on day one, and we managed to hold onto that lead for the rest of it.

"Everywhere I look [with the bowling attack], there's a lot of Test wickets there - even our part-timers are better than that. I've got loads of options and Hazlewood is just a captain's dream.

"Two games left, anything can still happen, but being ahead in the series always makes things a little easier."

Bavuma: Don't let Australia lead from the front

South Africa captain Temba Bavuma:

"It's not the way we wanted to start. You've got to give it to the Australians and the way they dominated the majority of the game.

"The way they got stuck into us, even after they were 124-6 [in the first innings], they showed their experience, showed their skills and got themselves into a very competitive position.

"For a lot of us who have the experience of playing against them, you don't want to give them that opportunity to lead from the front.

"There's a lot of questions and conversations we'll need to have - we can learn from them on a batting and bowling point view - but you've got to give it to them in terms of their performance."

Sports.title: A PL giant to fall? Newly-promoted clubs changing relegation equation

The Premier League's newly-promoted sides have often struggled to bridge the gap, with two consecutive seasons in 2023/24 and 2024/25 seeing all three newcomers relegated before Leeds and Sunderland helped buck that trend last season.

Three promoted clubs staying up would mean three other sides have to take their place, of course, potentially putting a supposedly safe mid-table club or a big-name team in genuine danger.

Hull, Ipswich and Coventry are outside the relegation zone and the early evidence suggests this is not simply a case of one promoted side riding a wave of momentum.

There is a collective challenge to the established order developing here.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United

Look at the early warning signs.

Fulham, Tottenham and Bournemouth fill the bottom three spots at the minute and are winless after six games, while, like Bournemouth, Sunderland have a European campaign to negotiate and only have a win over Fulham on the board this season.

Aston Villa and Newcastle are going through big transition seasons and the bookmakers have Manchester City as third favourites for relegation with the possibility of a points deduction on the table following the independent commission finding them in breach of the Premier League's financial rules - City have denied wrongdoing and have lodged an appeal.

The danger is that poor form and the increased workload from potential European commitments can quickly become a crisis when confidence drains away and the pressure starts to build. The early relegation picture already suggests some established sides have reason to be concerned.

With Hull, Coventry and Ipswich refusing to follow the script, nobody should assume the three pre-season favourites for the drop are going down.

The relegation equation has certainly changed.

Sports.title: Rowley appointed new Tigers head coach
Sports.content:
Paul Rowley has been confirmed as the new Castleford Tigers head coach after signing a three-year deal with the club.

Rowley left St Helens in July with the club on their way to missing out on the Super League play-offs for the first time, having previously been in charge of Salford prior to the club's financial collapse in 2025.

He takes over at the Tigers following the departure of Australian Ryan Carr for personal reasons two months ago.

"I'm looking forward to leading Cas Tigers as their new head coach," said Rowley, who becomes Castleford's seventh head coach since Daryl Powell departed in 2021.

"From meeting [director of rugby] Chris [Chester] and the board, it immediately felt like a place I wanted to be a part of. I'm keen to get started and enjoy a new journey with this proud club."

Chester said: "We're absolutely delighted to welcome Paul Rowley to Castleford Tigers as our new head coach.

"Paul is a highly-respected coach within rugby league, and we believe he is the right person to lead this club into an exciting new chapter."

Chester also admitted there is the prospect of further recruitment in the coming weeks and months, adding: "I'm looking forward to working closely with Paul as we continue to strengthen the squad, develop our young talent and create a culture that delivers sustained success.

"We're delighted to have him on board and look forward to seeing what we can achieve together."

Castleford finished second bottom in Super League with only eight wins from their 27 games.

Sports.title: Bethell and Archer return for England white-ball tour of Australia
Sports.content:
Jacob Bethell and Jofra Archer are set to return to action for England's white-ball tour of Australia, starting in November.

Bethell is fit again following the knee injury he sustained during the ODI Series win against India in July that also saw him miss the subsequent Test series against Pakistan and white-ball series against Sri Lanka in August and September.

Archer returns after being rested for the tri-series in Pakistan with Eddie Jack and Thomas Rew earning their first call-ups as part of the IT20 squad.

Rew, who at 18 is the youngest player in the squad, captained the Young Lions to the ICC Men's U19s World Cup final in February.

Phil Salt returns from the quad injury that ruled him out of last month's 3-0 T20 Series win over Sri Lanka while Aneurin Donald retains his place after making his debut in that series.

Image: Thomas Rew captained England under-19s to the World Cup final earlier this year

Luke Wood is also recalled into the IT20 squad.

Jos Buttler remains sidelined as he begins his rehabilitation following hamstring surgery while Saqib Mahmood misses out with a knee injury.

Sports.title: Football regulator chair insists he will resign if politically pressured over Manchester City
Sports.content:
The chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan, has said he will resign if he faces any political pressure on how to respond to Manchester City being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, insisting “my independence is absolute”.

Kogan could remove City’s Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) should the damning verdict of an independent commission be upheld at the end of an ongoing appeal process. Concern had been raised, however, that the proximity of City’s ownership to Abu Dhabi’s rulers could trigger a political intervention by the UK government and an immediate test of the new regulator’s powers.

Those concerns have been rebuffed by Kogan. “Our independence is absolute and my independence personally is absolute,” he said. “I [have] made it very clear … any form of political interference on the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely. And, just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic.”

Kogan was speaking on Tuesday at the launch of the long-awaited State of the Game report, a document that lays out the financial challenges facing the English football pyramid. The City case has cast a huge shadow as the regulator prepares to introduce a new licensing regime for clubs later this season. “We have powers within the legislation that allow us to review not only owners and directors and senior executives, but also whether those owners are fit and proper people to run clubs going forward,” said Kogan, describing the process by which the regulator might intervene.

“That process is reliant on us having very detailed knowledge and information, which requires a certain amount of investigation. Then we would take judgments based on the legal advice that we then receive.”

Should a club owner ultimately be found to have failed a “fitness” test related to “integrity, honesty and financial soundness”, the regulator could force the club to be sold. “We deal with issues of this type much more frequently than you might realise because we are constantly looking at clubs,” Kogan said, stating if any decision by the regulator became the subject of legal action then clubs would be asked to foot the bill through a funding levy.

View image in fullscreen David Kogan reiterated that the regulator had powers to determine whether owners such as Manchester City’s were ‘fit and proper’. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA

The acceleration of revenues among the Premier League’s biggest clubs is one of the key findings in the State of the Game report. The highest earning top-flight club currently earns 605 times the revenue of the lowest earning National League club. At the same time, spending has increased at all levels of the game, with 94% of the 116 clubs under the regulator’s regime posting a financial loss in 2025-26. In one particularly eye-catching statistic, the report found 11 Football League clubs recorded costs that exceeded their income even once player wages had been stripped out.

Kogan argued that a number of external factors that fall outside the regulator’s purview are affecting the game, including the expansion of the club calendar, the regulation of players’ agents and the recent rise in interest rates. However, he argued that one key measure – the agreement of a redistribution deal between the Premier League and EFL – could unlock change immediately.

Arguing that parachute payments to clubs relegated from the Premier League have had a “distortive effect that’s grown over the years”, Kogan made clear if a deal was done that reduced parachute payments but increased the amount going to all clubs then “that will go some way towards looking at the distorted effect”. Once that money was distributed, he said, “you’re going to see a softening effect going through down the 116 clubs”, meaning the top five men’s divisions.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour, and chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, are under scrutiny. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

The Premier League welcomed the publication of the report, arguing: “It recognises what English football has built – the world’s most popular league, the leading second tier, and a pyramid of unmatched depth.” The league argued that a recent offer of financial redistribution to the EFL – understood to amount to £320m per season – “meets the objectives the IFR has set out in its report” and said it “remains committed to concluding a long-term partnership with the EFL that is fair, generous and balances the interests of all clubs”.

The EFL said the report’s findings “reinforce the EFL’s longstanding position that English football generates sufficient revenue to sustain both a successful Premier League and a thriving pyramid” and said it remained “committed to working constructively with the Premier League and the regulator to secure a financial settlement in the interests of the whole game”.

Meanwhile, the secretary of state for culture media and sport, Lisa Nandy, said the stark figures covered in the report had “blown the doors off the game”. She urged football authorities to “consider these findings for the good of the game, for the fans, and for the communities of which they are so often the bedrock”.

Sports.title: Patrice Motsepe’s Caf presidency under pressure after Afcon U-turn as Eto’o waits in wings
Sports.content:
Patrice Motsepe’s leadership of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) is under growing pressure, with officials from across the continent warning they have lost trust in the president and rivals including Samuel Eto’o positioning themselves potentially to replace him.

A return to a biennial Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) cycle is expected to be confirmed at Caf’s executive committee meeting in Abidjan next month after Motsepe surprisingly announced the U-turn last week – 10 months after the decision was taken to hold it every four years. That move is said to have wide support within Africa, but several sources have said there has been a weakening of trust in Caf’s leadership, with some questioning Motsepe’s management.

Most national association presidents are said to have been unaware Motsepe intended to announce the proposed change to Afcon’s frequency until the issue was raised at a strategic conference in Cape Verde last week. Motsepe confirmed he was not intending to stand for re-election for a third time when his term expires in 2029 and pledged Africa’s “unconditional support” for Gianni Infantino’s re-election as the Fifa president in March on the “unanimous” behalf of all 54 of Caf’s member associations.

It is understood Infantino remains extremely popular in Africa even though there are 10 to 15 member associations who would consider voting against him, as revealed in August. Motsepe’s potential rivals for the Caf presidency are believed to be attempting to gain Infantino’s approval should the South African billionaire be persuaded to step down early.

View image in fullscreen Former Barcelona forward Samuel Eto’o is the president of Cameroon’s federation and a member of Caf’s executive committee. Photograph: Steve Luciano/AP

They include Eto’o, the former Barcelona and Inter striker, who is the president of the Cameroon’s federation and a member of Caf’s executive committee, Ahmed Yahya of Mauritania, Côte d’Ivoire’s Yacine Idriss Diallo, and Souleiman Waberi, a Fifa council member from Djibouti who has been charged with embezzlement and money laundering. He has denied the allegations. Other candidates may emerge from southern Africa.

Sources indicate that Infantino could hold the key to whether Motsepe continues. The other option would be to challenge Motsepe through Caf’s statutory mechanisms, which say an extraordinary general assembly can be convened after a written request from at least two-thirds of the members of the executive committee.

Infantino is thought to have fallen out with Motsepe after Motsepe allowed the Somali referee Omar Artan, who was denied entry to the United States for the 2026 World Cup, to take charge of Uefa’s Super Cup final in August amid growing tensions with European football’s governing body. However, sources have indicated their relationship has improved in recent weeks as Infantino has sought to solidify his support in Africa.

Motsepe promised annual distributions of about $700,000 (£528,000) from Caf to each association at the conference in Cape Verde – an increase of $500,000 – and is understood to have increased payments to executive committee members for attending meetings from $150 to $350, and to have introduced for them an annual bonus payment of about $8,000.
