That is despite growing concerns over Caf’s finances, with a broadcast deal signed with IMG due to expire after the 2027 Afcon. As reported by the Guardian in February, there are major doubts about whether that tournament will go ahead owing to questions over the readiness of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda to host in June and July. Some sources are predicting that tournament could be pushed back to Christmas and the new year, which would cause major disruption to the European club season.

Caf is believed to have broadcast offers for future tournaments from IMG and an unnamed firm, although it is not known how the package will be structured and whether the proposed return to a two-year cycle could affect its commercial value. A Caf spokesperson said the process remained ongoing and that no rights had been awarded.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Coventry come to life at last – are their slapstick days behind them?
Sports.content:
FRANK CHAT

After years of circling the drain, Coventry City didn’t so much drop out of the Premier League 25 years ago as face-plant through its floorboards in slapstick style. In the intervening period, they endured their first experience of the fourth tier and were forced to live as tenants in their own city, before suffering the indignity of having to go cap-in-hand to neighbouring villages, looking for sofas on which to crash. Even the more recent good times were frustrating for the Sky Blues, as they lost a Championship playoff decider on penalties and were cruelly denied a place in the 2024 FA Cup final within the space of 11 months. It was all a far cry from that joyous afternoon in 1987 when Brian “Killer” Kilcline limped up the Wembley steps to hoist the FA Cup aloft.

Given all they have had to put up with, most Coventry fans would probably have relished the prospect of seeing their team get beaten repeatedly upon their return to the Premier League, if only because it meant their arduous return to English football’s top table was finally complete. And for a while that is exactly what looked likely to happen, as they lost their opening four league games, shipping 10 goals without reply. More astute observers will have noticed that three of those matches were against Arsenal, Manchester City and Brighton, sides that currently occupy the top three places. But while they may have lost them all, Coventry were at least creating the kind of chances that they have since begun to convert with aplomb.

Following Monday night’s shellacking of a comically shambolic and charitable Newcastle side, Coventry have now put together back-to-back wins and won their first top-flight game at home since a semi-thatched John Hartson scored the only goal of their victory over Sunderland at Highfield Road in April 2001. “We have to keep very much our feet on the ground because it’s so hard in this league,” honked Frank Lampard, having seen his young and inexperienced side bag four goals against the hapless Magpies. “If we think we’ve cracked it, if we think everything is fine … well, it’s not.” Of course, Lampard is right not to lose the run of himself and Coventry have plenty of road left to run. But following a night when Jack Rudoni announced himself as the top-flight midfielder many Coventry fans suspected he might be, things are definitely looking up.

The Premier League season is still in its infancy but already shrouded in more uncertainty than any that has been played before, not least because the team currently occupying first place look far more certain to go down than any of the 19 sides propping them up. Given the signs of life being shown by the three promoted sides, the battle against relegation already looks like shaping up to be an eight- or nine-way fight, a skirmish that is likely to be eminently more entertaining and far less weird than the current phoney war being played out at the top. Of course, if historical precedent is anything to go by, there’s also every chance this is just a temporary blip and Coventry could be playing League Two football – possibly against Manchester City – again in three years’ time.

Sports.title: The Ballon d’Or doesn’t capture football’s wonder – Michael Olise is proof | Zito Madu
Sports.content:
When I was younger, I wanted to be the captain on my football team because back then, I assumed that the armband was given to the best player. It was a goal of mine for so long that, even as my youth teams won tournaments and trophies, and I won top scorer and best player awards, I still felt unsatisfied because someone else always had the armband. Whenever I saw another teammate sprinting around with the armband on, I took it as an indictment.

I had forgotten this childish way of thinking until France v Belgium in the Uefa Nations League last week. Ousmane Dembélé, who was wearing the armband for France, was particularly active. Had it not been for the wastefulness of his teammates, he would have had several assists during his time on the field.

That time came to an end in the 60th minute, when France manager Zinedine Zidane decided to make changes in order to galvanize his team. Dembélé was doing well, but Belgium were nullifying the threat that he presented. They would double or triple team him, knowing that he wasn’t the best passer and that he would often dally on the ball. Those extra touches and extra dribbles allowed the Belgium defenders time to close in, or to recover before the pass made it to a teammate.

On came Michael Olise as Dembélé’s direct replacement, with Dembélé handing Olise the captain’s armband. There’s a clip online of the moment zoomed in, which shows what the broadcast cameras seemed to miss. When Dembélé gave Olise the armband, Olise accepted it with a look of confusion, seemingly not understanding why he was being given the honor, since he is not usually the captain or vice-captain. Seeing this, I remembered that I used to believe that the best player on the team is – and should be – the one who wears the armband and in that moment, the exchange made perfect sense.

You can always tell the quality of a player by how the crowd reacts to them. When Olise came on, the crowd roared, behaving as if victory was inevitable, even though France were down when he made his entrance. Whenever he touched the ball, they rose and took a deep breath in anticipation. He had wowed them throughout the World Cup, where he provided seven assists and innumerable moments of magic, and he had already scored a late goal to beat Belgium at the end of September. The French crowd expected great things, because he had delivered for them over and over again.

The first goal would actually come not from Olise but from Désiré Doué, who had subbed on for Bradley Barcola before Olise came on. But once things were back level, Olise took over and ended the game as a contest. In the 80th minute, he beat his man with ease down the line and cut the ball back for Rayan Cherki to slot past the keeper. Seven minutes later, he got the ball on the right side of the box from Doué. Surrounded by several defenders who were grabbing him all over, he managed a weak shot with his right foot that took the goalkeeper by surprise and went in the bottom left corner. Then three minutes after that, in the 90th minute, he made a run through the middle where Doué once again found him with the ball. With one touch Olise slotted the ball home through the keeper’s legs. His fourth goal in the last four matches. He didn’t just win the game, he turned a tough match between two of the best teams in the world into a rout in the span of 10 minutes.

Olise is often accused of performing nonchalance. Maybe that’s true, and maybe it’s a case of social anxiety and shyness being so unusual in the professional football ranks that fans have to see it as something insincere. Regardless, if you watch Olise play closely, beyond the YouTube highlights of isolated moments, it’s impossible to accuse him of nonchalance. His playing style is one of ease and grace, but that is not a consequence of pretending not to try. His style is so similar to that of Zidane, in the sense that the grace comes from both a sense to entertain the crowd but also from an economy of movement.

View image in fullscreen Michael Olise looked confused after being given the armband. Photograph: Catherine Steenkeste/Getty Images

If the danger of Dembélé comes from the innumerable ways that he can beat you, options that are so numerous that they tend to sometimes weigh him down when he tries to do too much, Olise beats defenders and teams by doing the simple things extremely well. When he controls the ball, he sets it to lead up to his next move. When he runs with the ball, he pushes it with the exact amount of force that allows him to either get by the defender or set up a pass. And when he’s presented with a number of options of what to do in front of goal or to find a teammate on the run, he usually chooses the best one. That doesn’t mean that everything he does ultimately leads to success – his inability to score during the World Cup eventually made it seem as though he were under a curse – but he is usually making the right choices with the ball at his feet.

Armbands don’t actually signify the best player on the field or in the world. Rather, that conversation is now centered around the Ballon d’Or. Players and their teams openly campaign to be crowned, and fans of each player attack the other sides, with each denigrating the opposing side’s favorite player in order to boost the campaign for their own. The obsession with the award has completely atrophied how we understand and appreciate players, replacing it with a destructive kind of comparison where great players are torn down as being bad if they haven’t won enough, or scored enough goals, or had more assists than the others that they’re up against.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

This kind of engagement is intellectually silly and insincere, and leaves us no space for one of the best parts of watching football: The sense of wonder that players give us. And in the effort to boost one over the others whether through tribalism or idol worship, we miss the beauty of such a diverse group of players at the top of their game doing the ridiculous, match after match.

The joy that I get from watching Olise and Dembélé (or Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappé, Raphinha, Harry Kane, Rodri, and others) doesn’t come from the possibility that they might win the Ballon d’Or. What is wonderful to me is seeing how each player solves the same questions presented to them on the football field. How each one interprets the game, its constraints, and faces it with their own strengths and weaknesses. What matters is how each of them makes magic from a collection of rules and chaos of 22 people on the field.

When Olise steps out onto the field after checking the length of the grass, and looking in bemusement at the armband, my thoughts aren’t about whether he can prove that he’s the best player in the world. No, like everyone else who stands and gasps whenever he tries the spectacular, what I’m looking and hoping for is to be impressed by a player expanding what is possible on the field. And more often than not, he delivers.

Sports.title: ‘It changed me a lot’: how Japan’s academy system supercharged women’s team
Sports.content:
Japan have constantly pushed the boundaries in women’s football, whether it be with regular success in Asia or their ability to beat the biggest nations in the world.

Nadeshiko won the Women’s World Cup in 2011 and reached another final in 2015, while more established countries fell by the wayside. Japan have not replicated that success but did win the Women’s Asian Cup this year under the guidance of Nils Nielsen, who has since been succeeded by Michihisa Kano, and most of the biggest stars play outside the country, with 24 contracted to Women’s Super League clubs alone.

Japan are discreet about the secrets behind their success, particularly the easy-on-the-eye style that has become a trademark of the men’s and women’s teams, but one of those secrets lies in the Japanese Football Association (JFA) creating the JFA Academy.

There are three that take girls across the country of 123 million people: Fukushima, Sakai and Imabari. A fourth, Kumamoto Uki, is a boys’ academy only. Fukushima was the first to open, in 2006, with Sakai following in 2012 and Imabari in 2015.

Shota Mishio, an analyst for the national team when they conquered the world in 2011, recently coached in the Fukushima academy, which since the nuclear disaster that preceded their World Cup success by months has moved to Susono City. He offers an insight into how they are able not only to develop world-class individuals but to mould them into a successful unit for the national team.

The girls enter the academies at 13 and, other than in Fukushima, leave at 15. “The players are here until the age of 18,” Mishio says of Fukushima, which has five technical coaches dedicated to the girls. “We belong to the JFA, we are a coaching school with accommodation for players … the most important information I can give you is 25% of our original players have become senior national team players – that is a very high percentage.”

At the 2023 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand, five of Japan’s 23 players had come through the Fukushima academy. At the Paris Olympics a year later, it was seven, Mishio pointing to a “progression every tournament”.

One of them, Manaka Hayashi, is one of the more recent success stories. She graduated in 2022 and, after playing domestically for INAC Kobe, earned a move to the NWSL side Chicago Stars at the start of 2025. “We all had to apply for it, then the coaches come and watch us try out,” she says. “There could be 100 to 200 players who could apply, but only half a dozen get selected, so it’s not easy to get selected, it’s quite special.”

View image in fullscreen Manaka Hayashi joined INAC Kobe Leonessa after leaving JFA Academy Fukushima. Photograph: Aflo Sport/Alamy

View image in fullscreen Manaka Hayashi made 38 league appearances for Chicago Stars after joining the NWSL club in January 2025. Photograph: Zoe Davis/NWSL/Getty Images

View image in fullscreen Manaka Hayashi, who is capable of operating as a playmaker and box-to-box midfielder, joined Juventus in September. Photograph: Juventus FC/Getty Images

It is not just about football, with the girls getting an education. “The government helps,” Mishio says. “For example, the education department helps us. We here specifically work only on football as coaches, but we have our own original programme for things like English, languages in general, and even football-specific language for football players.”

Hayashi says: “We would go to school from morning to evening and then come back to train around 4pm to 6pm. At high school age, we would go to school only 9am to 12pm and train more, so there is much more time for football as you get older.”

Hayashi left the NWSL, where there is strong Japanese representation, for Juventus last month. The group of Japan internationals in England includes Manchester City’s Yui Hasegawa and Chelsea’s summer acquisition Manaka Matsukubo.

“More and more players want to go abroad,” Mishio says. “For example, one player recently went to Feyenoord and before that one went to Bayern Munich. Some others want to become professional in Japan first.”

Hayashi recalls stepping into the world of the JFA Academy, and how it provided more than a football upbringing. “When we entered the dorm at 13, the oldest players are 18. It’s a big life experience and you definitely learned how to communicate with other people, from different backgrounds and different ages.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea’s Manaka Matsukubo is one of 24 Japanese players in the Women’s Super League. Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

“Football-wise it changed me a lot. The JFA scouts are always paying attention, but you live it every day, so there is so much opportunity to talk about and learn about football. We would watch it just to help each other become better, analyse everything. That’s the difference between the JFA Academy and being at other clubs.”

The way of playing is drilled into them from a young age, and is a big reason why Japan have enjoyed such success. “I’d say yes,” says Hayashi, adding: “The coaches emphasised a lot we had to be better technically. When you play against foreign teams, they are faster and stronger than us, so we had to be smarter to compete against them with quality on the ball. We had to be skilful on the ball to become better than other countries.”

Mishio says: “The important thing is the technique and endurance. These are the main points of the training here, because it was the trademark of the Japanese style of play.”

Get in touch

If you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please email moving.goalposts@theguardian.com.

Sports.title: Viking’s two head coaches on Champions League adventure: ‘For us, it’s the best team in the world’
Sports.content:
“When we recruit players, we say something bold.” The morning’s training session at Lyse Arena has finished and, over lunch, Morten Jensen is explaining how he and Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim have propelled Viking Stavanger from mediocrity to an implausible place among Europe’s elite. “We always tell them: ‘If you come to Viking and play for us, we’re going to be the best coaches you ever had.’”

It is a story more than a decade in the making for Jensen and Aarsheim, who were appointed joint head coaches in November 2020. On Tuesday they will oversee the club’s first home Champions League game, against Bayern Munich, the latest step in a journey that has brought shared success in every sense.

“We were talking on the phone one evening, it must have been around 2012 or 2013,” Aarsheim says, sitting across the table and recalling one of countless conversations between close friends who had first met on the semi-professional scene. “I worked in a bank, he was in the oil and gas industry, we both had local teams part-time. And I remember we said: ‘Hey, we should take a team together one day.’”

They are outwardly an odd couple. Aarsheim had played almost 300 games for Viking during the 1990s and 2000s. He cemented club legend status as a classy midfielder and captain, combining modest league successes with a handful of short Uefa Cup runs before starting to coach at Randaberg. Jensen’s attempts to forge a playing career at Viking had been stalled by injury; he had played college soccer in the United States before landing back in Norway’s lower divisions and managing tiny Havørn.

“He’s always calm, collected, analytical,” says Jensen of Aarsheim, five years his senior at 51. “His personality is not to be stubborn, but find solutions, so he’s always interested and seeking to learn new things. He can explode and be aggressive when he needs to, but it’s at the right time and there needs to be a reason.”

It is Aarsheim’s style to weigh words deliberately, a dash of swearing added for effect. The rhetoric falls to Jensen. “What’s impressive with Morten is how big he thinks and that he dares to tell it out loud,” Aarsheim says. “He talks about winning the league, the Champions League, everything, while I’m thinking: ‘Let’s just get a good team first.’ But it transmits. We put dreams to the players and put that flame inside for them to dream bigger. We don’t want players simply to be satisfied to play here.”

Viking have become an outstanding side themselves under Aarsheim and Jensen. “I think we have shown many players, young and a little bit older, that we see potential and can develop them,” Jensen says.

View image in fullscreen Viking’s CEO, Eirik Bjørnø (left), and the sporting director, Erik Nevland, have helped change the Stavanger club off the pitch. Photograph: Carina Johansen/The Guardian

Their paths had converged, becoming assistants to the previous Viking head coach, Bjarne Berntsen, before both were due to be interviewed for his replacement. “They gave us the tasks independently,” Jensen remembers. “And we said: ‘What if we just come together? Would you fancy that?’”

“I’m sat there thinking: ‘Jesus, are we really going for this?’” remembers Eirik Bjørnø, who was 29 and newly promoted to Viking’s chief executive officer position, when Aarsheim and Jensen turned up for their interview. The pair had everything planned, down to a 120-page dossier on how their team should play. At Jensen’s instigation, they had also prepared a special slide.

“Suddenly there’s this photo of a bunch of sheep,” Bjørnø says. “They had a big spiel about all the sheep, everyone following the main sheep. Then up pop these two wolves on the photo.” The sheep were, quite plainly, Viking’s competitors. As Jensen tells it: “We said: ‘Are you going to hire these two badass wolves? We’re going to eat up all the sheep.’”

Bjørnø and Viking’s sporting director, the former Manchester United and Fulham striker Erik Nevland, were persuaded. “We were at a place in history where we needed to do something different to become better,” says Nevland, who played for Viking across three stints and scored twice in a Uefa Cup win against Chelsea. “It was kind of: ‘Let’s go for it.’ It just made sense. It was a bit of a gamble but we were in a position where we could do that.”

Joint managers are vanishingly rare at the highest level. “It comes up all the time,” Nevland says. “When I talk to sporting directors from other countries it’s not Viking any more, it’s: ‘Oh, you’re the club with two head coaches.’ It’s something different but it’s a dynamic thing; it’s not like we will necessarily do it this way whenever they move on. It’s special, but why change something that works?”

Their efforts bore spectacular fruit last year, beating a previously imperious Bodø/Glimt to the Eliteserien title. Viking had been a dominant force in Norway during the 1970s but had not been champions since 1991. They had even been relegated in 2017. “In the first two years we learned a lot of things that we’ll never do again,” says Jensen. Finishing 11th in 2022 brought a keener focus on developing local players; those who, like their managers and the similarly homespun Bjørnø‑Nevland double act, know what it entails to represent this mountain-fringed port city in Norway’s south-west.

View image in fullscreen Zlatko Tripic is Viking’s captain and talisman. Photograph: Carina Johansen/The Guardian

“We’ve done it with a lot of people that care for each other,” Bjørnø says. “We’re trying to enjoy the ride together, and that makes us a lot stronger. When you have success together, it makes such a big difference when you actually feel that you’re friends.”

Nevland sees more benefits from such an intense local flavour. “It just gives us a feeling that everything we do means more,” he says. “The decisions you make are a little bit more thorough because it’s so important for the region and everyone you know. If it’s for my brother or my neighbour, you know all the decisions impact them in some kind of way.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Stavanger, enriched hugely by the discovery of oil 200 miles off shore in 1969, can adore its football team again. “There had been something underlying that was missing for the people here,” Jensen says. “We wanted to play entertaining football and move our people. And maybe that’s the most fun part: it’s not the Champions League or the title win, it’s seeing how many kids are running around with Viking jerseys around the city and in the schools. A decade ago you would only see Manchester United and Liverpool shirts. That’s the one thing I am most proud of.”

A video meeting longer than 10 minutes would risk losing the players’ attention. This one earlier in the day has focused on ways to exploit the high press of SK Brann, fierce rivals from up the coast who Viking must visit for an awkward test four days before facing Bayern. “They killed us last year out there, remember that,” Jensen tells the squad, assembled in a television room next to the changing areas, shortly before it winds up. “We thought we were going to be there, but they ran over us, they challenged us, they had more energy.”

Aarsheim generally oversees Viking’s defensive drills; Jensen focuses on attack. They have shown Viking’s players 10 short clips, selected by a six-strong staff during a coaches’ meeting that started at 8.30am. All bets are off in these highly charged derbies against Brann. The focus is on how Viking can impose their style and minimise the effect of an intense, raucous environment. “We’re going to be better in the first duel, we’re going to be better than them in the second-ball phase, it’s going to be important,” Aarsheim says.

It is raining lightly by the time training starts. Aarsheim clenches his fists on the touchline when one of the crossfield switches Viking have been practising finishes with a tap-in. In the centre circle, Jensen is telling their forwards how to escape the Brann press. Later in the session, they watch side-by-side from seats in the stand.

The tone is businesslike, positive, collaborative. But who gets to play good or bad cop if necessary? “I think we mix it up and sometimes we plan it,” Aarsheim says. “Yeah, we do that as a tool sometimes,” Jensen continues. “But we don’t believe in shouting and yelling at them. It’s not going to make them better footballers. So we try to develop their football intelligence, but also the people. I think our strongest asset is in man-managing.”

View image in fullscreen The English-born New Zealand midfielder Joe Bell (centre) last season helped Viking to a first Eliteserien title since 1991. Photograph: Carina Johansen/The Guardian

They are often asked what happens if they disagree over, for example, a selection issue. “Then we’ll discuss, loudly sometimes, with the rest of our staff in the coaching room and will both have to defend our choices and reasoning to them,” Jensen says. “We’ll all discuss it until we have an agreement. But 99% of the time we are pretty agreed in terms of who to use in a particular game so it’s very seldom we waste time over that.”

Aarsheim takes over. “I can read Morten in one second. If he really wants something from his stomach then I sense it: ‘OK, let’s go with that.’ It’s never been a problem.”

The fit is instinctive and has become second nature to Viking’s team, too. “You can see the respect and loyalty they have to each other,” says Zlatko Tripic, the long‑serving captain, speaking under calmer skies after the session. “They give a lot of responsibility to the players and let us discuss things. If you ask everyone in the dressing room, there is huge respect for how they deal with things and have given us this comfort and confidence.”

It is a self-assuredness Viking hope can help them trouble Bayern. Nothing appears off limits in Norwegian football’s recent run of fairytales. “This should be the best period of their lives,” says Jensen of a squad that, 72 hours later, heed the warnings and win 2-0 in Bergen. “It’s our job to make them do the best they can,” Aarsheim says. “For us, Viking is Barcelona. The players have to understand that we see Viking as more than a club. In our heads, it’s the best team in the world.”

Sports.title: Carrick promises Manchester United will ‘come out fighting’ after sticky start
Sports.content:
Manchester United have endured their worst league start in 40 years but Michael Carrick insists he is “loving it”. United arrived in Madrid without Kobbie Mainoo and Luke Shaw, who both picked up knocks in the draw against Tottenham at the weekend, and with the coach admitting that his team are in “a spot”, but he vowed that they would “come out fighting”.

Despite collecting just six points in the Premier League so far, Carrick claimed he did not feel under pressure and backed his captain, Bruno Fernandes, who he revealed was still “carrying something”, to rediscover his form. As he talked about building, there was a reminder too of the fact that Arsenal, the champions, finished “seventh or eighth” in Mikel Arteta’s first two seasons.

“To do something good, to do something great, you have got to be able to do something difficult,” said Carrick, whose side take on Atlético Madrid at the Metropolitano Stadium in the second round of games in the Champions League league phase on Tuesday.

“We hoped for a lot more, we expected a lot more, and we are where we are,” Carrick added. “I was aware that, winning as many as we had [last season], it was going to get more challenging, stickier. I understand that when it is not going well there is a real clamour and a feeling that it’s a disaster, that it’s all wrong and that everything needs to be changed. I kind of get that, but that’s not our mindset and it’s certainly not mine. You have to deal with things and overcome them. That is what I did throughout my career. We have to accept reality but we are building and you can’t lose sight of the journey.”

On the pressure he is under, Carrick said: “It depends on how you define ‘pressure’. There is our own expectation: we know what we want, what we are capable of and that comes from us. I don’t look outside. I don’t feel the pressure from that at all.

“I’m pretty good at shutting off, to be honest; closing off and living a little bit in my bubble. And I think that’s what we do as a group. We look after each other, we all know what’s out there and it’s about managing it, controlling it and staying focused on what we can do. It is about us wanting to succeed, to win. That’s the drive. There is no negativity. It’s also fine lines sometimes. We are hugely confident and we have confidence in each other. I have the utmost confidence in the boys that we can win a lot of games.

“[That’s] because I know them, I know how much they care, I know how strong the group is. And, anyway, you’ve got no choice: that’s why we’re here. We’re here to test ourselves and that’s the opportunity that’s in front of us. If you haven’t got that little bit in you where maybe it’s a little bit crazy times but you actually love the challenge and really want to dig deep to find the answers, then this is not the place for you.”

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick backed Bruno Fernandes to rediscover his form from last season. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

Despite the poor domestic start, which also included exiting the Carabao Cup against Brighton at Old Trafford, Carrick’s side did win their Champions League opener convincingly against Sabah last month.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We need to do something about it now and accept the reality,” Carrick said. “I love this part of it: sometimes when it’s not quite going for you, you see who’s really there. You see within the group, the squad, the club, who’s really there and who wants to be there for the long term, [who] is really attached to it and [for whom it] really means something. The supporters are there: they know what they want, they’re desperate for it, and we’ve got to give them something. You have to embrace the challenge. I totally believe that we’ll work through it.”

Asked if he believed that Fernandes could recover his form, Carrick said: “I think it’s pretty obvious to say that he can, yeah. I mean, he’s a top player, Bruno. Sometimes things don’t quite go for you, but he’s done some incredible things for this football club and he will do the same in the future, there’s no doubt about that. I’ve seen that a lot was made of [his fitness]. He was carrying something.

“People don’t maybe realise it, but it happens a lot: players play with issues. I probably played 80% of the games with some sort of issue. It’s not ideal, but it’s manageable. Bruno was able to play the games; that’s the commitment he that he has. He’s pretty much over it. It’s not a major deal, he’s in good shape and he was really bright [in training] this morning, looking forward to the game.”

Sports.title: Christian Pulisic is no longer a focal point for the US or Milan – and that’s OK
Sports.content:
Usually, the second weekend of October sees Christian Pulisic flanked by compatriots as the Star-Spangled Banner plays. Last year, he was involved in US friendlies against Ecuador and Australia. But this year, with Fifa having folded the October window into September, Pulisic didn’t have the chance. On Sunday, his pre-match music was O Generosa, the Serie A anthem, which he observed with a soft smile.

Mark Twain’s first visit to Italy left him describing the country as “a vast museum of magnificence and misery”, and it’s a fitting summary of Pulisic’s three-plus years with Milan. The magnificence: 43 goals and 25 assists in 138 appearances. The misery: just one trophy since he arrived in July 2023, a 2025 Supercoppa Italia held in Saudi Arabia.

For years, Pulisic’s club career was a source of chronic frustration in between the reprieve of international duty. Now, after Mauricio Pochettino opened the team’s next era by selecting 13 top prospects (but not Pulisic, recently recovered from injury), his international standing is in a shakier state than ever, a decade after he debuted.

In a continuation of a frustratingly familiar theme, Pulisic’s fourth season with Milan hasn’t started smoothly. The lower-leg microfracture he suffered against Belgium at the World Cup this summer has kept him off Ruben Amorim’s teamsheet, with just two league starts. He opened Sunday’s visit to Sassuolo as the right half-space winger beneath Gonçalo Ramos.

Pulisic still commands quite a lot of attention. Mid-table Sassuolo were more willing to let the ball find Diego Moreira than Pulisic, with the American’s touches garnering additional defensive bodies. As opponents converged whenever he entered the final third, he often cycled possession to fellow US international Yunus Musah, trailing behind on the right side of midfield.

Pulisic dropped into the defensive half often in search of creating numerical advantages, part of a relatively free-roaming deployment. He led Milan players with 5.3km (3.2 miles) covered in the first half, although his industry failed to create much. He was a key part of the buildup to Milan’s only goal of the day, playing the pass before Luka Modric’s assist and offering the Croat a helpful decoy run.

By the 77th minute, Pulisic’s sole shot had been blocked and his only created chance was stifled by the goalkeeper. Pulisic has a goal contribution in just four of his last 22 appearances in Serie A.

Having turned 28 last month, Pulisic is in the next, veteran phase of his career. Teams expect an attacker nearing 30 to be prolific. A player who is steady if unspectacular at this point can fall down the depth chart if a younger, more dynamic alternative presents themself.

View image in fullscreen Christian Pulisic celebrates after scoring a goal. Photograph: Tiziano Ballabio/NurPhoto/Getty Images

With a quarter-hour left against Sassuolo, Amorim opted for one: Pulisic off, Alpha Cissè in.

Since arriving from Hellas Verona this summer, Cissè has been a bright spot for Milan. The 19-year-old was lauded by Amorim early in the season, starting as Pulisic recovered from his World Cup injury. In just 242 league minutes, Cissè has scored twice; Pulisic, now up to 190 minutes under Amorim, has one goal.

“I love Cissè. I love Cissè,” crooned the coach in late August.

That’s not to say that everything is against Pulisic. This week, Gazzetta dello Sport reported he is one of three key players the club hopes to renew early in the Amorim era. He has history to fall back on, having led Milan with 17 goals in all competitions two seasons ago.

“I can only say that I am very happy at Milan right now and for the near future as well,” Pulisic said at a San Siro meet-and-greet during the window, flanked by a wall of shirts bearing his name. “So, yeah, I’m not thinking about the contract renewal but I am very happy here. I want to stay at Milan.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Cissè’s rising presence mirrors Pulisic’s new reality with his national team. Pochettino ushered in the next generation as Pulisic remained in Italy, giving debuts to several teenage attackers who are hungry to work into the fold. Cavan Sullivan validated the hype with an audacious account-opener against Mexico, while others – such as wingers Mathis Albert and new Crystal Palace signing Zavier Gozo – began what they hope will be long careers representing the US.

Pulisic has struggled on international duty under Pochettino. He’s scored just once since the start of 2025, in a tune-up friendly against Senegal. His mostly poor performances at the World Cup hardly reinforced his bona fides to the Argentinian, who declined to directly address Pulisic’s situation during the recent international window.

It’s far too soon to write Pulisic off. He covers considerable ground. His more decisive touches can generate threats, though too often he appears caught in two minds about his best course of action. After years of being cast by Milan and, especially, the US as an attacking focal point, he may be more dangerous as an auxiliary option with a lower touch volume.

Internationally, his rising teammates could afford Pulisic a lower-pressure role. Sullivan has relished early acclamation of being the face of the program. Folarin Balogun weathered the pressure – well, the more normal kinds – of being the team’s chief goalscorer at the World Cup, bagging three goals in 316 minutes. With Pulisic absent, Pochettino used his usual spot at left-wing to shoehorn in both of his chief playmakers, Gio Reyna and Malik Tillman; given his past form at Milan, he could still slot in at right-wing while making Sullivan a useful alternative to all three from the bench.

Pulisic’s entire career had been framed in the context of a home World Cup. Perhaps being freed from that years-long pressure can enable him to rediscover his best form, to Milan’s benefit as well as his national team’s.

But with the World Cup gone and his performances leaving something to be desired, we’re left to wait and watch to see who Pulisic is, and will be, as a player.

Sports.title: Premier League and EFL respond to bombshell report from Independent Football Regulator
Sports.content:
The Premier League and EFL have both welcomed the Independent Football Regulator's State of the Game Report.

The landmark report assesses the financial sustainability of football in England.



3 Former prime minister Keir Starmer pledged to reform English football governance prior to winning the 2024 general election Credit: Getty

What is the report?

Reporter Ben Jacobs told talkSPORT: "The report highlights a game loaded with both revenue and risk.

"Professional clubs brought in £9billion in 2025/26. And Premier League clubs have actually grown on average 10 times faster than the UK economy itself since 1992.

"And yet at the other extreme, 94 per cent of clubs make losses, 32 clubs could not survive 30 days without owner funding, 60 per cent of EFL and National League teams are technically insolvent, 20 per cent of Premier League clubs fall into this category as well.



"The solution focuses on revenue distribution, with the independent football regulator confident that a funding deal will be finally reached between the Premier League and the EFL.

"And the independent football regulator has outlined plans to address financial losses, look into a National League specific strategy and tackle financial and corporate governance."



What have the Premier League and EFL said about the report?

The 250-page report has initially been released in draft format.

A statement from the Premier League read: "The Premier League welcomes the publication of the Independent Football Regulator’s (IFR) draft State of the Game Report.

"The Report recognises what English football has built – the world's most popular league, the leading second tier, and a pyramid of unmatched depth. It also identifies key challenges within the game that need to be addressed in partnership.



"The Premier League shares the IFR’s preference that there should be a football-led solution to revenue distributions. As the Report makes clear, new funding must go hand in hand with effective financial controls and wider reforms to strengthen clubs.

"We believe the proposal we have made to the EFL, which was unanimously approved by Premier League clubs in July, meets the objectives the IFR has set out in its Report. The League remains committed to concluding a long-term partnership with the EFL that is fair, generous and balances the interests of all clubs.

3 The report presents tough reading for Premier League and EFL cubs Credit: Getty

"We will now study the Report in detail before responding to the consultation, and will continue to work constructively with the IFR, and all stakeholders, to protect and strengthen the deepest professional pyramid in world football."



The report comes against the backdrop of Manchester City being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules, a verdict which the club have appealed.

An EFL statement, meanwhile, read: "The Independent Football Regulator’s draft State of the Game Report provides a significant and comprehensive assessment of the financial health of English football.

"On first review, many of the Report’s central conclusions reflect concerns the EFL has consistently raised since the publication of the Fan Led Review, particularly the disproportionate distribution of growing revenues and the financial cliff edges this has created, most notably between the Championship and the Premier League. These pressures are distorting competition and contributing to rising losses, debt and over reliance on owner funding, creating material risks for clubs throughout the pyramid.

"These initial findings reinforce the EFL’s longstanding position that English football generates sufficient revenue to sustain both a successful Premier League and a thriving pyramid. The EFL’s purpose is to help make Clubs sustainable and the challenge is not simply how much money flows into the game, but how it is distributed and spent. A more appropriate distribution of revenues must therefore be accompanied by effective and enforceable financial regulation, ensuring that additional resources strengthen clubs’ financial position, rather than contributing to further cost inflation.



"The EFL welcomes the Report’s focus on reducing financial losses, strengthening Clubs’ management of financial risk and ensuring that governance standards reflect the risks across the pyramid, including at National League level. We also recognise the importance of meaningful supporter engagement, strong corporate governance and greater diversity in club leadership. These priorities must form part of a coordinated programme of reform alongside improved revenue distribution and effective cost controls.

3 Sheffield Wednesday are among a number of EFL clubs to find themselves in financial difficulties in recent seasons, beginning the last Championship campaign with a points deduction for entering administration and committing financial breaches under former owner Dejphon Chansiri Credit: Getty

"In the more immediate short term, the EFL remains committed to working constructively with the Premier League and the Regulator to secure a financial settlement in the interests of the whole game.

"As the Report proceeds to consultation, we will consider its evidence and recommendations carefully, consult our Clubs and submit an appropriate response. We will also engage fully with the IFR’s six-point action plan, with the aim of delivering coherent, long-term reform that improves financial resilience, safeguards Clubs as community assets and supports the continued strength and competitiveness of English football at every level."



What is the Independent Football Regulator?

A non-departmental public body of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), the IFR was set up in September last year with the purpose of preserving and encouraging the sustainability of football, having first been announced back in 2023.

It followed the passing of the Football Governance Act 2025.

The body is chaired by Richard Kogan, with Richard Monks serving as chief executive.

A final version of the report is expected to follow next spring.

Sports.title: Ex-England goalkeeper Alex McCarthy was told to retire after doctors discovered heart condition
Sports.content:
Former England goalkeeper Alex McCarthy says doctors advised him to retire from football due to a covid-related heart problem.

The 36-year-old, who currently plays for League One side Leicester City., considered calling time on his career towards the end of the pandemic.



2 McCarthy has revealed that he was told to retire by doctors after he was found to have a heart condition Credit: Getty

McCarthy has not revealed the timeline of the diagnosis but he did not feature in a competitive match between December 2021 and May 2022 while contracted at Southampton.

The shot-stopper, who earned his only England cap in a friendly against the USA in 2018 admits to having no symptoms from the issue.

However, when doctors discovered the problem, he was strongly advised to hang up his gloves.



How was McCarthy's condition found?

“I don’t think I’ve spoken about it before. It was coming out the back end of Covid when I missed a year because I had a heart condition from Covid,” McCarthy told the Fozcast podcast.

"Not many people know this. I think it was during Covid, when you had to have all the tests. I had to wear a heart patch. I think a few of the lads in football who had Covid had to.



“They picked up some formalities with my heart. I had no symptoms or anything.

"So they monitored it for a while but I couldn’t get signed off to play.



“I ended up getting called in by the doc at Southampton to see a specialist down in Southampton. He was like, ‘Bring your agent and your wife’. I was like, ‘This can’t be good’.

“Turned up there and the guy basically said, ‘You can’t play football anymore, you need a defib fitted like Christian Eriksen and that’. This was out of nowhere. I felt fine.”

McCarthy opted for a second opinion from a London-based doctor before making any hasty decisions.

2 McCarthy, who has one England cap to his name, took a year away from playing and managed to make a comeback despite his condition Credit: Getty



And the veteran goalkeeper later underwent a procedure that enabled him to continue his career.

How did McCarthy continue playing?

“Long story short, I had to have a think about what I wanted to do. I said to Southampton that I wanted a second opinion. [I] go up to this guy in London and he said, ‘I think I can sort this’,” McCarthy added.

“A month or two later I had to go back to London. They cut my groin open, I had to be awake for this because they needed the heartbeat to be normal.

"They put a tube up to my heart and did an ablation where they burn a part of your heart.



“They found that when I was exercising, my heart would skip quite a few beats. They then put a chip in my chest, which is linked to my phone to them to always monitor it.

“I missed a good few months, and I had to go through all that to get signed off to play again.

"[I’ve] gone from nearly having to retire to still playing. It’s mental.”

Sports.title: Jamie O’Hara’s Tottenham hot take leaves Jason Cundy utterly speechless
Sports.content:
Jason Cundy was left gobsmacked by Jamie O’Hara’s claim that Tottenham are the best footballing team in the Premier League this season.

Roberto De Zerbi’s side sit 19th in the table and remain winless having picked up just three points from six league games.



6 Roberto De Zerbi watched his ten men salvage a point late on at Old Trafford Credit: Getty

6 Jamie O'Hara was hugely impressed by Spurs display at Old Trafford

Spurs have drawn three of their last four in the Premier League including a hard-fought point against Manchester United on Saturday.

Although Tottenham appear to have halted their losing run, Cundy does not appear ready to give the north London club any credit, just yet.



And faced with O’Hara’s ringing endorsement of De Zerbi’s men, Cundy was left dumbfounded by what was to follow.

“We’re 19th but that doesn’t read true with what I’m actually watching because when you’re actually watching us right now, we are playing some good stuff,” O’Hara said while his broadcast colleague listened with a smirk.



“We absolutely battered Man United. Yes, we’re a bit fragile and we concede poor goals but that result – we should have won 4 or 5-1.

“When I’m watching the overall play of the Spurs, I’m actually quite excited.”



O'Hara's bold claim

Then came the line that sent Cundy into a stunned silence.

O’Hara said: “I think we’re actually probably playing the best football in the Premier League. I do. We just haven't got the results yet.”

Cundy’s eyes then lit up in amazement at what he had heard from his Sports Bar colleague.

“Why are you looking at me like that? I’m actually being serious,” O’Hara added.

6 Jason Cundy promptly gave his broadcast partner a look of disbelief



6 Before bursting into hysterics

Cundy was unable to hold it together and burst out into hysterics at O’Hara’s notion.

But the die-hard Spurs fan was not ready to back down from his assessment and tried a little harder at convincing Cundy that his claim had some truth to it.

“When you watch the team play, the way we're gelling and the movements and patterns, it’s exciting mate, it is,” O’Hara continued.



“When it clicks, and it will click, we’re going to start slapping teams. It hasn’t happened yet but it’s coming.

“You can’t get away from the football we’re playing. That football is good to watch.”

Cundy’s continued silence was deafening as O’Hara urged him to say something in response.

6 O'Hara poured his heart out while Cundy lapped it up



The former Chelsea defender hilariously picked up a printed copy of the Premier League table before simply uttering: “19th.”

O’Hara came back at him with further justification for his claim saying: “I know we’re 19th but that’s because we had a sticky start. But the signs are there mate. You know there’s encouraging signs.

“Are you not seeing encouraging signs?”

Cundy stands firm

Cundy again responded with “19th” before pointing out why he felt O’Hara’s assessment was a flawed one.

“I’m sorry, Newcastle and Aston Villa had your pants down and gave you a whooping,” Cundy said.



“You’ve gone from 17th to 19th, to 19th. There’s no encouraging signs.”

6 Cundy then explained why O'Hara was completely wide of the mark

He then reeled off the 18 teams currently above Spurs in the table, telling O’Hara all of them were better than them before adding bottom side Fulham to the list to further wind up his co-host.

Cundy, who was not in the mood to take O’Hara seriously, left the final word to his pal.



“They are not better than us, they are just taking their chances. In terms of the football though, everyone’s in awe of the way we’re playing.”

Tottenham’s quest for a first league win continues when they host Coventry next Monday – live on talkSPORT.

Sports.title: Top four breakout players in Europe this season, including new Xavi Simons rival
Sports.content:
Top four breakout players in Europe this season, including new Xavi Simons rival

The 2026/27 season is well into its third month as leagues across Europe begin to take shape.

Clubs have already started establishing their positions in the table, with the Champions League already reaching matchday two.



6 Andy Brassell has highlighted Paris Brunner as one of four breakout stars so far this season Credit: AFP

Whilst a host of well-known players have continued their expected form into the campaign, several exciting talents have also emerged across the continent.

European football journalist Andy Brassell has now provided an insight into four of those phenoms.

Speaking exclusively to talkSPORT, he has revealed which players could be set for high-profile moves come next summer.



Here is a rundown of his biggest breakout stars of the season so far.

Gjivai Zechiel (Feyenoord)

The Feyenoord midfielder has established himself in the side since returning from a season-long loan spell with Utrecht last term.

Zechiel has started all eight Eredivisie matches for the unbeaten league leaders, scoring five goals and adding four assists.



His performances saw the 22-year-old sign a new three-year deal last month.

Meanwhile, he also made his senior debut for the Netherlands against Greece during the recent international break.



Brassell fears Zechiel's quality means he could soon be on the move, explaining: "Gjivai Zechiel has been really good in a Feyenoord team that are top of the table in the Eredivisie. So they have had a really good start under (Giovanni) Van Bronckhorst.

"You know when someone starts with such a focus in one of the second-tier leagues that you think it is going to be absolutely impossible for this club to hold him, as big a club as Feyenoord are, beyond this season. That’s how it feels with Zechiel.

6 Zechiel's form for Feyenoord earned him his Netherlands debut earlier this month Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

"He has been brought into the Netherlands team by Xavi as well, bearing in mind that that other Xavi, Simons, is not available at the moment.



"There is room for someone to be given creative license in that team so I think we will be seeing some more of him in November as well.

"Someone who is such an intuitive footballer, who is scoring and creating a fair lick already this season and you feel that barring injury Feyenoord are on for a really good season here.

"Zechiel will make it a fairly memorable one I think, both for him personally and for Feyenoord."

Alessandro Romano (Cagliari on loan from Roma)

Alessandro Romano's start to the season has already seen the 20-year-old win three caps for Italy.



The Switzerland-born youngster was handed his debut against Belgium in September before featuring in both matches against Turkey.

6 Romano chose to play for Italy despite being born in Switzerland Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

It comes after his loan move to Cagliari from Roma in the summer, with the deal including a conditional obligation to buy.

Romano has since played all but five minutes of their opening six Serie A matches, including scoring on his league debut against Parma.



Cagliari have lost just once so far this term and held Juventus to a draw on Sunday, leaving themselves fourth in the table.

Brassell has now tipped Romano to potentially succeed a Euro 2020 winner in Italy's midfield in the future.

He continued: "Alessandro Romano has been great so far this season. Picked of course by Roberto Mancini for Italy and making three appearances for him in the recent international window.

"Again I think a beneficiary of the fact that Cagliari are having a great start to the season.



"We talked about the Swiss connection, born in Winterthur, came over and joined Roma’s academy when he was near enough 16 and really impressed there.

"I think his palate sort of widened there because he was played for the first time as a more defensive midfielder and he’s really good at controlling the tempo, so that’s something that he can do pretty well.

"I don’t want to say that long-term for Italy he can replace (Marco) Verratti, but he has I think the ability to be that influential for them.

"He has made a choice of love by going with Italy because when he was at home in Switzerland he was picked for the Under-17s and he was also brought into this accelerated development program.



"As he has chosen to play for Italy, the Swiss FA have basically asked for all the money back that was spent on his training and he’s obliged to pay it back.

"So he owes them €1million or whatever, I’m not sure that necessarily influences him getting a big transfer down the line. I think he’ll be able to afford it in the very near future.

6 Brassell has tipped Romano as a potential successor to Marco Verratti Credit: Getty

"Mancini is aiming to make that (Italy) team younger and he’s aiming to give younger players responsibility, and Romano is good enough to deal with that.



"I think he is going to go a long, long way. Again, I think if he continues playing like he does and you look at the players around him, you look at Daniel Maldini for example who’s had a great start to the season as well, Cagliari could be a surprise package this season."

Flavio Goncalves (Sporting Lisbon)

Unlike Zechiel and Romano, Flavio Goncalves has been thrown straight into the first-team at Sporting Lisbon without a loan spell elsewhere.

The 19-year-old winger was promoted from the 'B' side this summer having joined the club's academy from Rio Ave aged 13.

Goncalves has since scored three goals and added an assist in seven Liga Portugal appearances this term.



He also made his debut for Portugal's Under-21 side last month with the France-born forward also eligible for Les Bleus.

Sporting have made an unbeaten start to the new league season, sitting third behind Porto and Benfica.

Goncalves also featured in their Champions League victory over Galatasaray in September as they began their campaign in style.

Providing his thoughts on the teenager, Brassell said: "Sporting’s identity is synonymous with producing young talent and Flavio Goncalves is one of the latest.



"I say one of the latest because you look at them this season, they’ve sold a cluster of key players including Pedro Goncalves, so they’re really substituting one Goncalves for another.

"Pedro, who’s gone to Fiorentina, was more of a No.10 being pushed into an inside-left position and his close control made him make it work rather than him being a natural winger.

"Flavio Goncalves is a proper wide forward, he’s got the capacity to score a lot of goals.

6 Goncalves has already shown an eye for goal since joining the Sporting first-team Credit: Getty



"He started this season very, very well in a season where a lot of people I speak to around Sporting came into the season not expecting that much because they’ve held onto the coach Rui Borges, which I think is a huge thing, but they’re aware of the turnover of players there is.

"That some key players, and not just good players, not just great players, but leaders like Pedro Goncalves, like Morten Hjulmand have moved on and they’ve been replaced by youth.

"But this is what Sporting have done throughout their history. They’ve not got the same financial means as Benfica or Porto and they never really have."

Paris Brunner (Monaco)

Monaco striker Paris Brunner has had to wait for his opportunity at the Ligue 1 leaders until this season.



Signed from Borussia Dortmund in 2024, the forward was subsequently sent on loan to Belgian side Cercle Brugge.

After returning to Monaco, Brunner failed to score in seven Ligue 1 appearances last season.

However, he has already found the net four times in five matches under Filipe Luis this term as well as scoring twice in as many appearances in the Conference League.

The 20-year-old also scored twice on his Germany Under-21 debut against Latvia last month.



Brunner's form has helped Monaco make an unbeaten start to the season as they sit a point clear at the top of Ligue 1.

However, he missed Saturday's draw with Toulouse through suspension after receiving a two-match ban for a throat-slitting celebration against Strasbourg.

Whilst he will also be unavailable against Lorient this weekend, he can face CSKA Sofia in the Conference League on Thursday.

Addressing Brunner's rise to prominence, Brassell explained: "I think it’s a nice surprise to see Paris Brunner really hit the ground running this Ligue 1 season.



6 Brunner's fast start to the season comes two years after he first joined Monaco as a teenager Credit: AFP

"Now bear in mind that when he signed from Dortmund, their youth academy had a big reputation.

"The feeling was he was going to Monaco really as his off-ramp to one of the elite European clubs because he thought he could go all the way.

"But it’s been a couple of years of not much really and I think a lot of people thought he was going down that same route as (Pietro) Pellegri where he’s never really going to make it in the first-team.



"Then, lo and behold, you have a change in management at Monaco with Filipe Luis coming in with them losing a few players. They thought Folarin Balogun was going for example as well.

"Brunner comes in, who is still a young guy, showing all the quality and the personality to be a big player since the start of the season.

"He scored goals in volume, he scored important goals. He doesn’t have one type of goal, he’s a good finisher.

"As we saw going back to his second goal against Marseille in the 2-0 win about four or five weeks ago, he can actually beat players and create his own shot from deeper in the pitch as well, and he’s massively confident."

Sports.title: Real Madrid legend Dani Carvajal lands new club despite LaLiga complications
Sports.content:
Dani Carvajal has joined Getafe on a free transfer despite the deal facing various financial issues.

The right-back was available as a free agent having left Real Madrid in May after a trophy-laden 13-year stint with the club.



3 Carvajal was getting increasingly agitated at being left on the bench at the Bernabeu Credit: Getty

The 34-year-old's arrival at Getafe has been heavily speculated, with the club's president Angel Torres confirming the club were working on a deal.

The Spain international has signed a one-year deal and also agreed to a significant wage cut to ensure himself and his family don't have to relocate away from Madrid.

Getafe have hailed the defender as the most significant signing in their history.



A statement read: "From Getafe CF, we want to welcome Dani Carvajal and wish him much success in this new stage. Welcome to the Coliseum, Dani!"

They added: "Getafe CF has reached an agreement with Dani Carvajal, who will be linked to the club until June 30, 2027. An international player on 51 occasions with the Spanish national team and with a long career in elite football, Carvajal faces a new stage in his sporting career in the south of Madrid.



"Throughout his career, Dani Carvajal has a record of 29 titles with the Real Madrid first team and the Spanish national team, including 6 UEFA Champions League titles and the 2024 European Championship with Spain.

"The Spanish right-back begins a new stage in the Azulones team, where he will contribute experience and leadership."



Salary cap complications

A direct phone call from manager Jose Bordalas proved pivotal in convincing Carvajal to join, with the coach planning to start him at right-back or as a right-sided centre-back in a three-man defence.

The deal almost didn't happen, despite the player passing his medical.

This was due to LaLiga's salary cap rules.

3 Carvajal was also linked with a move to the Premier League to help his former teammate Alvaro Arbeloa Credit: Getty

The league's independent committee determines a player’s minimum acceptable wage based on factors such as age, career history, previous earnings and market value.



Reportedly, the Spanish top flight valued the Los Blancos legend at around £2.2million; however, Getafe originally struggled to match it, yet eventually managed to meet the Financial Fair Play criteria.

According to Spanish outlet Marca, the 34-year-old has asked for a special transfer request in his contract.

It apparently dictates that the defender can leave Getafe in January if another club submits an offer.

After visiting the training ground on Tuesday, Carvajal confirmed his happiness, and said: "I'm really looking forward to getting to work."



End of an era

The club captain announced his departure from Los Blancos in May after he decided not to renew his deal.

3 Carvajal tasted huge success in European football at Madrid as he won 26 trophies Credit: Getty

He has suffered with injury issues in recent years, including a major knee problem which naturally impacted his playing time

Additionally, the arrival of Trent Alexander-Arnold last summer ultimately limited him to only 892 minutes in LaLiga in the 2025/26 campaign.



Florentino Perez said: "Dani Carvajal is a legend and a symbol of Real Madrid and its academy.

"Carvajal has always exemplified the values of Real Madrid. This is and will always be his home."

Under managers such as Carlo Ancelotti and Zinedine Zidane, he became fundamental to Madrid's tactical structure, providing width, supporting midfield build-up play, and helping the team transition between defence and attack.

Also, he delivered important moments like his performance in the 2024 Champions League final, where he scored and was named man of the match.

Sports.title: Why Arsenal are wearing black armbands for Champions League clash against Lille
Sports.content:
Why Arsenal are wearing black armbands for Champions League clash against Lille

Arsenal's players will wear black armbands in Tuesday's home Champions League clash with Lille.

It comes following the death of the Gunners' Life President Ken Friar aged 92.

2 Ken Friar was involved with Arsenal for most of his life Credit: Getty

An Arsenal statement read: "It is with profound sadness that we announce the death of Life President Ken Friar OBE.

"Since our formation in 1886, there have been many inspirational individuals who have driven our club forward, but no one has had an influence on Arsenal Football Club quite like ‘Mr Friar’ and he leaves an extraordinary life of service to the club as his legacy. One that will surely never be matched."

Born locally in Islington, Friar's association with Arsenal dates back to 1946, when he started working for the club part-time at the age of 12.

He went on to serve as club secretary and managing director and was appointed life president in September 2020.

In 2011, a bridge connecting the Emirates Stadium to Arsenal Tube station was named in his honour.

A statue depicting a young Friar playing football outside Highbury also stands at one end of the bridge.

Mikel Arteta's side will pay tribute to Friar as they welcome Lille to the Emirates for the second game of their Champions League campaign, live on talkSPORT 2.

Arsenal kicked things off with a 1-0 win away to Napoli last month.

And they'll be hoping to finally get their hands on European club football's most prestigious trophy this time around after agonisingly losing to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties in last season's final.

Having suffered the setback of their first dropped points of the season when they lost 3-0 to Brighton in their final Premier League outing before the international break, Arsenal returned to winning ways on Saturday.

2 Arsenal got their season back on track with victory over Leeds at the weekend Credit: AFP

Riccardo Calafiori and Bruno Guimaraes scored as the Gunners recovered from 1-0 to beat Leeds 2-1 at the Emirates.

Speaking ahead of the visit of Lille, Arteta urged his team to take emotional control on the pitch.

"We have to be emotionally dominant regardless of what the context is," he said. "It's easy to say, very difficult actually to do.

"We did it in the majority of the matches, which is great. We didn't do it in Brighton and we paid the price for that.

"There are always lessons and evolutions to make for the team and that's something extremely important because at the level that we played every three days, things will happen and you're going to have to be able to adapt and resolve those ones."

This will be the first-ever meeting between Arsenal and Lille.

Sports.title: ‘Cheating is cheating’ – Simon Jordan hits back at Jamie Carragher over response to ‘hypocrite’ claim
Sports.content:
‘Cheating is cheating’ – Simon Jordan hits back at Jamie Carragher over response to ‘hypocrite’ claim

Simon Jordan warned Jamie Carragher he is 'not beyond reproach' after the Liverpool icon didn't take kindly to being labelled a 'hypocrite'.

Jordan branded Carragher as such after a clip of the latter stating he'd cheat to win went viral.

2 Carragher has been extremely vocal about City needing to be sanctioned Credit: Getty

In the video, which stemmed from a podcast appearance on the Diary of a CEO in 2022, Carragher said: "I'd rather cheat and win than not win."

Carragher's resurfaced comments generated a social storm given how strong he has been on Manchester City after they were found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

The Reds great has called for City's owners to be turfed out and all the honours won in the period they committed the alleged breaches to be stripped.

Simon Jordan labels Jamie Carragher a 'hypocrite'

After hearing the clip involving Carragher, ex-Crystal Palace owner Jordan claimed the former defender had been caught in a 'hypocritical moment' .

However, Jordan believed it should not detract from the ex-defender's verdict on City's financial crimes.

"He'll feel that perhaps he shouldn't have said that," Jordan said on Tuesday's edition of White and Jordan.

"I think it doesn't alter the fact that what he is saying about Man City has resonance.

"Most people in life are hypocrites, they might just not choose to admit it. He's been caught in a hypocritical moment.

Carragher responded to Jordan's claims, just one hour after a clip of the ex-Palace owner's verdict was shared on X.

Jamie Carragher's response to Simon Jordan

"No it's not hypocritical," Carragher wrote.

2 Relegation, stripping of titles and hefty points deductions have all been mooted as potential City punishments Credit: Getty

"I'm talking about my striker diving for a penalty, me stopping a ball going over the line with my hand.

"I'm not talking about 900m in fake sponsorship over a number of years."

Although Jordan admitted on-field and off-field matters should be judged 'in different ways', he cautioned Carragher about continually beating the drum about City given his previous comments.

Simon Jordan: 'Cheating is cheating'

"If you're going to make imperious judgements, then you need to be beyond reproach," Jordan said.

"And if you're not beyond reproach because you've opened your mouth previously and said something I think was silly for Jamie... he has been caught in a hypocritical moment.

"I also went on to say that it doesn't alter what he's saying about Man City."

Jordan added: "Cheating is cheating. If you want to be judge, jury and executioner, and as much as it sticks in my craw, without allowing Manchester City due process, then expect to be judged by the standards you are wanting others to be judged by."

Sports.title: Lamine Yamal is not the most important player at Barcelona – on or off the pitch
Sports.content:
Lamine Yamal is not the most important player at Barcelona – on or off the pitch

Lamine Yamal may be a serious contender to win the Ballon d'Or, but that doesn't make him Barcelona's most prized asset.

Instead, European football expert Andy Brassell believes that honour belongs to Raphinha.

3 Raphinha has now scored just shy of 90 goals for Barca since he moved from Leeds Credit: Getty

The Brazilian leads LaLiga's goalscoring charts with an impressive haul of 12 goals from just seven fixtures.

He also bagged a double against Feyenoord in Barcelona's Champions League opener.

However, he was rested for Barcelona's 3-0 win over Getafe on Saturday and will miss the Champions League clash against Galatasaray on Tuesday.

The decision was made by Barca boss Hansi Flick after Raphinha picked up a thigh injury on international duty for Brazil.

"The tests show something," Flick said.

"It's not a serious injury, but we have to be careful because he had three injuries last year, and we have to take care of him."

Why Andy Brassell believes Raphinha is Barca's most important star

With fixtures against Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain to come later in October, Flick will hope his cautious approach with Raphinha, who turns 30 in December, can bear fruit.

For Brassell, Flick's decision also underlines the high regard in which the Brazilian is held at the club.

"Hansi Flick has been clear to say that he's not injured, he's just too valuable to us to muck about with," Brassell told talkSPORT.com.

"They've just extended his contract to 2030. He is their most important player, I would say, ahead of Lamine Yamal even, on and off the field."

3 Flick is hoping to lead Barcelona to a third consecutive LaLiga crown Credit: Getty

Key tactical tweak behind Raphinha's stunning numbers

Key to Raphinha's blistering goalscoring form this season has been his shift to a central striker role compared to his usual left wing position.

Barcelona had a serious hole to fill up top following Robert Lewandowski's departure at the end of last season.

The Spanish giants attempted to replace Lewandowski with Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez, but their efforts proved futile.

But Raphinha has seamlessly slotted into the position and it's proved to be a masterstroke from Flick.

How good has Lamine Yamal been this season?

Despite Raphinha's blistering start to the season, most of the spotlight remains firmly on teenage whiz Yamal.

Fresh after helping Spain win the World Cup, Yamal has eight goals and seven assists for Barcelona.

3 Yamal is the youngest player ever to debut for Barcelona Credit: AFP

Flick is evidently keen to maximise Yamal's youthful energy, having started him in all of Barcelona's fixtures this term.

Yamal's brilliance could soon be recognised with his first Ballon d'Or, with the winner to be named on October 26.

It is shaping up to be a two-horse race between Yamal and Harry Kane for football's most coveted individual prize.

Should Yamal win, he'd become the youngest player to win the Ballon d'Or while Kane is aiming to become the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to claim the gong.

Sports.title: Why Man City players should celebrate as much as they like despite rivals' demands to cower in shame for the 'sin' of winning a match - and how they're turning abuse into fuel
Sports.content:
Why Man City players should celebrate as much as they like despite rivals' demands to cower in shame for the 'sin' of winning a match - and how they're turning abuse into fuel

Antoine Semenyo has put his journey to the top of European football down to journaling. Scribbling stuff down, manifesting every goal and target since the age of 14. It’s safe to say that the circumstances around the past fortnight will not have made it into those notebooks.

Semenyo and his Manchester City team-mates didn’t account for this. It’s beyond their wildest nightmares, chastised as cheats for crimes committed before their time. Semenyo was eight years old when Sheikh Mansour completed his takeover.

There has been a prevailing wind of anger blowing towards these players since Sunday. Since their temerity to beat Liverpool and since their further unforgivable sin of basking in that feat once the whistle blew at Anfield. Rayan Cherki puffed his chest out, you know. Erling Haaland smirked at some fans waving bananas. Others shook their fists. One even shouted.

And their manager. What can be said of Enzo Maresca? He only went and danced down the touchline and stuck two fingers in his ears. Risible arrogance of a man who, whether the critics like it or not, might just be using the guilty verdicts and deluge of condemnation as a motivational tool. Because that is what football people do.

‘Criticised for what?’ Maresca said of commentators launching rebukes in their direction. He looked genuinely surprised. ‘We won 3-0 at Anfield! What do you want us to do? And even if it was 0-1, it would be exactly the same.

‘The rest? It's just things from outside that we need to deal with, but we were so, so happy inside the pitch, and you cannot imagine inside the changing room.’

There has been a prevailing wind of anger blowing towards City's players since Sunday. Since their temerity to beat Liverpool and their unforgivable sin of basking in that feat

What can be said of Enzo Maresca? He only went and danced down the touchline. Risible arrogance of a man who might just be using the guilty verdicts as a motivational tool

Having built Anfield up as the worst possible assignment for City’s first public outing since the independent commission handed down their judgment, attention immediately shifted as Maresca’s squad passed the test and then some.

Shifted to this unreasonable clamour for footballers to temper emotions for the demands of a section of the watching public – of course ignoring a sizeable number who support clubs lower down the EFL, who accepted that the Premier League ate itself long ago and are far more pre-occupied by the concept of Wrexham’s rapid rise through the divisions.

Shifted to this clamour to bow their heads in sorrow, to demonstrate embarrassment, to cower in shame as they simultaneously have the executives who pay their wages telling them in no uncertain terms that the club will have findings overturned on appeal.

The idea of that happening right now looks remote but the prospects of points deductions or worse cannot be in the minds of a group of young men whose sole aim now is to beat Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday night and continue a flawless start to the season on the pitch.

‘We’ll celebrate however we feel in the moment,’ captain Ruben Dias said. ‘It’ll be a show of how much things mean to us. Yes, there is a lot of noise and it’s almost impossible to not see something – even us being so private. But I feel like we’re also very good at focusing on ourselves.

‘We had conversations for everyone to be on the same page and be clear about our peace of mind. You build yourself against any kind of noise. I feel like I speak for the whole group when I say we’re very calm. We trust the club. We know the team we’ve got and want to win. It’s the same noise as before because people don’t love us.’

Dias hit upon something there. They very much do not love City and have not done for decades, when the club was more slapstick – regularly grasping defeat from the jaws of victory – and threw David James up as a striker and had furry mascots in the dugout for good luck.

They’ve never loved them because of the winning and the money and the sense of ill-gotten gains. So quite why Dias – who signed six years ago – cannot lead a charge of resistance against those who have never liked them anyway is anybody’s guess. What he effectively relayed during media duties ahead of PSG was that this is nothing particularly new to him.

‘Criticised for what?’ Maresca said of commentators launching rebukes in their direction. He looked genuinely surprised. ‘We won 3-0 at Anfield! What do you want us to do?'
