World.title: ‘Act five’: National Assembly opens budget debate amid ongoing student protests in France
World.content:
Another major day of demonstrations got underway in France on Tuesday, with students and trade unions taking to the streets to protest education conditions and funding as the National Assembly began its debate on the government's budget proposals for 2027.

 

Teaching unions told Euronews that they were dissatisfied with the government's response to concerns over long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down facilities, and teacher absences.

"It is clear that the responses that have been provided are inadequate and do not meet the needs set out," Elisabeth Allain-Moreno, secretary-general of SE UNSA, a teachers' union, said.

France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced on 8 October that 3,000 available supply teachers would be deployed across more than 500 priority schools by Tuesday in a bid to solve teacher absences.

On Tuesday, he announced that just 35% of the target had been achieved.

"We have a generation that is articulating demands that we identified years ago, which we have been advocating for and were never heard," Morgane Verviers, secretary-general of UNSA Education, told Euronews.

"It's clear that the responses provided are inadequate and don't meet the needs set out," Moreno added.

Budget proposal under fire

The government's budget proposal includes a €1.2 billion increase in funding for the National Education Ministry, as France grapples with one of the highest public deficits in the eurozone.

However, critics say this measure is insufficient, arguing that a 1.6% increase in funding falls short of inflation, which is forecast at 1.8%.

Sabrine Kharbach, a spokesperson for l'Union Etudiante, France's biggest student union, said she felt the government had underestimated students' ability to understand budget matters.

"They believe that students and young people are not aware of the economy and don't understand what's happening. But we truly understand, when we see that there's an additional $400 billion being allocated to the military," Kharbach told Euronews. France's government has allocated a total budget of €413.3 billion to its armed forces for 2024 to 2030 under its Military Programming Law (LPM).

"We have to ask ourselves if they want to invest in death or in the future," she added.

One secondary school student said she felt her generation was not being taken seriously, despite being the "future of France."

"We can't turn a blind eye to issues, especially in secondary schools in the suburbs, which really lack funding," she said.

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg also joined Tuesday's protests, telling the AFP news agency that "young people are not being included in the conversation."

"Our future is being robbed away from us," she added.

Thunberg's visit to France comes after French students' grievance struck a chord with young people across Europe, leading students in Belgium and Italy to stage their own demonstrations over the past week.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party, was also among those who joined the protests.

Taking to X on 8 October, he declared that the Bastille had been "retaken" after a mass protest on Paris' Place de la Bastille captured audiences worldwide.

Police violence sparks outrage

France's protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September, before rapidly spreading nationwide.

While many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by sideline riots and clashes with police.

Rights groups have accused officers of exercising disproportionate force whilst dealing with protesters following a wave of injuries to students.

According to figures shared by France's Ministry of Justice on Friday, there have been 6,877 arrests since the beginning of the movement, mostly involving minors.

More than 215 students and nearly 800 police officers have also been injured.

World.title: Russia funnels nearly half its budget into defence, cutting social spending
World.content:
Russia's parliament will vote later this month on a budget that allocates a record 44% of federal spending to defence and security — double the share for social programmes — as the Kremlin presses ahead with a fifth year of all-out war in Ukraine.

 

The State Duma, Russia's lower house of parliament, is due to begin examining the 2027–2029 draft on 22 October.

President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party won an absolute constitutional majority in September's parliamentary elections, making major amendments unlikely before it passes.

Military expenditure this year has reached 17 trillion roubles (€181 billion) against the 12.1 trillion (€129 billion) originally budgeted, showing the escalating cost of the full-scale invasion Russia launched against Ukraine in February 2022. Defence and security's 44% share of the 2027 budget is the highest on record.

The Finance Ministry's draft lists "fulfilling social obligations to citizens" as its top priority. The figures tell a different story. Social policy spending will fall 7% in 2027, from 7.1 trillion roubles (€76 billion) to 6.65 trillion (€71 billion), covering pensions, payments to veterans, maternity benefits and other support.

The government has pledged to index these payments against inflation. Russia's official inflation rate has exceeded 8% for much of the past two years, and independent economists put the real figure higher.

The Kremlin has announced a 10 trillion rouble (€107 billion) "children's budget" over the next three years, covering maternity payments, child benefits, and housing programmes. The ratio of those funds to defence spending is one to five.

Federal payments to servicemen and their families fall under the "national defence" section, whose spending will rise by roughly a quarter next year.

War at the expense of orphans and the poor

The federal budget is not the only source of pressure on social spending. Russia's regions partly fund war-related payments, many of which are already running deficits, forcing local authorities to cut civilian budgets.

In late September the Arkhangelsk region redirected more than 63 million roubles originally earmarked for social support — two-thirds from payments to foster parents, the rest from support for large families — to one-off war payments and death compensation.

A few days earlier the Tula region cut 54 million roubles from spending on foster children, low-income households, families with disabled children, housing repairs for orphans and support for labour veterans, redirecting the sum to servicemen's pay and compensation for the dead.

In St Petersburg, authorities have prepared a bill reducing spending on education, transport repairs and medical projects while increasing payments to servicemen.

'Coffin money' being cut

Regional lump-sum death payments — known informally as "coffin money" — have been cut across Russia since autumn of last year.

The payments are regional supplements to the federal one-time compensation paid to families of troops killed in action, and regions sharply raised them in 2022–2023 as they competed to attract recruits.

In Ulyanovsk region the payment stood at 1 million roubles (€10,700). By February it had been halved, then cut again to 50,000 roubles (€533).

In Bashkortostan, the initial 2 million roubles (€21,300) payment has fallen to no more than 100,000 (€1,100).

Kirov and Omsk regions have halved payments from 1 million to 500,000 roubles (€5,300). In Kemerovo the payment went down from 3 million to 1 million. In Saratov, families who received 1 million roubles until late September now receive a tenth of that.

The sums attracted fraud. In Primorsky Krai, a warrant officer was alleged to have arranged marriages between contract soldiers heading to the front and local women, with the compensation shared among participants if the men were killed.

In Khabarovsk, authorities detained six people in February on suspicion of orchestrating similar arrangements, using notarised powers of attorney to access soldiers’ bank accounts, with alleged damages reaching 2.4 million roubles (€25,600).

Some families receive nothing at all. Soldiers classified by the military as missing or as deserters rather than confirmed dead are ineligible for the one-time payment. Relatives of those killed say the designation is used to withhold compensation.

Healthcare insignificant

Healthcare spending will fall to 7 trillion roubles (€75 billion) next year, a 6.8% reduction according to calculations by independent Russian media, though the Finance Ministry disputes the figure.

Over the three-year period, healthcare will receive 28.6 trillion roubles (€305 billion) against 50 trillion roubles (€533 billion) for the military.

Funding for ambulance services has been cut by more than a quarter. The programme to build and repair outpatient clinics in the regions has been halved.

The national cancer programme will receive 3.9 billion roubles in 2027, down from 44.9 billion this year.

World.title: Women with autoimmune diseases face longer waits and more misdiagnoses than men
World.content:
Women are disproportionately affected by autoimmune diseases — conditions in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's healthy cells and tissues. Yet a new study has found they are significantly more likely than men to face prolonged diagnostic journeys, with nearly a third of surveyed women waiting four years or longer for a diagnosis.

 

While nearly half of men are diagnosed within a year of symptom onset, most women face longer delays, with 60.4% waiting more than a year for a correct diagnosis.

Such “stark” differences suggest that “historical gender biases remain a challenging aspect of the diagnostic journey,” said Shaista Tayabali, co-author of the study, with possible reasons including historical biases, limited research on women’s health, and sex-biased data feeding machine learning models.

Women account for 70% to 80% of autoimmune disease cases worldwide, with the most common conditions being type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, systemic lupus and multiple sclerosis.

While women suffer from autoimmune diseases more than men, their diagnosis takes longer.

“Although labels such as hysteria are outdated, and fortunately rarely used nowadays, as women we still often have a harder time having our symptoms believed and therefore addressed accurately,” said Tayabali.

The study analysed more than 6,000 patients with a wide range of autoimmune diseases. Participants were asked how long it took to receive a diagnosis from symptom onset, how many healthcare consultations they had, and which diagnoses they received before their autoimmune one.

Symptoms dismissed as psychological

Doctors often take symptoms such as fatigue, pain, sleep disturbance or low mood as psychosomatic or psychiatric without considering autoimmune diseases at first, which can lead to longer waiting times, untreated conditions and loss of trust in the healthcare system.

“Clinicians must be open-minded,” said David D’Cruz, consultant rheumatologist at Guy’s Hospital in London, calling on them to “consider whether there is an underlying autoimmune disease that has not yet been recognised – and to listen to patients”.

One of the reasons for long waiting times is that women were more likely than men to have their symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic, meaning that physicians believe symptoms are caused or worsened by psychological factors. This was reported by 34% of women compared with 22% of men.

The researchers also found that females were almost 50% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis and nearly 75% more likely to report a psychosomatic misdiagnosis than males.

“This is not about saying that a psychiatric diagnosis is never correct,” added D’Cruz. “People can have both autoimmune and psychiatric conditions, and it is increasingly understood that psychiatric symptoms can be part of an autoimmune disease, especially in diseases like lupus which can directly affect the brain.”

World.title: US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns
World.content:
US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle has resigned from her role following a series of allegations about her conduct.

 

"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," she wrote in a lengthy post on social media on Tuesday.

New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia said earlier in the day that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign.

"We have asked ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia told reporters.

The move follows a series of articles published in the Wall Street Journal alleging questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including a threat against a Greek official, the acceptance of inappropriate gifts and services, as well as an offer to use her influence within the administration in exchange for the settlement of a large credit card bill.

In her post on Tuesday, Guilfoyle said she also wanted to "address the recent allegations against me."

"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote. "I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

US President Donald Trump had said on Monday that his administration was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle and that they were "not happy" with the situation.

Guilfoyle previously responded to the allegations against her through her lawyers, rejecting claims made by American businessman and former political candidate Eric Deters.

The statement said that Deters owed her around $150,000 for speeches and consulting services and that Guilfoyle had previously turned down a $1 million proposal from Deters to promote a private legal case.

Regarding accusations of accepting gifts and travelling on private jets, her lawyers argued that the ambassador had requested and received guidance from the State Department and had fully complied with ethics rules and provisions governing the acceptance of gifts.

World.title: How will emergency rule in Pakistan's KP affect Afghan ties?
World.content:
Pakistan's decision to suspend Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's provincial government could further strain already tense relations between Islamabad and Kabul.

Pakistan on Sunday announced that the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's federal government defended the move, saying the provincial administration — led by imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party — was working "hand in glove" with the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

"The PTI government in the province has not equipped the police and security forces to counter militancy. Instead, they have links with TTP and did not cooperate with the federal government to fight terrorism," Talal Chaudhry, minister of state for interior affairs, told DW.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the government had "solid evidence" to support its allegations, the Associated Press news agency reported.

He said the suspension and imposition of a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would allow security forces and the new administration to better coordinate efforts to combat terrorism.

The move comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.

But the federal government has denied that its action was driven by domestic politics.

Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A stronghold of Imran Khan's PTI

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months, is a political stronghold of former PM Khan.

The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his supporters say are politically motivated.

His PTI party had long governed the volatile province, but Islamabad's decision to impose emergency rule has now effectively removed it from power.

Pakistan's constitution ​allows the federal government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency.

Islamabad said Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would now be administered directly by a new governor, assisted by an advisory council. This arrangement will initially be in place for six months, but could be extended for as long as necessary, authorities said.

Is governor rule the solution?

Khan's party has lambasted the suspension of the provincial government.

"This is more a coup disguised as emergency and governor rule," said PTI spokesperson Sayed Zulfikar Bukhari.

It has also sparked questions about provincial autonomy and the future of civilian rule, with critics warning that the abrupt removal of an elected administration risks weakening accountability and deepening political divisions.

"Governor's rule should only be imposed in extreme constitutional crises, not political disputes, and its legality should be reviewed by the Constitutional Court," Osama Malik, a senior constitutional expert, told DW.

"While it may temporarily reduce militant attacks, lasting security requires political engagement and stronger civilian law enforcement," he added.

Why Pakistan is fighting the Taliban it once backed To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Raja Qaiser Ahmed, assistant professor of regional security and foreign affairs at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, echoed this view.

"Federal rule can never be a substitute for an elected political authority. The argument of provincial autonomy would also definitely surface amidst this uncharacteristic measure taken," he told DW.

"It may, though, streamline coordination between the federal government and the province, which was a missing link for quite some time."

Surging militancy poses acute security challenges

Pakistan has seen a surge in militant violence in recent years.

Authorities have recorded more than 2,800 militant attacks since January, which have killed or wounded about 3,000 people, according to the AP news agency.

Islamabad blames Afghan-based elements for the attacks and has accused the ruling Taliban of allowing Afghan territory to be used to harbor militants.

Pakistan wants Kabul to clamp down on the TTP, which is a separate group but closely linked to the Afghan Taliban. The TTP seeks to impose a hard-line interpretation of Islam, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

"We have been asking Kabul to recognize terrorists as terrorists and take action against them. They must do so because their own peace, security, and future are linked to Pakistan," asserted Chaudhry, the deputy interior minister.

The Afghan Taliban deny the allegations and say they cannot be held accountable for security incidents inside Pakistan.

How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Will it escalate the Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict?

The dispute has fueled growing tensions between the neighbors, which have escalated into armed clashes in recent months, heightening fears of a wider confrontation.

Ahmed believes the suspension of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's provincial government is likely to aggravate tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan.

"Security measures taken in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would further impinge on the Pakistan-Afghan relationship, which is seemingly locked in a protracted cycle of offense and escalation," said Ahmed.

After announcing emergency rule, Islamabad also authorized the deployment of additional army troops and military equipment to the region to support authorities.

Ayesha Siddiqa, an independent military and security analyst, warned that the suspension of the elected provincial government could complicate counterterrorism efforts by deepening resentment among local communities.

"After ending the political government, I don't think the security situation will improve. In fact, there will be less willingness among local communities to support counterterrorism operations," she told DW.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: Saudi Arabia's military struggle against Houthi attacks
World.content:
Houthi attacks on airports and energy facilities are putting Saudi Arabia under pressure. Could a Saudi-led international military offensive succeed against the Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen?

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militia continues to escalate its attacks on Saudi Arabia targeting energy facilities but, above all, airports.

On Saturday, a missile attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300. In a second attack on Sunday, the militia killed another civilian and injured 11 others.

According to their own statements, the Houthis also attacked Saudi Arabia's airport in Dammam and two oil facilities within the past 24 hours. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud warned of the consequences for energy security and announced a strong response.

According to a report by the US think tank American Enterprise Institute, Saudi Arabia is targeting Houthi missile launch pads, storage facilities and other military infrastructure in Yemen. The institute quotes Saudi military spokesman Turki al-Maliki in its October 11 report as saying that 136 military targets have already been destroyed.

However, years of Saudi-led military intervention between 2015 and 2022 in Yemen have not succeeded in defeating the Houthi militia. Moreover, the Saudi-led international coalition formed in 2015 has fallen apart and the United Arab Emirates has withdrawn its troops.

The Iran-aligned Houthis not only control large parts of northern Yemen but also increasingly the western coastline from where they disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea and the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait. In early September, drones also severely damaged the Saudi East-West oil pipeline. The temporary shutdown disrupted oil exports and increased risks for the energy markets.

Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saudi Arabia calls on Pakistan, Turkey, the United States

For weeks, the Saudi government has been seeking allies in the fight against the Houthi militia. In late September, the United Kingdom and France pledged military support to defend Saudi infrastructure. London offered aerial refueling for Saudi fighter jets, while Paris announced it would provide troops, radar systems and air defense technology to protect the Yanbu oil terminal.

However, while the US recently refused to fight alongside Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, there could now be a change of heart in Washington, writes political analyst Osamah Al-Rawhani in a study by the Yemeni think tank Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies.

He notes that it remains to be seen whether this could actually lead to a successful offensive, as holding on to captured territories and launching counterattacks require significant financial resources, political commitment and the necessary resolve.

In his view, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia would be able to muster the necessary perseverance. The kingdom could, however, change its current strategy. "If the costs of the war continue to rise, Riyadh might look for a way to withdraw from the conflict," Al-Rawhani says.

Observers note that Saudi Arabia is facing an asymmetrical war as the Houthis don't need to win militarily for disrupting Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 and oil exports Image: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Saudi Arabia's asymmetrical war against the Houthis

Marcus Schneider, project manager at the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Center of Expertise on Peace and Security in the Middle East and North Africa, shares a similar view.

"To eliminate the Houthis, ground troops would be needed but Riyadh has no experience with this type of warfare, especially in a foreign country," Schneider recently told DW. As such, he believes the Saudi leadership is less concerned with achieving a military victory than with reducing its vulnerability, securing the broadest possible coalition of partners and gaining political maneuvering room.

"The Houthis are well-entrenched in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows. Above all, Saudi Arabia needs stability for its Vision 2030 reform set and that is currently further away than ever," Schneider said.

He added that military asymmetry is also a key factor: Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. The Houthis, on the other hand, do not need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to deploy missiles and drones, threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping traffic.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (C) is hoping for military support by his defense allies Pakistan and Turkey Image: Turkish Presidency/UPI Photo/newscom/picture alliance

Are the UAE, Pakistan, Turkey changing course?

Saudi Arabia may also be able to turn to another partner in the region: the United Arab Emirates (UAE). According to media reports, Anwar Gargash, a senior diplomatic advisor to the UAE president, spoke out in favor of closer security cooperation among the Gulf states. "We are all targets," he stated on X.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have undermined the security of the entire region, he notes. "It is necessary to revitalize cooperation among the Gulf states, particularly in the areas of security and defense, and to strengthen the collective security system," Gargash added.

Pakistan, which signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in early August along with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, also initially ruled out military intervention.

According to media reports, however, the country is now said to be carrying out airstrikes on Houthi missile and drone positions — a claim that Islamabad denies. Pakistan does not intend to deploy ground troops. Turkey, another member of the Mecca Pact, rules out an offensive military operation but is providing air defense equipment.

Saudi Arabia can thus build on additional military support, according to an analysis by the US think tank Soufan Center. Whether this will result in an effective strategy, however, depends on whether the partners go beyond limited airstrikes and political expressions of solidarity and on whether the fragmented Yemeni government forces can better coordinate their military operations.

Meanwhile, Iran has offered to act as a mediator between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. However, given Iran's support for the Houthis and the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia will accept this offer.

Saudi Arabia and the US are allies, whereas Iran and the US have been at war since February. It is also unclear whether Tehran wields sufficient influence over the Yemeni militia to persuade it to halt the attacks.

World.title: Kimberly Guilfoye : US ambassador to Greece resigns amid misconduct allegations
World.content:
Kimberly Guilfoyle has resigned as US ambassador to Greece. President Trump previously said he was unhappy with her amid reports of a bribery scandal and ethics violations.

Kimberly Guilfoyle has stepped down as US ambassador to Greece.

White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia earlier told reporters that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign, calling her "an incredible asset to the team."

Zacharia, continued by adding, "we wish her well," though did not say whether she had already stepped down.

Guilfoyle's position became untenable after the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on her supposed threats against Greece and her acceptance of improper gifts. Most recently, WSJ published an article with screenshots of text messages documenting her attempts to receive cash from a Republican donor in exchange for influence in the Trump administration.

Trump before firing: 'We're not happy'

The past week has seen much speculation as to whether Guilfolyle would have to go, with the Associated Press (AP) revealing that President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" over the former Fox News host's conduct.

On Monday, Trump said "we're looking at it" when asked if Guilfoyle could be fired, adding, "we're not happy."

Rubio initially defended Guilfoyle and continued to do so in Greece last week, saying, "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

Ultimately, however, he lashed out at journalists for asking about the allegations against Guilfoyle, accusing them of seeing their own reporting as "gospel" and insisting that he would not comment until he knew the whole story.

There have been mixed reports suggesting that the State Department's investigator general might look into the matter, though this has not yet been confirmed.

Top Democrats in the House of Representatives and the Senate have called for investigations.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reportedly 'extremely pissed off' at Guilfoyle over embarrassing allegations tied to accusations of attempted influence peddling Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

Guilfoyle calls posting 'honor of a lifetime,' vows to 'defend reputation'

After news broke of Guilfoyle's fall from grace within the White House, she released a lengthy post on X, lauding her own performance and calling her posting to Athens "the honor of a lifetime" as well as thanking Trump and Rubio for putting their trust in her.

Guilfoyle also said she wanted to, "address the recent allegations against me," writing: "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

Her most vocal accuser, Eric Deters, has vowed to sue Guilfoyle and her attorneys for defamation over her denials of wrongdoing in dealings with him.

What exactly is Guilfoyle accused of?

Guilfoyle, a TV personality who was formerly married to California Governor Gavin Newsom and later engaged to Trump's eldest son Don Jr., has been accused of numerous improprieties during her tenure in Greece.

Greece is an important NATO ally for the US, especially in the Eastern Mediterranean and in terms of Red Sea shipping security.

Among other things, she is said to have bragged about luxury travel and the perks of chumming with energy company executives before threatening that the US could easily undermine Greek democracy if it did not get what it wanted from the host country.

She also appeared to favor shady deals with individual Greek construction and energy company execs, going so far as to bring their lobbyists to top-level diplomatic meetings.

Guilfoyle was further reported to have alienated embassy staffers with her behavior and reportedly exploded after not being invited to a Greek-themed event at this year's World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, demanding she be allowed to attend.

The straw that broke the camel's back, however, was a media offensive started by GOP donor Eric Deters, who grew weary of Guilfoyle's insistence that he pay off her credit card in exchange for influence that she had been unable to deliver.

Deters began doing media interviews with any outlet that would listen after the WSJ story broke, publishing embarrassing text chains in which Guilfoyle implored him to transfer $100,000 (€89, 400) to her American Express card, writing, "Honey please, I need you to get this done for me today."

Deters, who said he had already paid her $300,000 and had gotten nothing in return, told numerous US media outlets the deal was "absolutely a quid pro quo" and that he had warned Guilfoyle that he would go public about their dealings if she could not rectify the situation.

World.title: Hungary's parliament votes to reverse anti-LGBTQ legislation from Orban era
World.content:
Hungary's parliament passed a bill amending the 2021 "child protection law." The move is considered the first significant reversal of Orban's curbs targeting the LGBTQ+ community.

Hungary's parliament on Tuesday passed a bill amending a 2021 law targeting the LGBTQ+ community that was passed under nationalist ex-leader Viktor Orban.

The 2021 "child protection" law introduced restrictions on the "portrayal" or "promotion" of sexual and gender diversity in content accessible to children. In reality, this meant that even books addressing these topics in an age-appropriate manner could only be sold in black plastic packaging with warnings.

Critics argued that the law promoted the bigoted view automatically linking homosexuality and child abuse. The European Court of Justice had also ruled in April that it violated EU treaties.

Tuesday's amendment repeals most of the statute, except the provision protecting under-18s from sexually explicit or violent material. It passed with the support of the governining majorty, with 139 lawmakers voting for in favor and 51 against.

Will Hungary's new govt. bring real change on LGBTQ+ rights? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What brought about this change?

Hungary's longtime Prime Minister Viktor Orban was voted out of office in April. While his successor Peter Magyar is also a conservative and an immigration hardliner, he promised to break with Orban's repressive policies on media, the judiciary, and other issues.

Magyar has promised to dismantle what he calls the rampant corruption and authoritarian structures put in place under Orban's government.

"We welcome this important signal of commitment for our common values," EU commissioners Michael McGrath and Hadja Lahbib said in a joint statement. The bloc then unfroze €4.2 billion ($4.7 billion) in funding to Hungary following the vote.

World.title: DR Congo: Kabila’s move towards M23 raises questions over peace
World.content:
Former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila has joined a new political-military front that brings together the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 coalition. Analysts say it could reshape opposition to President Felix Tshisekedi.

Joseph Kabila's decision to lead a new political-military movement, the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), puts the former president of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in more direct confrontation with President Felix Tshisekedi's government. Kabila announced the FRN on October 12 in Goma, eastern DRC, at his residence, where leaders of the AFC/M23 rebel movements joined him.

FRN coalition adviser, Claude Ibalanky, said the group would unite opposition forces, including figures associated with the AFC/M23 movement. The new structure succeeds the Congo River Alliance (AFC), which had been allied with the M23 rebellion. Its leadership includes former AFC leader Corneille Nangaa and M23 political leader Bertrand Bisimwa. Sultani Makenga, a senior M23 military commander, was also assigned a senior role in the new organization.

The announcement comes as diplomatic initiatives seek to end fighting between Congolese government forces and the rebellion.

Congolese authorities have accused Kabila of supporting the insurgency, allegations he has denied. On September 30, 2025, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia after convicting him of treason, war crimes and other offenses linked to the conflict in eastern DRC. Kabila has rejected the case as politically motivated.

Adolph Amisi Makutano, an official of the ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS), criticized the former president for taking a more public role.

"It was a lack of courage that made this gentleman drag his feet. They held several meetings and today he is being pushed to step out into the open. But it is a disgrace for the DRC," Makutano said.

Why is eastern Congo at war?

Eastern DRC has experienced decades of conflict involving armed groups, competition over territory andmineral resources, and tensions with neighboring countries.

The aftermath of Rwanda's 1994 genocide against the Tutsicontributed to successive regional conflicts, as armed groups and refugees crossed borders and neighboring states became involved in Congo's civil wars.

7 reasons why eastern DR Congo remains stuck in conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

M23 takes its name from a March 23, 2009, peace agreement. The movement says the Congolese government failed to honor commitments to integrate its fighters and protect minority Congolese Tutsis.

Kinshasa, the United Nations (UN) and Western governments haveaccused Rwanda of supporting M23 and exercising influence over its operations. Rwanda denies backing the rebellion and cites security threats posed by armed groups operating in Congo. In 2025, M23 captured Goma and Bukavu, two major cities in eastern Congo. Its territorial gains weakened government control across parts of the region, displaced civilians and intensified an already severe humanitarian crisis.

Kabila's leadership of the new front raises questions about whether he intends to consolidate opposition to Tshisekedi, strengthen the rebellion's political leadership, or pursue both.

Political implications of Kabila's move

Alex Vines, Africa program director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, sees the move as evidence that Kabila remains politically ambitious. "It shows Kabila's political ambition is alive and kicking and he is prepared to challenge Tshisekedi," Vines told DW.

Why are tensions rising in the Democratic Republic of Congo? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Timo Roujean, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's office in Kinshasa, cautioned against assessing Kabila's potential support based on ethnic identity alone. He told DW that economic performance and political dynamics in Kabila's home region of Katanga are also relevant.

The new front could give the movement more explicitly political leadership, but it remains unclear whether the reorganization will broaden its domestic support or alter its negotiating position. Conflict analyst Cliffton Chifuwe told DW the alliance does not rule out a negotiated settlement, but could make a durable agreement harder to achieve.

"The Kabila alliance with M23 does not make peace impossible. However, it raises the threshold for achieving that settlement and its ability to hold," Chifuwe told DW.

For Chifuwe, lasting peace requires more than a cessation of hostilities. It also depends on credible security arrangements, the restoration of state authority, humanitarian access, and conditions that allow displaced people to return safely. The new FRN coalition also raises questions for mediators about whether existing peace frameworks can accommodate the political realignment and whether the parties involved can ensure compliance with any agreement.

As this new development plays out, the central issue for civilians in eastern Congo remains whether the leadership change will open a path to settlement or make an already complex conflict harder to resolve.

Wendy Bashi, Saleh Mwanamilongo and Jean Noel Ba Mweze contributed to this article

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

World.title: India: Can 'cockroaches' threaten Modi's political grip?
World.content:
Thousands detained, leaders arrested on arrival, and a capital under lockdown: The youth-led protests against the election chief have the attention of the Indian government. But experts say toppling it is another matter.

India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) may have anticipated pushback from the government after its first round of protests in July, but the scale of barricading and detentions that greeted its leaders in a fortress-like New Delhi on October 10 was unlike anything they had anticipated.

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In its latest round of agitation, they are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were reportedly removed from electoral rolls nationwide.

What happened over the weekend?

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, accompanied by co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, was detained from the plane in which he landed in the national capital on Saturday.

Meanwhile, police were stationed outside the homes of several other faces associated with the movement, including social media personality Dhruv Rathee, who has nearly 20 million followers on Instagram.

In central Delhi, buses were loaded with protesters, many of whom were taken to far-flung centers, where they were kept for hours. According to local media, at least 3,000 people were detained across the city.

How the government is handling the protests

The protests come as Modi marks 25 uninterrupted years leading elected governments, first in Gujarat state as chief minister and then as prime minister of India.

Ironically, "this celebration has happened at the time when he's politically at his weakest," Delhi-based writer Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told DW. Mukhopadhyay is the author of Modi's 2013 biography "Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times."

Over 30,000 security personnel were deployed ahead of the October 10 protest Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

He contrasted the government's current response with its approach in July, when thousands of young protesters took to the streets to demand the resignation of Modi's education minister over repeated exam paper leaks.

At the time, authorities had used batons, detentions and pellets to disperse the crowds gathered in central Delhi, which had been on the streets for days.

This time, authorities shifted to mass security deployments and preemptive action on a large scale. This included notices to those associated with earlier protests, transport cuts, the internet cutoff and airport arrests.

Thousands of protesters were detained after CJP's call for agitation Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

"The government has learned from its previous experience. They didn't allow people to sit at Jantar Mantar for any length of time, so it couldn't balloon," Pearl Pandya, senior analyst for Asia at global monitor ACLED, told DW.

"What's worrying is whether this becomes a playbook for the future — that you are not allowed to protest in the first place," she added, referring to the government's decision to remove the 18th-century observatory Jantar Mantar in central Delhi from the list of designated protest sites.

Authorities, however, have announced three new designated protest sites in the national capital.

Mukhopadhyay had a different reading of the situation. "The scale of this deployment is actually a defeat for Mr. Modi," he said.

Mukhopadhyay argued that it was already a setback for the government if it was forced to deploy security forces on such a scale in response to protests from a completely new socio-political movement.

Why October hasn't matched July

Despite the momentum, the CJP has not been able to replicate its success from July, with the protests against Kumar being led primarily by opposition leaders and student organizations.

Indian authorities crack down on 'Cockroach' protest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Education was far more of a cross-cutting issue... the right to vote is still seen as an intrinsically political one, where it's the opposition versus the BJP," Pandya said.

The CJP, however, has long maintained that it is non-political. This is often cited as the reason for them amassing such a large following of young followers.

Mukhopadhyay criticized that stance, saying: "You cannot raise issues about electoral neutrality... without saying that these are political issues."

Despite the differences between the previous round of CJP protests in July and the current wave of demonstrations, sociologist Surinder Singh Jodhka emphasized continuity.

"I don't think they're qualitatively different. Once again, young people are the ones who are mobilized, and they are much more encouraged because the earlier round of protests was successful," he told DW. "And it's also asking similar questions about institutions, about democracy, about transparency and accountability."

"There is a new hope for those who had earlier given up on India, and felt like the right wing was in complete control," Jodhka added.

Abrupt change of government unlikely

Dismissing comparisons with volatile protests in neighboring Nepal and Bangladesh, which brought down their governments, the analysts pointed to India's strong institutions as a safeguard against a dramatic change of government.

"India has had a very strong state system and state institutions," Jodhka explained, highlighting that even the opposition parties were asking for "the revival of institutions, rather than an overthrow of the state."

Pandya also stated that faith in the judiciary "would prevent these protests from tipping over into a popular revolution which unseats the government."

Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nevertheless, she said, sustained discontent "might come to bite the government in 2029... or before that in the state elections."

It could also erode Modi's popularity, which has been a defining feature of Indian politics over the past decade, the expert indicated.

For Mukhopadhyay, the most troubling aspect of the current protests is the erosion of the electoral body's credibility.

Recalling the pride he felt when he registered to vote at 21, he drew comparisons with young Indian voters today. "The youngsters are now fighting for their vote."

World.title: Nuremberg airport briefly closed after in-flight emergency
World.content:
Police are investigating a suspected in-flight emergency on a Corfu flight. After the airport reopened, the airline said they believed the emergency code was a result of a technical malfunction.

Police gave the all-clear at Germany's Nuremberg airport after a suspected in-flight emergency involving a plane arriving from the Greek island of Corfu.

The alert prompted police to cordon off the airport and Eurofighter jets to escort the aircraft, which landed safely, an airport spokesman said.

Authorities confirmed later on Tuesday that the airport had resumed normal operations.

Coredon Airlines, which was operating the flight in question, said they believed an emergency signal had been sent due to a technical malfunction.

Why was the airport closed?

The DPA news agency reported that the plane had transmitted an emergency code before landing, alerting air traffic control to a possible problem on board.

"Checks at the scene established that there is no danger," police said in a statement. The nature of the alert was not immediately clear.

Earlier in the morning, three pilots independently reported seeing an object that may have been a drone while taking off or landing at the airport.

An onboard alert on a Corendon flight from Corfu prompted a temporary closure of Nuremberg airport Image: Daniel Löb/dpa/picture alliance

Airport officials, border police and Germany's air traffic control service immediately launched a search involving a police helicopter, but no drone was found.

Six flights were delayed, while two arriving aircraft diverted to Cologne and Prague before continuing to Nuremberg. It was initially unclear whether the two incidents were connected.

Drone incidents disrupt German airports

German airports have faced drone-related security alerts previously. In August, an explosives-laden drone was found near a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, prompting a police investigation.

Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In May, a possible drone sighting halted flights at Munich airport for about an hour, forcing more than 20 arriving aircraft to divert. Police found no drone.

World.title: Nord Stream: Germany puts suspected Ukrainian pipeline saboteur on trial
World.content:
A Ukrainian citizen faces court in Hamburg, accused of attacking the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022. It raises questions about Kyiv's possible role in the explosions. German support for Ukraine is also under scrutiny.

The aerial photos made headlines worldwide: On September 26, 2022, massive quantities of methane gas bubbled on the surface of the Baltic Sea near the island of Bornholm. Unknown people had blown up three of the four sections of the Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines from Russia to Germany.

The attack, which occurred seven months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, meant the end of a mega energy project between Germany and Russia in which both sides had invested billions, and which secured affordable Russian gas for Germany. However, the flow of gas via Nord Stream 1 had been restricted or stopped several times by Russia since the Ukraine war began; Nord Stream 2 was not yet operational.

From October 14, Ukrainian citizen Serhii K. is facing trial before a court in the northern German city of Hamburg. He was arrested in Italy in August 2025 on a European arrest warrant and later extradited to Germany. This week he must answer for the attacks before the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court. He is accused of being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.

5 things you need to know about Nord Stream To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine aid criticized

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly said that Ukraine was not involved in the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines.

"Ukraine has never officially taken part in any operation related to the blowing up of Nord Stream," Zelenskyy told reporters again in August in response to a question about the ongoing investigation.

The fact that the accused is Ukrainian is especially politically sensitive. Germany continues to support the country after it was attacked by Russia: militarily, financially, with humanitarian aid and by taking in about 1.3 million refugees.

Critics of Germany's support for Ukraine, especially the right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Moscow, resume energy deliveries from Russia – including via a repaired Nord Stream pipeline — and stop supporting Ukraine. Some of them have practically delivered their verdict on Serhii K., although the trial has not yet begun, and assume that Ukraine's political or military leadership was behind the attack on the pipeline.

Sahra Wagenknecht, former leader of the BSW, told news agency Reuters in 2025 following Serhii K.'s arrest: "It is totally absurd that Germany spends many billions on aid for Ukraine but never demands an explanation from [President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. Questions should also be raised about possible compensation."

Alice Weidel, co-leader of the AfD, has shared similar sentiments. In early 2026, she asserted that the German government must seek financial repayment from Ukraine. If the AfD came into power, she would demand Kyiv compensate Germany for blowing up the pipeline and pay for its repair. According to her, a country that does such things is "no friend of Germany." She has, however, failed to provide proof that Ukraine was behind the attack.

Who benefited from blowing up the pipeline?

In an interview with public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk in 2023, German naval commander Göran Swistek pointed out that, given the technical, financial, and organizational effort involved, “there is likely a state-run structure behind it.” In his opinion, a group of amateurs could not have carried out the act.

However, he considered it unlikely that this state could be Ukraine, since Ukraine, after all, would not want to jeopardize German support. At the time, Swistek thought a false lead pointing to Russia was possible.

The German-Russian Nord Stream project had many opponents from the beginning, including Poland, the US, the Baltic countries and — especially since Russia's full-scale invasion — Ukraine. That is why investigators always ask: Who benefits from the explosion?

Henning Hoff from the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) thinks it is important to shed light on the background context.

"By halting supplies or using the threat to do so as leverage, Russia exerted immense pressure on Germany at the time, and gas markets went haywire," he told DW. "The explosion thwarted Russian attempts to extort Germany, prices for natural gas sank. I think one could say: The explosion was in German interests."

Can Ukraine still count on Germany? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Berlin's dilemma

But what will happen if the Ukrainian Serhii K. is found guilty and a connection to the military or political leadership of Ukraine is proven? Could the German government still continue its current course regarding Ukraine?

The German government faces a dilemma: On one side, judicial independence must be preserved and consequences for the sabotaging German infrastructure must be pursued. On the other side, the German government wants to prevent Russia from instrumentalizing the case. However, pressure on Germany would increase enormously, also from within the country.

Roderich Kiesewetter, a lawmaker with the ruling center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), said there is no reason to deviate from the current course of support, even in the case of involvement by Kyiv: "Irrespective of the outcome, no consequences at all are appropriate, because our support for Ukraine is carried out in the interest of our own national security and stems from a sense of responsibility for a free Europe."

The debate around support for Ukraine is escalating in Germany, regardless of the court process. Public backing for Ukraine is decreasing, especially for deliveries of weapons.

The AfD gained significant support in three state parliament elections held in eastern Germany during September. The party could potentially supply the state premier in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD has also led nationwide polls for months, far ahead of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

In addition, the AfD and BSW have drawn a connection between planned government spending cuts on social services and aid to Ukraine.

Wagenknech told a campaign event before the state parliament elections that the federal government was "Sinking billions upon billions into the black hole of Ukraine, while in Germany, in our schools, the children are no longer properly learning reading, writing and arithmetic." Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of the AfD, raised the question of whether citizens were prepared to spend so much money on a non-EU and non-NATO country.

Germany's chemical industry hit by high energy prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Repair of Nord Stream unlikely

Given very expensive energy costs, it is not only the AfD and BSW who suggest repairing Nord Stream and receiving new deliveries of gas from Russia. Some CDU politicians favor this too, such as Saxony state premier Michael Kretschmer. He views a repaired gas pipeline as a possible bargaining chip for talks with Russia. Kretschmer's position, however, contradicts the federal CDU party line and European Union sanctions policies.

His party colleague Kiesewetter considers it dangerous: "Russia has always used energy as an instrument of geo-economic extortion. It would be extremely dumb if we were to again learn nothing from history and cling to a special path with Russia. That would fuel mistrust among our partners in Europe. I can only advise everyone, including people from the CDU, to keep their distance from such calls, because they are against German interests."

Hoff from the DGAP also rejected positions like Kretschmer's. "That is an illusion. There is no returning to the time before Russia's war. The supposedly cheap Russian gas, which has cost Germany dearly, will never flow again, if only because Putin has no interest in it doing so. It serves only as an instrument of propaganda for polarizing German politics and weakening support for Ukraine."

In any case, the outcome of the trial in Hamburg will undoubtedly influence the public debate about further support for Ukraine.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Última hora de la visita de los Reyes a Ceuta, en directo | Los Reyes riden homenaje a las víctimas de la entrada masiva en el cementerio musulmán de Sidi Embarek
World.content:
Vivas entrega la llave de Ceuta a los Reyes

“Hoy es un gran día. Hoy recibimos a los Reyes”, ha dicho Vivas en el Salón del Trono en un discurso pronunciado antes de la entrega de la llave y ante distintas autoridades de la ciudad y mandos militares. “Contamos con el aliento del jefe del Estado”, ha añadido Vivas. “Gracias por venir a generar confianza, para resistir y para alumbrar la salida del túnel en el que nos encontramos. Vivimos uno de esos momentos, sin duda el más difícil de los reciente. Una invasión que ha causado la pérdida de ajenos 141 vidas con la intención de poner en riesgo la línea de flotación de nuestra ciudad”, ha continuado. El Rey asentía con la cabeza cuando Vivas ha narrado los orígenes de la ciudad y su “historia rica”. Luego, Felipe VI y Letizia han saludado a los miembros de la Corporación local.

Vivas ha mostrado el “cariño y admiración” de la sociedad ceutí a los Reyes “por la manera en que ejercen las funciones que la Constitución les atribuye; por su cercanía y humanidad; por su implicación en favor de los más vulnerables y de las causas justas; por su templanza y valentía; por su sentido del deber; por su decencia e integridad; por su amor a España”.

Tras explicar los orígenes de la ciudad de Ceuta y recordar que, en 1640, cuando se separan los reinos de Portugal y España los ceutís “tomaron la decisión de elegir a España”, Vivas ha asegurado que Ceuta es “España hasta la médula”: “Lo acredita el derecho, lo avala la historia y lo quieren los ceutíes, recen como recen y se llamen como se llamen”. “Viva Ceuta, viva España y viva el Rey”, ha zanjado el presidente.

World.title: Miles de personas reciben con entusiasmo a los Reyes en Ceuta: “Hoy toda España es caballa”
World.content:
Los Reyes saludan a los ciudadanos a su llegada al Ayuntamiento de Ceuta, este martes.

El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

Felipe VI y Letizia se reúnen con miembros de la sociedad civil para conocer el estado de la ciudad dos meses y medio después de la entrada masiva, tras saludar a los ceutíes en el centro de la ciudad

En 1640, Ceuta tuvo que tomar una decisión crucial: decantarse entre permanecer en España o quedarse en Portugal, cuyos territorios se dividían entonces. Desde esa fecha, los ceutíes han llevado a gala su sentimiento español, una reivindicación que se ha acentuado aún más si cabe con la entrada masiva de finales de julio. Y cuya emoción ha explotado al máximo durante la visita histórica de los Reyes a la ciudad autónoma, la primera de Felipe VI, y justo un día después de la Fiesta Nacional. Miles de ceutíes han copado este martes los distintos puntos de la urbe por donde discurre el periplo de los monarcas, con las calles engalanadas con la bandera rojigualda. En cada rincón por donde pasan, los vecinos le gritan “¡Viva España!“, ”¡Viva el Rey!“ y ”¡Ceuta es España!“. También proclaman el lema que resuena en la ciudad autónoma desde el cruce multitudinario. ”¡Ceuta no se vende!"

La visita ha arrancado a mediodía en las inmediaciones del Palacio del Ayuntamiento, ubicado en el centro histórico. Sobre las 12.15, tras aterrizar en el aeropuerto, Felipe VI y la reina Letizia han iniciado un paseíllo con saludos a los vecinos que ha durado unos 45 minutos, tras aterrizar en helicóptero en el puerto. A esa hora, las campanas de la iglesia de Santa María de África, patrona de la ciudad y cuyas fiestas fueron suspendidas a principios de agosto por el shock de la entrada masiva, han empezado a repicar para anunciar que el jefe del Estado pisaba Ceuta. “¡Yo soy español, español, español!”, exclamaban los ceutíes conforme avanzaban los Reyes por la Gran Vía.

Carmen Mateo, de 54 años, llevaba esperando desde primera hora de la mañana para tener un sitio en primera fila. “Quiero decirle que no se olvide del pueblo ceutí”. Mientras caminaban por la Gran Vía, rumbo al Ayuntamiento, Felipe VI y la reina Letizia han ido acercándose a las vayas donde estaban los ceutíes para darles la mano y mostrar su afecto. Los Reyes iban acompañados del presidente de la ciudad, el popular Juan Jesús Vivas, que ha entregado el bastón de mando al jefe del Estado a su llegada. También han estado escoltados por el nuevo delegado de Gobierno, David de la Encina, y el ministro de Política Territorial y dirigente de La Moncloa al frente del mando único, Ángel Víctor Torres. Ya sobre las 13.00, los Reyes han llegado a la puerta de la sede del Ejecutivo ceutí, donde han saludado a los miembros de la Corporación local y han entrado al edificio.

Poco después, Felipe VI y Letizia han salido al balcón del Ayuntamiento y los ceutíes han arrancado en aplausos y más proclamas. “¡Ceuta es España!, ¡Felipe, Felipe!”. Luego ha aparecido en la terraza Vivas, lo que ha elevado aún más el volumen de los vítores. “¡Presidente, presidente!”. El jolgorio se ha tornado en abucheos cuando ha aparecido salido el ministero Torres. Dentro del edificio, los Reyes se reúnen a esta hora con miembros de la sociedad civil ceutí, también de la Policía, para conocer cómo está la ciudad después semanas del cruce masivo.

Tras terminar el encuentro, Vivas ha entregado las llaves de la ciudad a los Reyes en el Salón del Trono del Ayuntamiento. “Hoy es un gran día. Hoy recibimos a los Reyes”, ha dicho el presidente ceutí en un discurso pronunciado ante distintas autoridades de la ciudad y mandos militares. “Contamos con el aliento del jefe del Estado”, ha añadido Vivas. “Gracias por venir a generar confianza, para resistir y para alumbrar la salida del túnel en el que nos encontramos. Vivimos uno de esos momentos, sin duda el más difícil de los reciente. Una invasión que ha causado la pérdida de al menos 141 vidas con la intención de poner en riesgo la línea de flotación de nuestra ciudad”, ha continuado. El Rey asentía con la cabeza cuando Vivas ha narrado los orígenes de la ciudad y su “historia rica”. Luego, Felipe VI y Letizia han saludado a los miembros de la Corporación local y a continuación han escrito en el Libro de Honor que “agradecen el cariño de los ceutíes en una visita largamente deseada y pendiente”. “Había una deuda que hoy saldamos al tiempo que transmitimos la cercanía y el afecto de toda España”, han plasmado. También han señalado que han estado “muy atentos y pendientes de las circunstancias tan difíciles” que han “padecido” los 83.000 ceutíes y han reflao que “quieren mostrar el compromiso de todo el país con el futuro de los ceutíes, que es el futuro de España”.
