A team of Railway Protection Force (RPF) apprehended him following the incident. A 50-second video of the entire episode has also gone viral on social media. The incident took place at Shivnarayanpur Railway Station in Bhagalpur district under Eastern Railway Zone (ERZ)

RPF subsequently took him into custody; however, the identity of the youth involved and other details have not been made public.

While speaking to The Hindu, the Chief Public Relations Officer (CPRO) of Eastern Railway said that the video is old and he was unable to share more details.

World.title: Houthi media says Saudi Arabia hit oil facility near Sanaa
World.content:
Houthi media reported that Saudi Arabia struck an oil facility near Sanaa on Tuesday (October 13, 2026), after the Saudi-led coalition ordered civilians to evacuate the site.

An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported hearing an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthis’ Al-Masirah TV said “Saudi aggression targets the oil company in Al-Sabaha, west of Sanaa”.

The Saudi-led coalition had earlier warned civilians to evacuate the Al-Sabaha station near the Houthi-held capital, which belongs to the Yemen Petroleum Company (YPC), following a spate of deadly Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, particularly on Riyadh airport.

Following the warning, AFP’s correspondent reported that many civilians rushed to queue at fuel stations in Sanaa, fearing shortages.

But the YPC sought to reassure the public, saying it had taken all necessary precautions in the event of an “emergency” to “meet people’s needs.”

“Al-Sabaha facilities currently do not contain any stock of petroleum products, and therefore, targeting them will not affect fuel stock or supply chains,” it said in a statement.

Stocks for consumption are “available in safe facilities and locations, and in sufficient quantities” to meet demand for long periods.

World.title: Over 50 members of Makkal Adhikaram arrested for rail roko
World.content:
The police arrested over 50 members of Makkal Adhikaram after they blocked a train at the Egmore railway station on Tuesday.

The protesters demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. They assembled on Platform 5 and staged a blockade in front of the Bikaner-Madurai Superfast Express. The police personnel removed them from the tracks and took them to a community hall. The protest delayed the train’s departure by 10 minutes.

Makkal Adhikaram general secretary Chezhiyan alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah, and Mr. Gyanesh Kumar deprived 13 crore people of their voting rights through the SIR. Kovan, general secretary of Makkal Kalai Ilakkiya Kazhagam, demanded the annulment of elections held since 2024.

World.title: Transport department pensioners launch sit-in demonstration over long-pending demands, benefits
World.content:
Members of the Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation Retired Employees Welfare Association (REWA) and the State Express Transport Corporation Retired Employees Welfare Association on Tuesday staged a sit-in protest outside the TNSTC head office here.

The demonstration was organised to emphasise the urgent need to resolve mounting grievances and long-standing issues faced by the pensioners across the State.

The protesters raised several key demands, prominently calling for unconditional implementation of the medical insurance scheme for State Transport Corporation pensioners as stipulated in Government Order (G.O.) No. 123.

Addressing the gathering, REWA president S. Alagar demanded the immediate disbursal of retirement benefits of workers who retired from April 2026 and implementation of the Old Pension Scheme, based on wage settlement agreements, for employees who entered service after 2003.

The participants further urged authorities to immediately clear outstanding wage settlement arrears, ensure that retiring employees received all terminal benefits on the exact day of their retirement, and provide compassionate employment without delay to legal heirs of deceased workers.

In his inaugural address, V. Pichai, president, Retired Employees Welfare Association State Federation, outlined the gravity of the pensioners’ plight.

R. Vasudevan, general secretary, Madurai REWA, detailed the struggles of the retired workforce, while Madurai District CITU vice-president G. Rajendran delivered the concluding address.

The association leaders urged the government to intervene immediately and take concrete steps to fulfill their demands.

World.title: Bengaluru court restrains media, tech platforms from disseminating defamatory vidoes on Siddaramaiah
World.content:
A Bengaluru civil court on Tuesday issued an ad-interim ex-parte temporary injunction restraining further circulation of two videos telecast on two private YouTube channels making allegedly defamatory remarks against former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah.

The interim order restrains 42 media houses, including newspapers, television channels, digital platforms like YouTube, Yahoo, Google and Facebook, from disseminating the impugned videos, their captions, clips, extracts, or substantially identical versions through any medium.

B. Pushpanjali, judge of the 19th additional city civil and sessions court, Bengaluru, passed the interim order on a suit filed by Mr. Siddaramaiah.

Additionally, the court directed YouTube, Yahoo, Google and Facebook, to forthwith disable access to and block the specified URLs of the two videos telecast on the YouTube channels on September 27, 2026, with title “Karnataka Honey Trap Nexus Part-1”, and October 2, 2026 with the title “Live: Biggest CD Blast in Karnataka Politics?”.

In the suit, Mr. Siddaramaiah categorically denied all the allegations made in the two videos. In one of the videos, a woman narrates a 2011 incident, allegedly when she was 14 and links it to him in a conversation with two men, “the recording of which was in a manner intended to resemble a clandestine or hidden-camera recording,” it has been stated in the suit.

The caption, it further says, “is deliberately framed to place the plaintiff at the centre of a sensational political and sexual narrative,” sans any material.

It has been pointed out in the suit that the caption to the video links the alleged recording of conversation as a reason for him to demit the office of Chief Minister, alleged blackmail, an alleged honey-trap network, the present Chief Minister, statements of other political leaders, the Congress High Command, and Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi.

“...The attempt to retrospectively connect a political transition with an alleged secretly recorded conversation is false, baseless and designed to injure Mr. Siddaramaiah’s reputation and political standing,” it has been claimed in the suit.

Since Mr. Siddaramaiah has challenged the authenticity, credibility, intent of the videos, the court observed that permitting their circulation at this stage could seriously harm his dignity, reputation and privacy. It noted that if media houses are not restrained from broadcasting or sharing the videos or their clips, the resulting damage would be irreparable.

World.title: PM Shehbaz takes allies into confidence on KP governor's rule, says Centre made every effort to avoid 'extreme step'
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday took the allies of the ruling PML-N into confidence on the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, saying that the Centre made every effort to avoid this “extreme step”.

The Centre on Sunday imposed governor’s rule in KP and emergency in 12 of its districts, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism.

PM Shehbaz held a meeting with leaders of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P), as well as a separate huddle with a parliamentary delegation comprising representatives of PML-Q, Balochistan Awami Party (BAP), Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP) and PML-Zia.

During the meeting with the MQM-P delegation led by Education Minister Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui, the two sides exchanged views on the country’s overall and political situation, the PM Office (PMO) said.

The prime minister said the government had to take this “most difficult decision” in the interest of the people of KP.

“We made every effort to avoid taking this extreme step in any way. We engaged in negotiations with an open heart, but did not receive a positive response from the other side,” he was quoted as saying.

The premier noted that rising terrorist attacks in KP were targeting ordinary citizens and security forces, while the provincial government “failed to openly raise its voice against terrorist groups”.

PM Shehbaz also termed the PTI’s long march a “conspiracy to destroy the country’s improving economy”.

According to PMO, the MQM-P delegation assured the prime minister of its full support for the government’s decisions regarding KP.

On the MQM’s side, the delegation included Health Minister Mustafa Kamal, Senator Amir Waliuddin Chishti, Senator Khalida Ateeb, MNA Farooq Sattar, Syed Waseem Hussain, Aasia Ishaque Siddiqui, Javed Hanif Khan, Muhammad Moeen Aamir Pirzada, Muhammad Iqbal Khan, Hassan Sabir, Sadiq Iftikhar, Arshad Abdullah Vohra, Syed Hafizuddin, Syed Aminul Haque, Khawaja Azharul Hassan, Ahmad Saleem Siddiqui, Farhan Chishti, Nighat Shakeel Khan, Sabheen Ghoury, Rana Ansar, Sofia Saeed Shah, and Sanjay Perwani.

In the second meeting with other parties, PM Shehbaz explained the reasons behind the federal government’s decision to take constitutional measures, state-run APP reported.

He said the conduct of the PTI-led KP government in the province and its failure to adopt an unequivocal stance against terrorism had posed risks to Pakistan’s growing economy.

The premier highlighted that the federal government had provided more than Rs800 billion to KP under the National Finance Commission (NFC) arrangements to support efforts against terrorism.

However, he said, the provincial government had failed to take effective measures to strengthen the capacity of its Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and establish Safe City projects to improve its counterterrorism capabilities.

According to the PM’s Office, the parliamentary delegation expressed its support for the federal government amid the prevailing situation and appreciated the prime minister’s leadership during what it described as difficult circumstances.

The delegation also said the people of KP had remained deprived of adequate development in health, education and infrastructure during the PTI’s tenure in the province.

It expressed confidence that, with the federal government’s cooperation, development and prosperity in KP would advance in line with other parts of the country.

The delegation included BAP President and Science and Technology Minister Khalid Magsi; former Senate chairman Sadiq Sanjrani of BAP, senators Manzoor Kakar, Abdul Qadir Baloch, Dinesh Kumar and Samina Mumtaz Zehri; PML-Q President and Human Resource Development Minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain; and representatives of the IPP and PML-Zia.

From the government, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry and PM’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah attended both meetings.

‘What other path did we have?’

Later, he addressed a parliamentary meeting of his PML-N and said, “When terrorism is spreading, sacrifices are being made day and night, and this party (PTI) is exhausting all its resources and time round the clock to create instability.”

The premier emphasised that the people of KP had been wanting “projects of development and prosperity for the past 13 years”, such as schools, universities, hospitals, better law and order, and an end to corruption.

However, he contended, there was “not zero, but negative attention” towards these matters, and “all attention and resources” were instead diverted towards long marches and protests.

“Can any respectable society tolerate this? Even the question does not arise. So what other path did we have?” he asked, quipping if the Centre should have remained as “silent spectators”.

The prime minister noted that the Centre was “compelled to make this decision” after the Oct 3 talks between the government and the opposition collapsed.

Elaborating on the dialogue process, PM Shehbaz said, “There was a moment when it was set in stone that an agreement was about to be reached, all demands were settled.”

He added that a consensus-based draft was ready, but the PTI team sought some more time to consult Sohail Afridi — the KP chief minister whose role now stands non-functional.

“The rest is history. […] They were ordered that you have to create another May 9, even go beyond it and wreak havoc; you must not accept anything,” the premier added.

He went on to recall his engagement with Jamiat Ulemai-i-Islam–Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman to reduce tensions, which was followed by the Oct 11 cabinet meeting.

“After all consultations and arguments, it was decided that this is the moment to save Pakistan. We must not wait any further, else everything will be set on fire and we will be left with regret.”

PM Shehbaz reiterated, “We were compelled to make the decision of imposing emergency. This is no other choice because Pakistan is first.”

He expressed his hope that the newly appointed KP Advisory Council, which will work under the governor, would work to improve the living conditions and safety in the province.

The prime minister asserted that terrorism had been eradicated in most parts of the country several years ago, but had resurged recently.

He lamented that law enforcers were being martyred daily in KP and Balochistan. “If this bloodshed is not brought to an end like it was in 2018, then the journey of development made in the past 2.5 years… this journey is continuing gradually.”

“If one provincial government is not only determined to end that journey […] but that party is determined on destruction and comes to thinking that if they make progress, what will be our value; how regrettable it is.”

The prime minister recalled the November 2024 protest by the PTI in Islamabad, as well as its 2014 rallies at the federal capital’s D-Chowk.

“When someone is bent on ending the country’s progress, they are engaged in sit-ins, verbal abuse and allegations, instead of standing with the Centre and the armed forces and empowering the police and CTD,” he said.

PM Shehbaz said even an enemy would not make the remarks made by Afridi in recent weeks. He criticised the PTI leader for not expressing sympathies with the martyrs’ families and for “not willing to say a single word” against terrorists.

At the outset of his address, the premier highlighted his government’s efforts to cooperate with the PTI-led governments in KP.

He recalled his meeting with former KP chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur, saying, “We told him in every way that we will cooperate with them … combatting terrorism is our shared responsibility.”

He noted that he had also met with Sohail Afridi — whose role as the KP CM is currently non-functional due to governor’s rule — and asserted that the Centre tried its best to work with the KP government.

At one point, the premier said International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva recently told him, “This is a new Pakistan”, as she praised the country’s economic reforms.

He recalled his meetings last month with international financial institutions and stressed that praise from such independent firms for Pakistan “restored” his faith in the country’s progress.

World.title: In Senate, Dar says federal cabinet 'rightly decided' to end process of reconciliation with PTI
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Tuesday that the federal cabinet “rightly decided” last week that the process of political reconciliation with the opposition PTI was over.

He was addressing a Senate session following the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and emergency in 12 of its districts, for which the Centre had cited the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism.

Regarding the collapsed negotiations between the federal government and PTI earlier this month, the deputy premier stressed that the PPP and PML-N had both made efforts to reach a point of understanding with the PTI, but failed.

“They said they would talk about it, then consulted with their chief minister, and after that, virtually, they refused,” he said.

He added, “Political reconciliation can be secured when other things are … equal. Other things have gone in a very bad, very wrong direction in this country and particularly in the province.”

Addressing the session, DPM Dar stressed that “everybody has the right to get elected” but that it mattered where you “take” the government.

He noted that he himself had been among those who supported the granting of an extra one per cent of the gross pool to KP during the National Finance Commission (NFC) negotiations, so that it could “prepare itself for the war against terror”.

“Rs800 billion has gone in this,” he said, questioning where this money had been spent in the province, including on a Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) or in funding for law enforcement agencies (LEAs), or even the establishment of a forensic lab.

While stressing that “we are all Pakistanis” and shared the same loyalties, Dar urged reflection on the state of the country and especially the province.

Regarding arguments that terrorism was also prevalent in Balochistan, he highlighted that the Balochistan government was “fully on board” with fighting terrorism.

The deputy premier added that when Maulana Fazlur Rehman of the JUI-F came to play his part in breaking the deadlock in negotiations, “things had gone far beyond”. He said that he had told Fazl that the matter would be presented in the Cabinet and that the results of this would be shared with him.

“His proposal was presented to the Cabinet, but the Cabinet asked: ‘How long will this go on?’” Dar said. “‘The CM (chief minister) is sometimes in Sindh, sometimes Punjab, and now they are mobilising people.’”

He also claimed that there was proof KP’s resources were being used by the PTI’s private account and not the provincial account.

“We are all common citizens of this country,” he said. “For 13 years, we have seen this ruin happening.

“I think the Cabinet rightly decided … the political reconciliation is over.”

He added that “reconciliation” could be talked about 100 times, but first the issue of ending terrorism in the province needed to be addressed.

Dar slammed the conduct of now non-functional KP CM Sohail Afridi since he came to power last year, saying, “He has been unable to perform, to do anything, (make) any improvement.”

He also highlighted the external problems being felt in Pakistan, including the Middle East conflict that spiked energy prices sharply this year, asking whether the country could really afford to deal with increased numbers of terrorist attacks.

The deputy premier said that the Cabinet had told the JUI-F chief four demands for the PTI, including that it change its chief minister and denounce terrorism — “Hand on your heart… how many times have you heard the PTI and its leadership denounce terrorism?” he challenged.

“Listen to his (Afridi’s) speeches! The things he was saying in these few weeks? Just to mobilise and provoke people against the country — do they want to set fire to the whole country?” he emphasised.

“The Cabinet rightly said that this will not happen.”

He added that the changing of chief ministers happened constantly and should not be an issue: “If he can’t perform, and if his conduct is totally unbecoming of a chief minister,” then he should be removed, he said.

He further criticised the now non-functional chief minister, questioning how many days he had actually spent in the province and slamming his use of KP’s resources to mobilise people of other provinces. He alleged that Afridi’s goal was to “bring back May 9”.

“The matter has gone far beyond political reconciliation,” the deputy prime minister stated, adding that it was “established” that the KP government had done nothing in 13 years to equip its institutions to combat terrorism.

“Whatever has happened is according to the law and Constitution,” he added.

Parliament approval for governor’s rule

President Zardari had on Sunday issued proclamations of emergency and governor’s rule under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, respectively.

According to Article 232, in case the president “acts on his own” — which was not the case for KP as he acted on PM Shehbaz’s advice — the proclamation of emergency is to be placed before both houses of Parliament for approval by each house within 10 days.

It also empowers Parliament “to make laws for a province, or any part thereof, with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Federal Legislative List” during emergency.

Meanwhile, a proclamation for governor’s rule issued under Article 234 “shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months, unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolution of the joint sitting and may by like resolution be extended for a further period not exceeding two months at a time”.

In the upper house, Senator Kamran Murtaza of the Jamiat Ulemai-i-Islam–Fazl (JUI-F) had submitted a resolution on Monday opposing the imposition of governor’s rule in KP.

President Asif Ali Zardari had summoned the Senate and National Assembly sessions after he and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif agreed on it during their weekend meeting on the country’s political and security situation.

NA session

When the NA session began at around 7pm, Speaker Sadiq administered the oath of membership to PML-N’s Malik Munir Iqbal Channar, who won the Bahawalpur polls last month held to fill the seat of his late father Malik Muhammad Iqbal Channar.

Lawmakers then offered prayers for late MNA Chaudhry Mahmood Bashir Virk, who died last month after a prolonged illness.

As MNAs from various parties took their turns to recall the services of Virk, there was slight commotion, which prompted the speaker to urge PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan to respect the late MNA.

Gohar remarked that sessions are usually adjourned after prayers for a deceased member. Referring to the governor’s rule in KP, he said the “funeral of this house was also held on Oct 11”.

“We tried to give you very much in dialogue, but you (PTI) were not ready to take what we had offered,” the speaker replied, then switched off Gohar’s mic.

The speaker said political discussion will not be allowed today, but tomorrow (Wednesday).

PPP’s Syed Naveed Qamar also urged the PTI chairman to acknowledge the services of Virk, who had stood by the Constitution. He said the PTI could raise its issues later as well.

Lawmakers then continued to pay tribute to Virk, with Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal among those who highlighted his professional life.

The proceedings were then adjourned till 11am on Wednesday.

PTI seeks production orders for 9 MNAs

The PTI requested the NA speaker to issue production orders for its nine “detained” MNAs ahead of NA and Senate sessions on Tuesday.

In a letter to NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq, Chief Whip Amir Dogar claimed that the nine MNAs were “currently detained” and requested him to issue production orders for them to enable them to attend the 30th session starting today.

The lawmakers comprised Haji Imtiaz Ahmad Choudhry (ΝΑ-68), Muhammad Jamal Ahsan Khan (NA-89), Mian Ghous Muhammad (ΝΑ-170), Sanaullah Khan Mastikhel (NΑ-91), Dawar Khan Kundi (NA-43), Junaid Akbar (NA-09), Amjad Ali Khan (NA-02), Fazal Muhammad Khan (ΝΑ-25) and Adil Khan Bazai (NA-262).

“As the speaker of the National Assembly of Pakistan, the impartiality of your esteemed office requires that production orders be issued for all detained members, irrespective of their political affiliation, to ensure that no constituency remains unrepresented during the proceedings of the House,” the letter read.

It requested Sadiq to issue the production orders under Rule 108 of the 2007 Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the National Assembly.

World.title: Army conducts successful test launch of hypersonic Fatah-2 extended range missile: ISPR
World.content:
The Pakistan Army successfully test-launched the Fatah-2 extended range (ER) hypersonic ballistic missile, the military’s media wing said in a statement on Tuesday.

According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Fatah-2 ER is equipped with advanced navigation and state-of-the-art avionics.

“It is capable of engaging targets with high precision and defeating [the] enemy’s missile defence systems due to its unique trajectory and manoeuvrability features,” it added.

“Fatah-2 ER, with its extended range, will further enhance [the] army’s reach and capability of engaging deep targets.”

The test launch was witnessed by Army Rocket Force Command (ARFC) chief Lt Gen Nauman Zakaria, senior army officers, scientists and engineers.

The ARFC commander “appreciated the dedication and technical prowess of scientists and engineers”, ISPR said.

It further said the president, prime minister, and the chief of defence forces congratulated the scientists and engineers on the successful test launch of the “extended range version of Fatah-2 weapon system”.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi congratulated the nation on the success of the test and termed it an important advancement in the defence sector.

Last week, the indigenously developed extended version of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile also underwent a successful test launch.

In a statement, ISPR said, “Equipped with advanced avionics and state-of-the-art navigational aids, the weapon system is capable of engaging targets at extended ranges with high precision and lethality.”

“The test also validated additional technical parameters of various sub-systems incorporated for improved accuracy and enhanced survivability,” it added.

World.title: Violence in response to a woman's refusal to marry 'profound shame' on society's conscience: Supreme Court
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Criticising patriarchal customs and gender-based violence, the Supreme Court (SC) on Tuesday said it was a profound shame on the conscience of any civilised society when a man, having failed to win a woman’s affection, answered her refusal with violence rather than acceptance.

“The sole reason he takes her life is to appease his wounded ego, as he was unable to secure her hand and marry her,” regretted Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar in a nine-page judgment he authored.

The observation was made by a three-member bench, which also included Justices Salahuddin Panhwar and Ishtiaq Ibrahim.

In its judgment, the bench rejected a criminal review petition by Muhammad Kamran, who sought the commutation of his death sentence to life imprisonment.

Kamran, who has already served around 15 years of his sentence in the death cell, was convicted for murdering a woman after she and her family rejected his marriage proposal.

Dismissing his review plea, the court ruled that a condemned prisoner could not claim, as a matter of right, that him having served 14 or 15 years of his sentence placed him in the same position as a person sentenced to life imprisonment.

“The latter entered prison under a sentence of life imprisonment; the former entered it under a sentence of death. The distinction does not lie in the number of years already spent in prison, but in the sentence which the court actually imposed,” the judgment emphasised.

Woman’s consent considered irrelevant, regrets SC

The court further observed: “Marriage is a mutual, voluntary covenant that necessitates free consent of both parties. But in a variety of patriarchal systems, it is accepted that men have the exclusive right to select, demand and enforce possession over a woman, irrespective of her wishes.”

The judgment stated that a woman “challenges the suitor’s perceived ownership when she exercises her fundamental right to say ‘no’”.

“Under a patriarchal mindset, this rejection is taken by that man as a blow to his ‘honour’ (ghairat), which results in stalking, home invasion, acid violence or femicide,” the judgment added.

The judgment also referred to several customs, such as that of ghag, to illustrate the manifestation of this mindset.

Ghag (proclamation in Pashto) is an archaic customary practice where a man unilaterally claims a woman as his bride without her or her guardians’ consent.

The court observed that historically, ghag was executed by firing gunshots outside the woman’s residence or making a public declaration.

“Ghag acts as an informal seal or taboo intimidating other perspective suitors away, holding a woman’s marital status hostage as if she is a territory, which is now marked by this man,” the judgment said, adding if the woman or her family resisted, the suitor would frequently employ violence to enforce his claim.

As a result, a woman may remain unmarried for years, or even decades, solely due to a declaration that was never followed by a legal or religious ceremony, engagement, or marriage, the court said.

It added that the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Elimination of Custom of Ghag Act, 2013, had already declared the custom a cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable criminal offence.

The judgment then referred to the customs of suara, also known as vani or badal-e-sulh, which it said operated differently from ghag, despite the fact that both portrayed situations where the decision to marry a woman was made by others for a purpose that was not in accordance with her own desires nor benefit.

Suara involves a girl or young woman from a family that has committed an offence, such as homicide, given in marriage to a man from the victim’s family as a form of compensation through decision made by a jirga, and serves as a substitute for a criminal proceeding or financial compensation, the court observed.

The practice was criminalised through Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2004 and further solidified by Prevention of Anti-Women Practices Act, 2011, it noted.

Similarly, there was the custom of watta-satta — another example where the setting of marriage was at the cost of the bride’s well being, the judgment said.

Watta-satta, which translates to “give-take”, is a “reciprocal marriage that is prevalent in our country involving a brother and sister from one family marrying a sister and brother from another family”, the judgment said.

“The common thread that unites all of these customs is that in this male-dominated society having patriarchal customs and traditions, a woman’s assent to her own marriage is considered irrelevant,” the court regretted.

It further stated that it is impossible to reconcile this mindset with Islam, which required woman’s free assent as a prerequisite for a valid nikah. Any adult person, either a man or a woman, was equally entitled to decide whether, when and with whom they would marry, the judgment said.

That entitlement, the judgment said, was not a concession that her family, tribe or society, as a whole, had granted to her, the judgment emphasised, adding that a woman possessed this privilege in her own right.

“There is no excuse for such behaviour, regardless of whether it is committed in the name of honour, custom, injured pride, or emotions.”

The judgment further highlighted that Pakistan was party to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW). Its Article 16 obliged states to ensure that a woman had the same right to freely choose a spouse and to enter into a marriage only with her free and full consent, the court noted.

“A domestic custom or such prevalent mindset that nullifies this choice by force cannot be permitted to survive under the guise of local practice,” the judgment said.

In the case at hand, the petitioner, who murdered a woman in cold blood, seemed to have “suffered from the mindset which led to beliefs that a woman is a commodity and it was the right of the suitor to have her, with no possibility of refusal because commodities cannot express”, the court held.

The court further said that the attempt to present a woman’s lawful refusal as “provocation” or as a mitigating circumstance was a very “absurd ground” for the plea at hand because no individual had the right to deprive another of their life just because of refusing a marriage proposal.

Accepting such an argument would constitute judicial endorsement of the notion that a woman’s will was subordinate to a man’s preference, the court declared.

The court held that the petitioner had failed to point out any error to justify the SC’s review jurisdiction under Article 188 of the Constitution. “The submissions advanced are, in substance, a request to rearrange and reweigh matters, which this court, sitting in review, cannot undertake,” it said.

World.title: Omani FM arrives in Pakistan for Joint Ministerial Commission session
World.content:
Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi arrived in Pakistan on a two-day visit on Tuesday, during which he would head his country’s delegation at the eighth Pakistan-Oman Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC) session.

According to the Foreign Office (FO), he was received upon his arrival by the Economic Affairs Division secretary and the foreign ministry’s additional secretary (Middle East).

He would also hold a bilateral meeting with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar during his stay in Pakistan, the FO statement said.

In an earlier statement, the FO had said the JMC session would “serve as an important platform to review the entire spectrum of Pakistan-Oman bilateral relations and to further strengthen cooperation in diverse fields”.

The visit “reflects the longstanding fraternal relations between Pakistan and Oman and is expected to further deepen mutually beneficial cooperation across multiple sectors”, it had added.

On Saturday, DPM Dar chaired an inter-ministerial meeting in Islamabad to review the preparations for the upcoming JMC session, according to state-run Radio Pakistan.

The meeting reviewed the agenda, bilateral agreements and arrangements for the co-chairing of the JMC session, it said.

According to Radio Pakistan, the session will focus on “deepening cooperation in trade, investment, industry, agriculture, finance, oil and gas, labour, consular affairs, security, defence, climate change, civil aviation, education, media, and culture”.

Dar highlighted the importance of the commission in strengthening bilateral relations. He directed stakeholders to ensure thorough preparations and effective follow-up to “secure tangible outcomes”, the report added.

World.title: Pakistan’s growth during FY27 projected at 3.5pc, inflation at 9.9pc: IMF
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Pakistan’s economic growth at 3.5 per cent during the current fiscal year and inflation to remain close to double digits for another year, notwithstanding global growth rebounding to 3.4pc.

In its flagship World Economic Outlook, released at the launch of the World Bank-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, the fund estimated Pakistan’s current account deficit to widen to 1pc of GDP from a surplus of 0.5pc in FY2025. Headline inflation is projected to rise significantly to 9.9pc from 7.1pc last year.

However, the Washington-based lending agency projected Pakistan’s unemployment rate to decline to 6.5pc this year, compared with 6.9pc last year and 7.1pc a year earlier.

The fund, which concluded its review of Pakistan’s economic situation last week, did not explain the projected decline in unemployment despite the rising population and its other economic forecasts, including higher inflation and a widening current account deficit.

The fund’s growth projections are significantly lower than the government’s 4pc target for the current year and the 3.8pc forecast by the World Bank last month. Its estimated 3.5pc growth rate for Pakistan is slightly lower than the 3.6pc recorded last year but higher than the 3.2pc in FY2025.

Saying global economic activity had proved resilient despite multiple challenges, the international lender projected global growth to slow to 3.1pc in 2026 before rebounding to 3.4pc in 2027. Global headline inflation is projected to rise notably to 4.7pc in 2026 before easing to 4.1pc in 2027, it added.

The IMF attributed global economic resilience to the technology upturn, buffers and adaptations that helped mitigate the damage from geopolitics-driven disruptions.

“In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events. The pandemic and the ensuing disruptions to global supply chains; the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with the consequent sharp increases in the prices of energy and other commodities; and significant changes in trade barriers and trading relations have tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets, and governments,” it said.

“Individually, each of these major developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary. Yet, despite this barrage of shocks, the global economy has held up,” the IMF said.

It added that labour markets had remained unexpectedly strong, financial systems had broadly withstood the shocks and the sharpest monetary tightening in half a century, while inflation had receded from its peaks in many economies, although it remained persistent in some cases.

The IMF warned that energy-importing economies like Pakistan, which have limited links to the technology value chain, face the most difficult outlook. The margins of adjustment that have helped sustain resilience, however, are not limitless, and risks are skewed to the downside.

Further escalation in conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence (AI), renewed trade tensions and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken growth. On the upside, stronger momentum in AI investment and productivity gains from AI, or a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions, could strengthen growth, it said.

The fund advised its members that fiscal frameworks must deliver better results in dealing with disruptive shocks and build policy space through revenue measures. During cost-of-living crises, governments should preserve price signals and rely primarily on temporary, targeted income support for the most vulnerable, it said.

The stable global aggregate masks a reallocation of growth across economies. Countries with limited direct exposure to the war shock and strong participation in the technology upturn are seeing activity hold up or strengthen. Energy exporters outside the immediate conflict zone are benefiting from favourable terms of trade.

Conversely, energy-importing economies with little connection to the technology value chain face the most difficult combination of higher import costs and exchange rate pressures, weaker real incomes, more constrained fiscal space and fewer offsetting demand impulses.

Many low-income and vulnerable countries belong to this latter group, increasing the risk that recent shocks will widen income gaps across and within countries.

The IMF projected world trade volume growth to slow in 2026 and stabilise in 2027, reflecting the drag from tariffs, adjustments in production chains and continued strength in technology-related trade.

Global imbalances are expected to decline only modestly over the medium term, as large fiscal deficits, limited domestic rebalancing, technology-driven capital flows and differing demand compositions across major economies under current policies continue to sustain external gaps.

The medium-term growth outlook remains lacklustre by historical standards and uneven across countries, partly reflecting varying degrees of AI preparedness and the robustness of energy mixes.

Risks are skewed to the downside, the IMF warned, adding that a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East could keep energy and food prices elevated and volatile, revive inflationary pressures, worsen fiscal and external balances, and weigh on growth.

Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyberattacks or extreme weather events could amplify these effects.

A day earlier, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb told Reuters that the government expected the economy to grow by more than 4pc this fiscal year despite elevated oil prices. He also said the government was looking to privatise five to six entities during the year, potentially raising more than $1 billion.

Pakistan’s economy remains vulnerable to a prolonged conflict in the Middle East because of its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing support from the region.

World.title: Trump asks Greece ambassador to resign amid ethics scandal
World.content:
US President Donald Trump’s administration has asked its ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, to resign, the White House said on Tuesday, amid allegations that she sought money from a Trump supporter and accepted lavish hospitality from wealthy Greek businessmen.

“We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters at her first White House briefing.

The announcement came a day after Trump acknowledged that he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

“She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump told reporters after the announcement, adding that he had not spoken to her, but that “she will not be there”.

In a statement on X, Guilfoyle rejected the allegations against her and defended her record as ambassador, highlighting efforts to boost US energy exports and strengthen security ties with Greece.

“These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity,” she wrote.

Guilfoyle thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, pledging her continued loyalty to the president while acknowledging that her time as ambassador “may be coming to an end”.

Guilfoyle has faced mounting scrutiny following a series of reports by The Wall Street Journal about her financial dealings and relationships with wealthy businessmen.

The newspaper reported that she asked Eric Deters, an influential Trump supporter, to pay off $100,000 in personal credit card debt shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025.

“Honey, please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote to Deters in a message accompanied by instructions for paying her credit card company, according to the Journal, which published screenshots of the exchanges.

Luxury trips

Deters refused to make the payment, telling the newspaper that doing so would have cost him his marriage.

Guilfoyle’s lawyer has disputed the authenticity of the messages and denied wrongdoing.

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek businessmen, citing hundreds of messages, emails and other records, including recorded conversations.

She travelled to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, aboard a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction company Aktor Group, according to the newspaper.

Guilfoyle also spent Christmas at the exclusive Swiss ski resort of Gstaad with Greek shipping magnate Nikolas Tsakos, and stayed at a luxury Paris hotel on a trip with him, with Tsakos footing the bill, The Journal reported.

The State Department’s inspector general is investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts, according to US media reports.

The revelations emerged as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Europe last week, including a stop in Athens, where he declined to comment on the allegations.

Guilfoyle, a prominent figure in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, was appointed ambassador after her engagement to Donald Trump Jr ended. A former prosecutor and television commentator, she was previously married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom.

World.title: PM Shehbaz, EU official discuss Pakistan's efforts to curb migrant smuggling
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: European Union Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday to discuss strengthening Pakistan-EU cooperation in migration and mobility, one of the eight pillars of the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan 2019.

Welcoming Commissioner Brunner on his first visit to Pakistan, the prime minister underscored the importance Pakistan attaches to its partnership with the EU, according to a press release by the PM Office.

The premier highlighted Pakistan’s sustained efforts to curb irregular migration and combat migrant smuggling and human trafficking through legislative reforms, institutional strengthening, effective enforcement and international cooperation.

He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to further strengthening cooperation across all pillars of the Pakistan-EU Strategic Engagement Plan.

PM Shehbaz emphasised that efforts to address irregular migration should be complemented by practical opportunities for safe, orderly and regular migration.

He noted that expanding legal pathways for Pakistani skilled workers and professionals would help meet the labour market needs of European countries while reducing prospective migrants’ vulnerability to smuggling networks.

Brunner appreciated the measures taken and cooperation extended by the government of Pakistan, PMO said.

He expressed confidence that these efforts would contribute to expanding legal migration pathways and promoting mutually beneficial labour mobility between Pakistan and the European Union.

Naqvi, EU commissioner discuss border security

Separately, Brunner also met with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi in Islamabad, where they discussed enhancing cooperation in border security, legal migration and border management.

The meeting was followed by delegation-level talks.

Brunner appreciated Pakistan’s measures against illegal migration, describing the 64 per cent reduction in illegal migration to Europe resulting from the country’s efforts as commendable.

He said the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) had demonstrated professional competence despite limited resources, which was commendable. He added that the decline in illegal migration would pave the way for legal migration.

Naqvi said Pakistan had adopted a zero-tolerance policy towards illegal migration.

“After a 64 per cent reduction in illegal migration, our next target is its complete elimination,” the interior minister said, describing illegal migration as a serious global issue.

The two sides also discussed the promotion of legal migration and enhancing opportunities for skilled workforce between Pakistan and the European Union.

Both sides agreed to further strengthen cooperation in immigration, institutional coordination and border management, and to work together on the EU’s Eastern Corridor Initiative to eliminate illegal migration.

They also discussed increasing mutual cooperation to enhance the capacity of Pakistan Coast Guards and agreed to increase collaboration to promote border security and legal migration.

Brunner assured Pakistan of all possible cooperation in this regard.

The meeting was attended by the interior secretary, special and additional interior secretaries, FIA director general, Federal Constabulary inspector general, NCCIA director general, passports director general, Islamabad chief commissioner and other officials.

Last month, Naqvi said Pakistan had recorded a 64pc reduction in illegal migration to Europe, describing the achievement as challenging despite limited resources.

He said Pakistan’s next target was to eliminate illegal migration completely, stressing the need to expand legal migration opportunities, adopt modern technology and strengthen institutional capacity.

In February, Pakistan and three European countries — Italy, Spain and Greece — reached a consensus on promoting legal pathways to “effectively combat illegal migration”. The three countries endorsed Naqvi’s proposal to establish legal pathways as a strategy to combat illegal migration and human smuggling during a conference.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.
