World.title: Georgia to raise pensions for under-70s by 45 lari instead of 20
World.content:
Pension increase in Georgia

From 1 January 2027, the Georgian government will increase pensions for people under 70 by 45 lari instead of the planned 20 lari. Their monthly pension will therefore rise to 415 lari (around $160). Meanwhile, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze argues that setting a minister’s salary below 12,000 lari encourages officials to engage in corruption.

As of August 2026, 905,000 people in Georgia received an old-age pension. Of these, 420,000 were under 70, while 485,000 were aged 70 or older. The initial draft budget for 2027 allocated up to 5.6bn lari (around $2.16bn) for pensions. The announced change will increase this amount by 128m lari (around $49.4m), bringing the total to 5.7bn lari. Under the law, an ordinary member of parliament’s salary, before tax, should rise by 1,080 lari, from 12,800 to 13,880 lari (around $5,359). The Georgian Dream party may decide not to implement this increase.

Kobakhidze said the indexation mechanism under current legislation would have increased pensions by just 20 lari. However, the government decided to raise payments further. The change does not apply to pensioners living in mountainous settlements, where different rules govern pension supplements.

Implementing the decision announced today will require an additional 128m lari in state budget spending.

What did Irakli Kobakhidze say?

According to the prime minister, social spending accounts for more than 33% of the state budget. Available figures show that the government allocated more than 5bn lari for old-age pensions in 2026, while 540m lari went towards co-financing the funded pension system. For comparison, Kobakhidze noted that pension spending totalled 1.065bn lari in 2012.

Kobakhidze said further increases in social spending carry fiscal and macroeconomic risks. He stressed that social spending had already reached the upper limit recommended by international financial institutions. Exceeding that threshold, he warned, could slow economic growth, fuel inflation and undermine Georgia’s access to international financing.

Nevertheless, he promised that the Georgian Dream government would continue looking for ways to increase pensions for people under 70 beyond the statutory indexation rate in the coming years. He added, however, that any increase must remain within acceptable budgetary limits.

Alongside the pension announcement, Kobakhidze addressed public sector pay, linking low ministerial salaries to potential corruption risks.

“Paying a minister less than 12,000 lari means pushing them towards corruption,” he said, explaining that new figures put a minister’s take-home salary at around 12,000 lari.

Kobakhidze argued that a private sector role with comparable responsibilities and workload could pay between 50,000 and 100,000 lari a month. He rejected the suggestion that 12,000 lari was a high salary for a minister.

“Given the work a minister does and the responsibilities they bear, they would earn at least 50,000–100,000 lari in a comparable private sector role. Yet we are expected to accept that 12,000 lari is a high salary for a minister. Is that reasonable? Is it really that high?” Kobakhidze said.

He noted that ensuring public officials receive decent salaries forms part of the government’s anti-corruption policy. In this context, he recalled the previous government’s time in office, saying that Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of Georgian Dream, had used his own money to pay salary supplements to public servants. Kobakhidze presented this practice as a measure to combat corruption.

How much will the pension increase cost Georgia’s budget?

Paata Kvizhinadze, chairman of the parliamentary Finance and Budget Committee, said that raising an MP’s salary by 1,080 lari would cost the state budget 1–1.3 million lari. By contrast, increasing the old-age pension by just 1 lari would require 11 million lari.

“MPs’ salaries are not set to increase under the initial draft budget. Even if the increase had been included, it would have added only slightly more than a million lari to budget expenditure — around 1.3 million lari. Meanwhile, raising pensions by 10 lari requires 111 million lari, while an increase of just 1 lari costs 11 million lari. Therefore, we should not link MPs’ salary increases to pension increases,” Kvizhinadze said.

Pension increase in Georgia

World.title: From Uzbekistan to EU: Where Armenian goods are exported after Russia imposes restrictions
World.content:
Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

On 10 October, a preferential trade regime for Armenian goods exported to the European Union came into force. Under the EU decision to apply autonomous trade measures, the bloc will liberalise around 80% of imports from Armenia by removing import duties. The measures will cover a wide range of goods, including agricultural products.

The European Union has decided to support Armenia in response to restrictions that Russia has imposed on Armenian goods. Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian agencies responsible for enforcing the restrictions cited alleged failures to meet quality standards. However, it later became clear that Armenia’s closer integration with Europe had prompted the measures.

Exports of Armenian-origin goods to EU countries have grown for several months. In effect, this trend began before the preferential trade regime came into force. From January to June 2026, Armenia exported more than $516m worth of goods to the EU. This marked an increase of more than 80% compared with the same period last year.

Exports to EU countries are now expected to grow further. At the same time, Armenia is seeking other markets.

The local outlet Factor TV analysed the results of these efforts. Drawing on data from the Ministry of Economy and the Food Safety Inspection Body, it compiled a list of countries that received significant volumes of Armenian goods. The findings show that products traditionally exported to Russia now go to Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Georgia, Ukraine and Iraq.

More than 94% of exports went to three countries

According to data from the Food Safety Inspection Body, Uzbekistan, Georgia and Ukraine accounted for more than 94% of Armenia’s fruit exports in June 2026:

48% of fruit exports went to Uzbekistan,

around 34% went to Georgia,

approximately 12% went to Ukraine.

Georgia took the lead in July, accounting for around 35.3% of exports. Uzbekistan followed with 21%, Kazakhstan with 13%, Ukraine with 10.5% and Iraq with around 8.2%.

By comparison, in June 2025, Russia alone accounted for 86.7% of Armenian fruit exports. The figure rose to 87.2% in July.

State budget compensation for exporters

In response to the restrictions Russia imposed, the Armenian government launched support programmes for local exporters. These include subsidies and cash compensation, including payments to cover export duties in other markets.

In June and July, the government paid around 3.96bn drams ($10.3m) in compensation to exporters of strawberries, apricots, sweet cherries, plums, nectarines and peaches.

Over these two months, the state covered costs associated with around 90% of the export volume:

“The total volume of strawberry, apricot, sweet cherry, plum, nectarine and peach exports reached around 16,752 tonnes. The state budget provided compensation for 15,083 tonnes.”

Support programmes also continued in August. The government allocated around 4.52bn drams ($11.8m) that month to support exports and purchases of agricultural produce. This sum also covered costs for exporters of vegetables and flowers.

How the compensation was distributed

The figures for June and July show that apricots and sweet cherries accounted for 81% of the 3.9bn drams ($10.3m) allocated to fruit exports:

The government allocated around 1.86bn drams ($4.8m) for apricots.

Sweet cherries received around 1.33bn drams ($3.5m).

The government also paid compensation for strawberry, peach, nectarine and plum exports, but the amounts were smaller.

Exporters do not receive compensation automatically for every kilogram of produce they ship abroad. They must apply to the Ministry of Economy and submit customs or transit declarations, along with invoices confirming the exports. The ministry reviews each application and pays the compensation if it finds no discrepancies in the documents.

Under the government’s decision, compensation rates per kilogram stood at 770 drams ($2) for strawberries, 200 drams ($0.5) for apricots, 250 drams ($0.6) for nectarines and 400 drams ($1) for sweet cherries. For some fruits, the compensation came close to the average market price. In June, for example, strawberries sold for an average of 933 drams ($2.4) per kilogram.

Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

World.title: Non-medical support during childbirth in Armenia: who are doulas and what do they do?
World.content:
Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

The first certified doulas appeared in Armenia six years ago. Yet few women know that they can turn to doulas for support during pregnancy, childbirth and even after giving birth.

Doulas are not medical professionals. They help women manage labour pain through massage and breathing techniques, while also providing emotional support. Women now have a choice about who accompanies them during these hours. Some still prefer to have their husbands, mothers or sisters by their side. Others choose to give birth with a doula.

A doula with a woman in labour in the antenatal ward. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Most doulas enter the profession after a negative personal experience

Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova says women decide to become doulas after giving birth themselves. Sometimes they want to share a positive experience. More often, however, they turn to the profession because of a negative experience.

“I took a long journey to get to this point. I gave birth twice. My second birth was therapeutic and healing. I realised that a woman’s preparation, knowledge and expectations largely determine how childbirth unfolds. The problem is that women often have expectations that do not match reality. This can lead to traumatic consequences,” she says.

Иветта с мужем и сыновьями

Yvetta says her husband stayed by her side during both births. The first was a terrifying experience for both of them. The second went differently because they had both prepared for it. This time, they could talk to each other, joke and even dance during labour. She remembers the birth as “a wonderful process”.

She recalls that seven days before her second child was born, she listened to a lecture by an American doula. She remembers everything that might prove important during childbirth:

“Before that lecture, I was determined not to let anything that happened during my first birth happen again. For eight months, I told my doctor that I refused to give birth naturally. I insisted on a caesarean section. But that one-hour lecture changed everything for me. I realised I could understand my hormones and my surroundings, and that I could control many things. Ultimately, I could simply give it a try.

“My second birth went smoothly, without anxiety, and so quickly that after I was discharged, I kept telling my husband I wanted to offer to help pregnant women during labour and reassure them. Of course, those plans never came to fruition because they were unrealistic expectations.”

Yet the idea stayed with Yvetta for the next ten years. Eventually, she began working with pregnant women and women in labour, but as a photographer. Her family was living abroad at the time, where maternity photography was very popular. When she moved to Armenia, she expected to find plenty of clients for similar photo shoots. However, she says, almost all women in labour there turned down her offers.

“Either they invited me into the maternity ward not to take photographs that would capture this important moment in their lives, but simply because they did not want to be alone. But a photographer cannot intervene; they are like a shadow. Their presence should be as discreet as possible. I realised that, ultimately, I could not help women.”

Immediately after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Yvetta’s dream of becoming a doula came true during the coronavirus pandemic, when many training centres moved their courses online. Yvetta completed a course, passed her exams and received an international doula certification. She became the first doula in Armenia.

Who are doulas?

Doulas are trained professionals who support pregnant women, women in labour and those who need help during the postnatal period. They prepare women for childbirth and stay by their side throughout labour in the delivery room. Doulas provide informational, emotional and physical support.

During labour, doulas help women through massage, pressure techniques and touch. Sometimes they simply offer encouragement; at other times, they explain what is happening in a woman’s body at that moment. They suggest different positions and help women feel comfortable and safe throughout the process. This can increase the likelihood of a positive birth outcome.

Yvetta helps a woman in labour manage the pain.

According to Yvetta, in countries where many women use doula services, they start looking for a doula in the early stages of pregnancy, sometimes even when planning to conceive:

“Since doulas can take on only a small number of pregnant women each month, women book their services well in advance. They try to avoid complications this way, as there may be no available doulas when they go into labour. The situation in Armenia is different. Women who have given birth before usually contact us earlier in their pregnancy. First-time mothers tend to get in touch later, around weeks 28–30, when they start preparing for childbirth.”

Yvetta believes women should not leave the search for a doula until the final weeks of pregnancy. Sometimes doulas have to turn women away because the medical facility where they plan to give birth does not allow them into the maternity ward.

Armenia’s Ministry of Health has yet to recognise how much the work of a trained doula differs from the support a husband, mother, friend or anyone else can provide. Armenian law also contains no regulations governing their work.

There are only five or six doulas in Armenia

Most trained and received certification through Doula Link, a platform run by Russia’s Institute for Perinatal Support. They thereby became members of the European Doula Network. This allows them to provide doula services in Russia, Germany, Switzerland, Serbia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Spain, Italy, Israel and Panama.

In Armenia, people regard doulas as unqualified assistants.

A 2020 order issued by the health minister gives all women in labour the right to have a companion present during childbirth. However, some medical facilities still refuse to let doulas into the delivery room.

Moreover, some maternity hospitals charge a fee for allowing a companion to attend the birth. The Ministry of Health does not regulate this practice.

Why do women turn to doulas?

Yvetta says women in Armenia mainly choose to give birth with a doula because they want someone they trust by their side. They need someone who understands what is happening and what to do, can keep track of the situation and looks after them. They also hope to avoid traumatic experiences, including obstetric violence.

“Of course, having a support person present cannot guarantee that a woman will never experience abuse. But a doula is someone who will listen to her and understand her. I am convinced that in 99% of cases involving abuse, doctors do not intend to cause harm.

“They often intervene to reduce certain risks. Yet they do not answer the woman’s questions or explain why they have decided to intervene, even when the intervention involves surgery. A doula will at least ask why the intervention is necessary and why it needs to happen at that particular moment. Women feel safer when a doula is by their side,” Yvetta says.

A mother with her baby after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

In 2024–2025, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) conducted a study of women’s experiences during pregnancy and childbirth in 16 countries across Eastern Europe and Central Asia, including Armenia.

The study found that 67% of the women surveyed had experienced at least one form of obstetric violence.

In Armenia, around 55% of respondents said medical staff had performed obstetric interventions without their consent or any explanation. Meanwhile, 32% reported mistreatment by medical staff, highlighting a lack of information or pressure to make them agree to certain interventions.

Another 27% reported poor-quality care, such as inadequate staff qualifications. Around 15% of women experienced verbal aggression, while 5% reported physical violence. Eleven per cent of respondents reported various forms of sexual violence, including excessive or inappropriate touching.

Why don’t women turn to doulas?

Yvetta admits that 80% of the pregnant women who contact her are foreigners who, for various reasons, give birth in Armenia. Local women tend to be more cautious. The main problem, in the doula’s view, is a lack of information. Stereotypical attitudes also play an important role. Many people see childbirth as something women must go through on their own, without any need for additional support.

Waiting for childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

“But this is the wrong approach, because every woman in labour is vulnerable. It is very important that, by the end, she feels like a winner because she has brought a new person into the world, rather than feeling broken and miserable after enduring unbearable suffering. Unfortunately, most women still prefer to overcome their fears of childbirth and pain not with a doula’s help, but by paying for a caesarean section. They believe this will solve the problem,” she says.

Sometimes women do not turn to doulas because they assume their services will be expensive. Yvetta does not specify how much she charges. However, she says she sometimes helps pregnant women entirely free of charge because she sees this work as her mission.

“Being a doula is a calling. This work is first and foremost about your inner world and your heart, and only then about your skills.”

She recalls that when she first started working as a doula, she sometimes returned home exhausted and upset. She even considered giving it up. Poor working conditions and hostility from doctors and hospital administrators were the main sources of stress. She also felt distressed when her presence created additional difficulties for the woman in labour.

Now she knows which maternity hospitals allow her to do her job most effectively. Some doctors there see doulas not as competitors but as professionals who support their work. Every birth has therefore become a wonderful experience for her.

“Now I come home happy because I no longer suffer alongside a woman during labour; instead, I help her avoid suffering. I can see that my work makes a difference. I see a woman who was screaming in pain and fear stop screaming, get up and start dancing,” Yvetta says.

Yvetta with the parents of a baby born with her support

Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

World.title: Capitalization period for housing in Azerbaijan reaches 23 years – CBA
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Housing prices in Azerbaijan increased by 8.4% over the past year, while the median monthly rent offered nationwide stood at 917 manat ($539.41) and the real estate capitalization period reached 23 years.

According to the Central Bank of Azerbaijan's (CBA) Financial Stability Report, the capitalization period increased by 2.1 years compared with the end of last year. This change reflects rising housing prices alongside a relative decline in rental prices.

The pace of housing price growth has shown signs of moderation. Compared with the same period last year, prices rose by 12.7% in the primary housing market and by 8.3% in the secondary market. While the rate of price growth in the primary market remained stable over the past year, growth in the secondary market slowed somewhat, the report noted.

The report also assessed how household incomes affect mortgage affordability. The affordability index, widely used internationally, is calculated as the ratio of average monthly disposable income per capita to the average monthly mortgage payment.

An index above 100% indicates that disposable income is sufficient to cover mortgage payments, while a reading below 100% means that the monthly mortgage payment exceeds disposable income.

According to the CBA, positive growth in household disposable income over the past two years has driven a sustained increase in the affordability index, keeping it above the benchmark level.

This trend indicates that households have maintained their ability to meet mortgage payments, the report said.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan eye joint ventures and industrial projects - minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan possess significant resource potential, which opens up opportunities for the creation of joint ventures and industrial complexes, the country's Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov at a gala reception in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence, Trend's correspondent reports.

“Our countries possess significant resource potential. This opens up broad opportunities for the creation of joint ventures, industrial complexes, and the processing of natural resources,” the minister noted.

Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan are developing cooperation in the political, trade and economic, energy, transportation, and humanitarian spheres. A declaration on strategic partnership was signed in 2017. An important mechanism for coordinating bilateral relations is the Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, which has been in operation since 2008. To date, the parties have signed more than 120 bilateral documents.

In 2025, trade between the two countries totaled $208.39 million: Azerbaijan’s exports to Turkmenistan reached $63.85 million, while imports from Turkmenistan amounted to $144.54 million. In June 2026, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and President of Turkmenistan Serdar Berdimuhamedov held talks in Baku, signed a joint statement, and exchanged documents on cooperation between customs services. The priorities for further cooperation include energy, transportation and logistics, the development of transit routes across the Caspian Sea, and the expansion of trade and economic ties.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Laos discuss expanding interparliamentary ties (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Sahiba Gafarova, Speaker of the Azerbaijani Parliament, discussed interparliamentary relations with the President of Laos, Thongloun Sisoulith on October 13.

This was reported by the Press and Public Relations Department of the Azerbaijani Parliament.

Meanwhile, President of Laos, Thongloun Sisoulith on an official visit to participate in the summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), which will take place in Baku.

Speaking about the significance of the guest’s participation in the upcoming CICA summit in Baku, the Speaker of Parliament noted that she highly values Laos’s representation at this forum. Emphasizing that this visit marks the first official visit by a Lao head of state to Azerbaijan, Speaker Sahiba Gafarova expressed confidence that it would open a new chapter in bilateral relations.

During the conversation, the important role of high-level contacts in the development of bilateral relations was highlighted. In this regard, special attention was paid to the significance of the guest’s meetings with President Ilham Aliyev, the talks that took place, and the documents signed.

In addition, it was noted that ties between Azerbaijan and Laos are developing successfully in various areas. It was emphasized that the countries actively cooperate and support one another within the framework of international organizations, in particular the UN and the Non-Aligned Movement.

The President of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Thongloun Sisoulith,, noting that his last visit to Azerbaijan was 44 years ago, shared his thoughts on the remarkable progress Azerbaijan has made in recent years. He talked about the contribution of National Leader Heydar Aliyev to the development of Azerbaijani-Lao relations and highly praised his work.

Expressing his impressions of today’s meeting with President Ilham Aliyev, the Lao head of state noted that his country is interested in developing bilateral relations with Azerbaijan in the areas of inter-parliamentary cooperation, education, technology, agriculture, tourism, and other fields, as well as in exchanging experiences.

The guest noted with satisfaction that he had met today with students at Baku State University and that Azerbaijani higher education institutions had trained up to 2,000 specialists for Laos during the Soviet era, and he emphasized the importance of continuing this tradition.

During the conversation, the sides also discussed the importance of reciprocal visits by parliamentary delegations, promoting cooperation between parliamentary committees, and coordination on international platforms.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan cooperation boosts Middle Corridor efficiency - minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Cooperation between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan plays an important role in enhancing the efficiency of the Middle Corridor, and transit volumes are growing year after year, the country's Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov at a gala reception in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence, Trend's correspondent reports.

“Cooperation between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan plays a key role in enhancing the efficiency of the Middle Corridor. Transit volumes are increasing year after year,” the minister noted.

According to him, Turkmenistan has a modern transportation infrastructure and has made significant investments in its seaport, railways, and other logistics facilities.

The international transport route across the Caspian Sea connects Central Asia with the South Caucasus and, further on, with Türkiye and European markets. The ports of Baku (Alat) and Turkmenbashi are important hubs on this route, facilitating the transshipment of cargo between maritime and land transport.

In February 2026, representatives of railway companies from Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Georgia discussed expanding cooperation within the framework of the Middle Corridor, increasing freight traffic, and digitizing transportation. In April, during talks in Baku, representatives from Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan explored opportunities to more fully utilize the potential of seaports and increase transit shipments.

In June 2025, the first freight train departed from the Chinese city of Jinhua for Baku via Turkmenistan along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR). The train, consisting of 100 containers, traveled to the port of Turkmenbashi, from where the cargo was to be transported across the Caspian Sea to Baku. This route expands the options for delivering cargo from China to Central Asia, the South Caucasus, and onward to Europe.

World.title: Azerbaijan's SOCAR eyes Turkmenistan oil and gas field projects - minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Azerbaijan’s state-owned oil company, SOCAR, is interested in participating in projects to develop promising oil fields in Turkmenistan, the country's Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov at a gala reception in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence, Trend's correspondent reports.

“SOCAR is interested in participating in projects to develop promising oil and gas fields in Turkmenistan,” Jabbarov said.

According to him, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan have significant potential for further deepening cooperation in the energy sector.

Energy cooperation between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan includes discussions on the joint development of hydrocarbon resources in the Caspian Sea. In January 2021, the parties signed a memorandum of understanding on the joint exploration and development of the “Dostlug” field. In June 2026, representatives of SOCAR and Turkmenistan also discussed prospects for expanding cooperation in the energy sector.

SOCAR is the main partner of the international conference and exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan — 2026” (OGT 2026), scheduled to take place in Ashgabat on October 21–23. The event is organized by the state-owned concerns “Turkmengaz” and “Turkmennebit,” the state corporation “Turkmengeology,” and the Turkmen Energy Forum. Key topics of the forum include the development of gas fields, hydrocarbon exploration in the Caspian Sea, and attracting investment to the energy sector.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s trade with Central Asia rose over 50% in 2025, minister says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Azerbaijan’s trade volume with Central Asian countries increased by more than 50% in 2025, the country's Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov at a gala reception in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence, Trend's correspondent reports.

“There are more than 400 companies operating in our country with capital from Central Asia,” Jabbarov said.

According to him, Azerbaijan’s cooperation with Central Asian countries goes beyond simply increasing trade and is moving into a new phase involving joint investments, the development of production, and expanded access to foreign markets.

Jabbarov emphasized the special importance Azerbaijan attaches to developing economic ties with Turkmenistan. He noted that the economic potential of the two countries provides a foundation for exploring new opportunities and diversifying cooperation.

The minister also highlighted the role of the Joint Intergovernmental Commission as an important platform for expanding bilateral ties.

“At the ninth meeting of the commission, held in July in Ashgabat, we had productive discussions on strengthening our partnership in the areas of trade and economic cooperation, energy, transportation, agriculture, food security, environmental protection, water infrastructure, and other priority areas,” he said.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s full membership in Central Asian forum boosts regional ties - minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Azerbaijan’s participation as a full member in the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan in Turkmenbashi in October 2026 opens up new opportunities for strengthening regional cooperation, the country's Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov at a gala reception in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence, Trend's correspondent reports.

“This is the first Consultative Meeting in which our country has participated as a full member of the format, thanks to the historic initiative of Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov and the unanimous support of our brotherly Central Asian countries,” Jabbarov said.

According to Jabbarov, the meeting served as an important platform for further strengthening Azerbaijan’s partnership with the countries of the region, expanding regional cooperation, and discussing issues of mutual interest.

The minister also noted the importance of political dialogue between Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan, highlighting the role of trusting relations between the heads of state, mutual support within international organizations, and regular high-level reciprocal visits.

“Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan are united by a shared history, culture, and friendly and fraternal ties,” he noted.

Jabbarov recalled that during the state visit of Turkmenistan’s President Serdar Berdimuhamedov to Azerbaijan on June 22–23, 2026, the two sides signed important documents in various fields, including economic cooperation. The heads of state also familiarized themselves with the large-scale reconstruction and construction work being carried out in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur.

The minister made a special mention of the construction of a mosque in Fuzuli, an initiative of the National Leader of the Turkmen people and Chairman of the People’s Council of Turkmenistan, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov.

“The mosque being built in the city of Fuzuli at the initiative of the National Leader of the Turkmen people and Chairman of the People’s Council of Turkmenistan, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov, is a symbol of friendship between our brotherly peoples,” Jabbarov emphasized.

The minister congratulated Turkmenistan on its national holiday and expressed confidence in the further strengthening of the partnership between the two countries.

World.title: Turkmenistan to host MAMA Mother Nature art exhibition, ambassador says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. The MAMA “Mother Nature” International Art Exhibition, aimed at drawing attention to environmental protection and the relationship between humans and nature, will soon open in Turkmenistan, Turkmenistan’s ambassador to Azerbaijan, Gurbanmammet Elyasov said, at a reception in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence, Trend's correspondent reports.

According to the diplomat, the exhibition will be organized in collaboration with the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and the Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov Charitable Foundation for Assistance to Children in Need of Guardianship.

“The cultural and humanitarian sphere is undoubtedly an integral part of Turkmen-Azerbaijani relations,” Elyasov noted.

He emphasized that the regular holding of Culture Days, exhibitions, festivals, and other cultural events contributes to the further strengthening of relations between the two countries.

The ambassador recalled that in October 2025, Turkmenistan Culture Days were held in Baku and Ganja, and from June 5 through 7, 2026, Azerbaijan Culture Days took place in Ashgabat and Arkadagh.

The international MAMA project, “Mother Nature,” was first presented in Baku in November 2024 as part of the 29th Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP29). The exhibition was subsequently shown in several countries, including Italy, the United Kingdom, Bahrain, and Switzerland.

World.title: Quick hits: Carey's classic starts the rot and Hoff finishes it off
World.content:
Alex Carey breaks the game open with a spectacular take, Pat Cummins confuses Beau Webster for Muttiah Muralitharan, and Josh Hazlewood's career-best wins it for Australia.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Smith returns to the field

The Australians were worried they might have to push to victory without the fielding brilliance of Smith. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

After not taking to the field after Pat Cummins's tea time declaration on day four, there were serious concerns that Australia would have to push for victory without the fielding brilliance of Steve Smith.

The Australia vice-captain was hit in the helmet by an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting and was held back over fears of a delayed concussion.

But Australian fans would have been delighted to have seen Smith out on the field and warming up ahead of the final day's play, with the slipper supreme right to re-assume his role in the cordon.

Speaking on Fox Cricket, Mitch Starc said Smith appeared to have "the light back in him" and he certainly seemed to as he snared a sharp chance at first slip, his fifth of the match, to get rid Kyle Verreynne in the 67th over.

2. Carey's screamer starts the rot

Alex Carey's brilliant catch ended a troublesome Wiaan Mulder-Aiden Markram partnership. (Supplied: Fox Cricket)

Australia tried a lot of tricks to break the Aiden Markram-Wiaan Mulder partnership on the final morning of the Test at Kingsmead.

For 154 balls, near misses elicited plenty of "Ooh"s and maybe even the occasional "Aah", but little more despite some sensational bowling.

Then, in the space of four balls, everything changed.

Josh Hazlewood swung one towards the pads of Mulder, facing his 110th delivery, and it kept going down the leg side.

Mulder tried to help it on its way to fine leg as he'd done many times before, but only managed to get a faint tickle on it and that wasn't enough to evade Alex Carey.

Australia's phenomenal wicketkeeper shuffled and leapt to his left, sticking his gloved hand out and plucking the ball out of the air just centimetres off the grass.

The partnership broken, wicket-taking suddenly looked straightforward as Matt Renshaw nicked off Kyle Verreynne just three balls later to allow the Aussies to breathe a little easier.

3. Australia's shocking review

Webster would have needed to produce some serious turn for it to be a successful review. (Fox Cricket)

With six overs still remaining between lunch and the new ball, Cummins had time to kill.

The Australia captain decided that cycling through his part-time spinners would be the most efficient way to get the 80th over.

But with the pitch offering some substantial turn and the South African tail exposed, the Australian fielders were an in excitable mood.

And in the first over after the break, that excitement was channelled into one of the most questionable reviews of Cummins's captaincy career.

Beau Webster, who has never been a big spinner of the ball to start with, pitched his off break far enough from the stumps that Jansen felt comfortable kicking it away.

Webster would have had to have transformed into a prime Muttiah Muralitharan to have gotten that one back towards the pegs — and he hadn't. The DRS projected the ball to be missing by a considerable distance.

4. Hazlewood's career-best figures

Hazlewood ripped through the South African lower order. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Jansen and Markram made it to the new ball, but things went downhill pretty quickly after Starc and Hazlewood got their hands on the fresh cherry.

Hazlewood, who had started things off with the first two wickets of the innings on day four, produced a sensational 85th over double strike to all but end the South African resistance.

First, he found some movement off the pitch to castle Jansen, then, he procured some extra bounce to have Simon Harmer caught for a three-ball duck.

Mitch Starc then got in on the act to have the brilliant Aiden Markram caught behind on review, before Hazlewood fittingly ended the Test with the dismissal of Anrich Nortje.

The Proteas had lost their final four wickets for five runs and Hazlewood had career-best figures, with his 6-49 eclipsing the 6-67 from Bengaluru in 2017.

5. Markram in his element

Aiden Markram has a habit of doing this to Australia. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Every time Aiden Markram bats in Tests against Australia, many of us find ourselves perplexed by his Test average in the mid-30s.

But all the ingredients were there to turn him into a modern Graeme Pollock.

Markram averages over 60 against Australia, comfortably highest among any of his Test opponents. His fourth-innings average is in the mid-40s — for reference, Steve Smith's run-chase average is 31.65. And, among grounds he's played more than two Tests on, Kingsmead is his best.

Australians may remember him for his fourth-innings 143 in Durban back in 2018, but more recently for a match-winning 136 in the World Test Championship final run chase last year.

And Markram was almost chanceless as he held South Africa's innings together with a marathon 237-ball 75, before his late dismissal spelled the end for the Proteas.

World.title: More than 300 scientists say AI oversight needed after 'preventable' hacks
World.content:
A group of 350 scientists from more than 30 countries has written an open letter calling for greater AI security by establishing an international body to record and publish security failures due to AI.

In several incidents in recent months, both overseas and in Australia, AI models have hacked into the systems of external organisations, including startup Hugging Face and multiple government websites.

"[These incidents] can also be seen as an irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices, preventable with stronger sandboxes and procedures," the open letter reads.

The scientists are from 31 countries, including Australia, and are based across Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, and said that without immediate change, future incidents could expose critical infrastructure.

It had three recommendations, including:

adopting high-assurance containment systems, and initially defaulting to air-gapping, which means disconnecting from the internet for cyber-capable AI models

creating an international body to record and track AI containment failures

reporting security incidents to the body and making them public.

Toby Walsh, chief scientist at the University of New South Wales AI Institute, was among the signatories and said now was the time to act.

"We're lucky so far because the hacks that have happened have been incredibly modest cyber events," Professor Walsh said.

"But you can imagine what would happen if an AI [model] was trying to hack into the air traffic control system. It could easily cause significant harms to our day-to-day lives."

Safeguards will ensure incidents won't repeat

Following the Hugging Face hack, where an AI model broke into the company's systems, OpenAI described it as a "warning shot", saying without proper safeguards AI agents could take "dangerous actions" without human direction.

But Professor Walsh said one of the recommendations in the open letter would have prevented the hack entirely.

"We wouldn't have had the Hugging Face attack if they just air-gapped the test environment from the internet," he said.

"We wouldn't have had the Medicare hack if they'd been careful about giving the agents minimal permissions for the task it was needed to do.

"I mean, these are all incredibly basic things."

Professor Walsh said the most important element of the open letter was the creation of an international body to provide both information sharing and oversight of incidents.

He said similar bodies existed for industries such as banking, aviation and pharmaceuticals.

"Every time there's an aviation accident, independent inspectors go in and find out what happened, so that everyone can learn and not make that same mistake again," he said.

"We could do the same with AI because it's advancing rapidly and we need to make it as safe as possible."

International cooperation needed to prevent incidents

Last week, Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton echoed those sentiments surrounding regulating AI similar to banking and aviation in a speech.

Regulate AI like banks and airlines The federal government is looking to banking and aviation regulation as it develops laws that would make AI companies demonstrate they can identify and manage risks.

The government is finalising its national AI standards, and plans to legislate the new rules next year.

But Professor Walsh said there needed to be broad international consensus on AI because the technology was not being developed in isolation.

"So we need to cooperate internationally … in terms of perhaps reporting of incidents and sharing of information that doesn't mean that we have to regulate internationally," he said.

Cyber security improved after it became a requirement for companies to report incidents, Professor Walsh said.

"[Otherwise] no-one knew what was happening and we weren't able to learn from all of the mistakes that companies made," he said.

World.title: Germany scrambles jets after airline radio glitch sends false hijack alert
World.content:
One of Germany's biggest international airports says that flight operations have resumed after they were suspended following an aviation emergency.

A flight from Corfu to Germany landed safely as planned in Nuremberg after a hijack alert issued from the cockpit was put down to a "malfunction in the radio communication system", according to the airline.

Corendon Airlines said it wanted to "emphasise that no emergency situation occurred and that at no point were the passengers, flight crew or aircraft in any danger".

The incident forced a brief suspension of operations at Nuremberg Airport, where the plane was planned to land, the airport said.

Flight operations later returned to normal.

"From the cockpit, the code '7500' (hijacking case) was transmitted, and furthermore, the pilot could no longer be reached by radio," police said earlier on X.

"For safety reasons, various alarm scrambles were then triggered."

The alert comes less than a month after the co-pilot of a jet flying from Dubai to Israel attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe.

An aviation emergency halts flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. (Reuters: Michaela Rehle)

The airline said the emergency code had been transmitted on Tuesday while the plane, a Boeing 737-800, was in Croatian airspace "due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system".

"The situation was immediately monitored, investigations were promptly initiated and all necessary preparations were made.

The aircraft landed safely at Nuremberg Airport," it said.

An airport spokesperson had no additional information.

Crash axe used in flydubai attack on pilot The co-pilot who allegedly attempted to down a flydubai plane had been barred from flying in his home country of Oman.

German authorities have also been on heightened alert since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia.

Russia denied any involvement.

A possible drone sighting had already disrupted air traffic at the airport overnight into Tuesday, the airport said in a separate statement.

Three pilots independently reported an object they had seen during take-off or landing, the German media outlet Bild reported.

An airport spokesperson said six flights were delayed and two inbound flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution.

Authorities across Europe have stepped up surveillance of the skies in recent weeks amid an increasing number of mostly mysterious drone incidents.

Germany says Russia responsible for Leipzig airport drone attack Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that after assessing the technology used and other intelligence information "the government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack".

Drones at German airports

In August, a drone disrupted flights overnight at Hanover Airport, located in northern Germany.

The incident came a week after an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport.

Runways at the airport were closed for 90 minutes before normal operations resumed.

The Der Spiegel weekly, citing an internal police report, reported that "the possibility of a hybrid activity cannot be excluded".

The drone went undetected by authorities and airport staff, flying freely for about two hours.

German authorities use the term "hybrid attack" to describe a wide range of incidents — including sabotage and espionage as well as propaganda operations — that have increased since the start of the war in Ukraine and are mostly blamed on Russia.

According to the magazine, the police report concludes that it is "currently impossible" to link the Hanover incident to the explosive drone found at Leipzig Airport.

Following the Leipzig incident, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt warned of "a new dimension of threat" and mentioned a potential "hybrid attack scenario" without blaming anyone or any state in particular.

Germany has become Ukraine's leading military backer in Europe following the 2022 Russian invasion.

ABC/wires

World.title: Labor can't count on One Nation fading away, Chalmers warns
World.content:
Labor's senior figures are projecting confidence the party can overcome One Nation's surge, while acknowledging the economic frustrations driving voters towards the populist right.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has declared he is not "spooked" by the challenges facing Labor and denied he had sought to soothe the nerves of MPs fearful of a mid-term slump.

Meanwhile, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has warned the federal government cannot simply hope the far right "goes away or implodes", urging progressives not to "mock" or "talk down" to voters attracted to the One Nation message.

In an address to the Australia Institute, Jim Chalmers said Labor needed to assess what was driving voters to One Nation. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The political challenge for Labor has intensified as high inflation and four interest rate rises this year added to financial pressures on households and businesses.

Earlier on Tuesday, Mr Albanese told his Labor colleagues the party would once again "kick with the wind in the fourth quarter" and prevail over its political opponents when it mattered.

It was the same AFL metaphor he deployed to calm caucus jitters about Labor's chances leading up to the last election.

Mr Albanese claimed the Greens, One Nation and Coalition were now fighting for the "fringes" of politics, while Labor's policies were aimed at "long-term investment for the future".

The prime minister later said he was not "spooked" by the 24-hour news cycle driving pressure on Labor to respond to poor polling, One Nation and speculation about the next election in 2028.

"What I am doing is, we act as an orderly government, we are not halfway through this (term)," he told Afternoon Briefing.

Don't wait for One Nation to fade

In a speech to the Australia Institute, Mr Chalmers said One Nation's political momentum was unlikely to disappear quickly and acknowledged Labor must address the economic frustrations driving voters toward the party.

"Nobody expects polls to change much any time soon — it would be more surprising if they did," he said.

"Same goes for consumer confidence."

Mr Chalmers said economic pressures had "shifted the ground" under Australians and made them feel "disconnected from opportunity" and "disregarded" as change happened around them.

"All of this is then fed and fuelled, monetised, politicised, and catastrophised by algorithmic rage bait," he said.

Mr Chalmers said One Nation had been the "most obvious beneficiary" of this, but argued Labor must fight against the idea it was preferable to go back to a "more nostalgic version of the world".

Treasurer Jim Chalmers warned economic pressure and rapid change is driving voters toward One Nation. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

"We have all the facts to push back on this, but facts don't beat feelings," he said.

"When a significant swathe of our fellow Australians find that message of returning to an idealised version of the good old days appealing — we shouldn't turn on them.

"Our role as progressives is not to scold those who see appeal in that message. It's not to mock them or 'cancel' them or talk down to them."

But Mr Chalmers also argued progressive parties had contributed to their own political difficulties by becoming associated with defending existing institutions and economic arrangements.

Greens see red-hot anger as an opportunity David Shoebridge has big ambitions for the Greens, but his party is still wrestling with how to turn voter disillusionment into greater support.

"Perhaps a key mistake made by parties of the left is that in their defence of democracy and institutions they've also inadvertently become the party of the status quo," he said.

He said Labor's tax and housing reforms were central to demonstrating it could deliver economic change.

Albanese says 'focus' is on Australians

Despite One Nation's consistently high polling this year, Mr Albanese said he was focused on the "needs of Australians".

"We need to make sure we address immediate issues such as cost-of-living pressures, which are out there, such as the need to get inflation down but do so in a way that builds strength in our economy," he said.

Senator Pauline Hanson earlier took aim at Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's economic record. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Mr Albanese said in that time Australians would have to decide whether One Nation was best placed to solve their issues.

"I understand that people are under financial pressure, we live in very turbulent times, they are angry," he said.

"The question for people to ask is are [One Nation] capable of government, or would they make the situation which many people find difficult … better or worse."

Meanwhile, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson took aim at the Albanese government's economic record and said recent policy backdowns, like delaying the Australian Tax Office's ban on credit card payments, had hurt the business community.

"Too many people in this government have never run a business," she told the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) conference in Canberra.

"Yet, they're very confident telling people who do run businesses how to do it.

"We now have a treasurer with no private sector experience, and his Labor government thinks it knows better than you how to run your business."

World.title: World Cup revenge, Olympics firing Mooney beyond 100
World.content:
Veteran batter and wicketkeeper Beth Mooney is a star performer of the Australian women's cricket team, and there is plenty of incentive for her to continue well beyond her 100th ODI.

The 32-year-old will reach the milestone in the third and final one-day international against Bangladesh at Allan Border Field on Wednesday.

She is seventh on the all-time Australia aggregate list in ODIs with a stellar 3,288 runs at an average of 49.81, including six centuries.

Last year's loss to India in the World Cup semi-finals still sticks in the craw.

Aussies reflect on World Cup semi loss Australia captain Alyssa Healy says her side only have themselves to blame as the defence of their World Cup crown comes to an end.

Australia previously lost the crown in 2017 when England beat India in the final, and that was a big driver for Mooney and the Australians to win back the trophy in 2022, which they did.

Now it is a case of deja vu after what transpired last year.

"I think there was a lot of bitter disappointment from that World Cup loss in India 12 months ago now, and looking ahead, we've obviously come off a T20 World Cup win, we've got a Champions Trophy, there are a lot of ICC events and Ashes series and big series coming up," Mooney said.

"But the 50-over one is what you want to win as well, so I guess the motivation for me now is to play well enough in the next few years to put my hand up for selection in that (2029) World Cup, but also contribute in a positive way to a format of the game that is constantly changing and evolving."

Cricket will be played at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and likely again in 2032 in Brisbane, Mooney's hometown these days.

She will be 38 in 2032, but do not discount her still being around.

"Certainly the Olympics is definitely an enticing one for players to hang around a bit longer," Mooney said.

Concerns over summer gap for women's cricket Concerns are growing about the lack of women's cricket in school-friendly slots over summer, amid warnings the schedule will hurt the game's growth among girls.

"We're obviously seeing the game a bit more modern and are remunerated well, so it's probably more likely people will start retiring a bit later. But I think the exciting part is there's always something on the calendar, so it'd be pretty hard to retire at this point."

Mooney said that if she was still performing and contributing to the success of the team, a swan song in 2032 was on the table.

"Hopefully I'm still around, but that's a long way away," she said.

"There's a lot of cricket to be played between now and then, a lot of tournaments to play with this Australian team and in franchise cricket, so my main focus is to contribute as much as I can to those, and also help the younger players along the way as well."

Current openers Georgia Voll and Phoebe Litchfield, who added 162 inside 20 overs in the nine-wicket win over Bangladesh in game two of the series, are two young guns changing the way the game is played.

"I guess that's what excited me the most is the fact that the 50-over game is becoming a lot more modern, and we're seeing Phoebe and Georgia really take the game on," Mooney said.

"Who knows how many runs we might be able to score in a 50-over game one day? That's sort of driving me at the moment."

AAP

World.title: Driver who allegedly crashed into Newcastle Knights crowd faces more charges
World.content:
An 18-year-old who is accused of driving a car that hit and injured a crowd of Newcastle Knights fans has been served with eight more charges.

P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe allegedly injured 10 people, all of whom were hospitalised after the October 3 incident.

This included a five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man who were in a critical condition at the time.

Thousands of fans had lined the streets to wave the Newcastle Knights off to their first NRL grand final in 25 years.

The new charges include dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, and six counts of causing bodily harm by misconduct using a motor vehicle.

This brings the total number of charges to 17.

'Everyone was yelling'

Loading...

Knights supporters had gathered hoping to catch a glimpse of the bus carrying players to Sydney Olympic Park ahead of Sunday's game.

At about 9:30am a car police allege was seen driving erratically crashed into a number of spectators.

Witnesses could be heard screaming in videos taken at the scene.

One attendee told the ABC "everyone was yelling and hysterical, yelling at the driver".

Officers arrested Mr Samarasinghe shortly after the incident, with crowds recorded shouting at the man as he was put into a police car.

Authorities removed two other people from the car, as some members of the crowd allegedly turned on them as well.

The bus was diverted from its planned route for public safety reasons.

Police at the time thanked members of the crowd "who provided first aid and even CPR to different people".

Accused granted bail

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe is out on bail. (Supplied: Facebook)

Less than 24 hours after being arrested, Mr Samarasinghe faced bail court where he did not apply for bail which was formally refused.

His lawyer then lodged a successful bail review application on Friday.

The legal representative argued his client had no history of violence and had sustained a suspected spinal injury from the incident.

Prosecutors had opposed granting him bail, arguing the accused posed an "unacceptable risk" to the community.

At the time, Judge Trevor Khan said some of the injuries were "very serious" and that a child was left with brain injury.

"It certainly appeared on the basis of reporting that at least two of the victims were at some risk of death," he said.

Ten people were hospitalised. (ABC News)

Mr Samarasinghe was released after spending six nights in custody.

He left Silverwater prison with his parents by his side to live at his mother's home in Sydney under bail conditions.

The accused is obliged to report to police daily between 8am and 6pm and is banned from entering Newcastle except to attend court.

He is scheduled to face Newcastle Local Court on Thursday.

World.title: The secret to a long-term happy relationship may not be what you expect
World.content:
Amanda's husband Caleb is her best friend.

"I would prefer to hang out with him than anyone else," the 43-year-old from Canberra/Ngunnawal country says.

"If people ask me to go out, it's really hard to say yes, because I'd prefer to stay home with him.

"I know I'm just going to have a really nice time."

Amanda says while their relationship may seem "vanilla and boring", they're a safe space for one another.

"Our relationship is really comfortable. We're not looking for something new and exciting. We're really looking at investing in what we already have."

That's partly how they've been able to stay happy in their long-term relationship, Amanda says.

And experts would agree.

Yumi Stynes, host of ABC podcast Ladies, We Need to Talk, explores what couples who like each other are doing behind closed doors to keep the love alive when life gets busy and unsexy.

Good friendship key to long-term happiness

Gemma Cribb is a clinical psychologist and says happiness in long-term relationships "basically boils down to a really good friendship".

Ms Cribb says research has found that "keeping in touch with each other's internal world" is key to that foundation.

"Actually asking each other ongoing questions, not just 'How was your day?' but 'What's going on for you that I need to know about?'"

Fondness and admiration are also important, she says.

"Making a conscientious effort to appreciate what your partner brings to your life, not just focusing on the negative.

"Looking for how they add value and how they make your life easier and feeding that back to them."

Lastly, Ms Cribb says couples need to respond to one another's needs. For example, noticing when your partner seems stressed and offering support.

Listen to the episode Yumi Stynes speaks to women about how they found love that's stable, healthy and fun. And clinical psychologist Gemma Cribb talks through the foundations that all happy couples build their relationships on.

We're often told shared interests and humour are what keeps couple together, but Ms Cribb says those factors can be overrated.

"People's interests change over time, so if you connect purely over your shared interests of yachting and somebody gets a permanent injury, which means they can no longer yacht, we want to have something else underneath that … keeps that friendship alive."

Not trying to change one another

Ms Cribb says real love is "accepting your partner, warts and all".

She says research on happy couples shows they had "no change agendas" for the repetitive issues in the relationship.

"Most couples argue about money, sex, time, mess, and kids, and most of those arguments will never get resolved because it's just based on who you are as a person. Someone's messy, someone's not as messy. Someone's always late, someone's always on time.

"Healthy couples still talk about those sort of friction points, but they do so with humour and affection, not with a change agenda."

Amanda and husband Caleb make time for one another when their kids have gone to bed. (Supplied)

Amanda says when she was first with Caleb, his introverted nature bothered her.

"I always imagined someone who would kind of match me as … someone who was social and had a lot of friends.

"I would definitely be frustrated with him for not wanting to go to social events."

She eventually decided to "love Caleb no matter what and have his back".

"If he never changes, that is totally fine."

But then to her surprise, he did.

"When I accepted him utterly and completely for every bit of him, including his introvertedness, that was when I think he felt totally supported and he was able to start to change," Amanda says.

Rituals to connect

Sarah, not her real name, has been with her partner since she was 15 — although for a long time they were just friends.

The 35-year-old from Melbourne/Naarm says no matter how chaotic life gets with their little one, they always make time to connect.

"We always kiss each other goodbye. And now our son will say, 'Dad, kiss Mum.' So he'll give us a little reminder, which is really helpful.

"Also just little things like the end of the day when the baby's gone to bed, I will always lie my head on [my partner's] lap and he will just comb my hair, and we'll just sit together and watch crap TV."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Sarah says finding time to be intimate can be hard with a toddler, but they know it's just a phase in their lives.

" We wrote on our whiteboard on the back of the front door, 'We still love each other, we're just tired.' "

Ms Cribb says intentionally creating rituals to connect keeps couples together.

For example, spending a few minutes chatting over a cup of tea in the morning about what is coming up for the day.

We don't see enough happy relationships

Sarah says it's kind of expected that couples "bitch about" their partner, and that her happy relationship doesn't always fit the stereotype of parents of young children.

Women 'quiet quitting' relationships "Quiet quitting" began as a social media trend where workers were encouraged to avoid burnout in their jobs by doing only the bare minimum. Some women are applying that to their romantic relationships.

"Sometimes I do find when people are complaining about their partners, I have to almost not lie, but just highlight things about [my partner] that annoy me so I can join in the conversation."

Ms Cribb says we're not shown what relationships should look like after the Hollywood ending of sparks and passion.

"We don't actually get taught the skills of how to keep that interest and connection alive.

"It requires as much work as anything else in your life that you want to maintain for the long-term."

World.title: Anne Aly accuses Liberal MP of racism after 'stoning' comment
World.content:
Small Business Minister Anne Aly has accused a Liberal MP of making racist and misogynistic comments in parliament, saying they are contrary to Australian values.

During a fiery speech in the lower house, shadow minister Angie Bell called for the prime minister and Ms Aly to be "shamed and stoned in the square" over the tax office's decision to ban credit card payments.

The ban has sparked backlash from the business community, with the government last week intervening to ensure the ATO delays the measure until July next year.

In her speech to parliament, Ms Bell, who holds the arts and sport portfolios on the opposition frontbench, called on the government to overturn the credit card ban.

Angie Bell called for the prime minister and Ms Aly to be "shamed and stoned in the square" over the tax office's decision to ban credit card payments. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"We're talking about millions and millions of Australians who are employed by small business," Ms Bell said.

"And this minister and this prime minister should be absolutely shamed and stoned in the square."

Ms Bell subsequently withdrew the comments after Leader of the House Tony Burke raised concerns with what he described as "some physically violent imagery".

Ms Aly, the first Muslim woman elected to federal parliament, later posted a video on social media, describing Ms Bell's comments as racist and misogynistic.

"This past week alone, I have had 19 death threats on my social media, and in the past I have had death threats that are couched in that exact same language," she said in a video posted to Instagram and TikTok.

"It's not just something that a parliamentarian shouldn't say in terms of advocating violence against another parliamentarian.

"It is something that stands against our Australian values. We are a country that proudly stands against violence against women, and against regimes that use brutal methods like stoning against women."

Bomb threat reveals crisis Spitting, assault and online abuse are rising signs of a dangerous political culture in Australia.

A spokesperson for Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was appropriate that Ms Bell had withdrawn the remarks.

But the spokesperson also demanded Prime Minister Anthony Albanese show the same accountability, referring to comments he made earlier this year about melons being gifted to him by the Japanese prime minister.

"Australians are still waiting for him to apologise to Japan's prime minister and [for] his own litany of broken promises.

"The prime minister cannot demand accountability from others while refusing to take responsibility for his own failures."

Speaking on Afternoon Briefing, Shadow Foreign Minister Ted O'Brien also said Ms Bell did "the right thing" by withdrawing the remarks.

He also praised her as someone who is doing a "wonderful job" on the frontbench and as a local member in her Gold Coast electorate of Moncrieff.

World.title: Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct Matthew Lee October 14, 2026 — 3:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. US President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday (US time) after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she’ll “vigorously defend” herself. Trump’s administration said earlier on Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as US President Donald Trump listens at the White House in March 2025. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr. The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing on Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well”.



Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. “Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.” White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior US official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week. In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.



Guilfoyle addressed the allegations directly in a post on X, saying, “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.” “I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.” View post on X In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services – public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination – that had not been paid. The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations”.



After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” But after another report appeared later, Rubio – speaking on Thursday before leaving Athens – berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. Related Article Trump's White House Trump picks Fox News expert for next White House press secretary “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. A second US official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general (IG) was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.



The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament on Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary. Related Article Updated

US politics Federal agents raid home of Democratic congresswoman targeted by Trump Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens, as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law. The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Representative Robert Garcia, Democrat for California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.



Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $US100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behaviour appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.
