World.title: Renshaw had the game of his life at five. Cummins says he could open next Test
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Renshaw had the game of his life at five. Cummins says he could open next Test Daniel Brettig October 14, 2026 — 1:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Durban: Pat Cummins has hinted that Matt Renshaw may be on the move back up the order following his match-winning turn at number five in Durban, as the victorious tourists stressed their desire for a flexible batting line-up. With 190, 82 and a pair of wickets in South Africa's fourth innings, Renshaw was the outstanding contributor to one of Australia's finest contemporary wins overseas against the team that upset them in last year's World Test Championship final at Lord's. Matt Renshaw and Pat Cummins on day five in Durban. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Cummins, who lauded Renshaw's batting as a blueprint for the rest of the top six, suggested it was possible that the left-hander could move back up the top for the second Test in Gqeberha from Sunday, with Travis Head and the recalled Nic Maddinson also capable of shuffling around. Head, who vigorously defended his role as an opener before the Test, had another quiet match with the bat, and has tailed off in performance since the first three Ashes Tests.



“We’re always big on how the order functions as a whole,” Cummins said. “Seeing the way that he played spin in the one-day series led me to the thought [that] he would look pretty good at number five. “Give us a few days, we’ll look at the conditions of the next Test and whether that’s still the case. I mean, it’s got to be pretty compelling to move him from there. But we’ve seen Travis Head down at number five as well, [he] can do a job. Related Article Test cricket Australia claim series opener with 214-run win over Proteas; Waugh says Marnus needs to do more “We’re always working out the six batters or seven plus Kez [Alex Carey]. How’s that going to function as a whole? So if anything, I still think he can be a great opener, and now he’s got another string to his bow.” Cummins talked through how he came to decide that Renshaw should move down to number five this week, in consultation with tour selectors Andrew McDonald and George Bailey.



“So particularly between me and Ron, and you know, George as a selector as well, we kind of nut out what we think is going to be the best batting order,” he said. “We’re pretty certain that, yeah, we like Marnus at three, Smithy at four, and then the six and seven felt pretty locked up. “So I think bringing Maddo [Maddinson] in, we really like the idea of bringing that flexibility. That unlocks a lot – Trav back to number five, Renners down at number five, even Maddo himself at number five. We haven’t had that option the last few years where we feel like we’ve got plenty of options at the top. You know we’re very big on that flexibility. “I know you’re sick of us talking about it, but why not next week have different openers with the conditions somewhat different, or swapping out the batting orders between innings? I think having the structure that we do now with a few guys that can open, that’s really unlocked it.” Loading Maddinson worked his way into the game after a 33-ball duck on day one, cracking 48 from 38 balls in the second innings then being one of six spinners called upon by Cummins as the victory was completed by a yawning 214-run margin.



“It was good to see him get a bit of time out there in the middle in the second innings. I mean, open the batting day one as a Test batter, that’s as hard a test as you’re going to get really. So, yeah, we didn’t read into that too far,” Cummins said. “He was great around the group. Bowled a few handy overs at the end, but yeah ... kudos again to the selectors of whenever you’re presented with a problem, it’s how do they go about solving it. I think George and Ronnie [McDonald] and Dods [Tony Dodemaide] keep finding ways to solve them.” Back in touch: Nic Maddinson cracked 48 in Australia’s second innings in Durban. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Cummins also spoke about Steve Smith's recovery from a potential concussion to take a fifth sharp catch for the match at slip. Had he entered concussion protocols, Smith may have been ruled out of the next Test and potentially the whole series. “Yeah, he just manufactured a couple of wickets, he’s just so good to have in the cordon there,” Cummins said of Smith. “So it was good news this morning when he woke up and told Marnus to get out of his way. He was going to go back there.



Related Article Australian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball “I think he just took a couple [of] hours just to make sure he was kind of okay, and then woke up this morning, passed all his tests, was feeling really good, and obviously desperate to get back out there. So that’s great, a huge relief. “It’s always nice having him out there – feels like anything that gets nicked behind, he’s going to make sure he grabs it.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Apple’s latest launch will help you stay off your phone at home
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsHome tech Apple’s latest launch will help you stay off your phone at home Courtney Thompson October 14, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. On an unassuming street in Tribeca sits the six-storey loft that Apple calls home in New York City. A ceiling of skylights, exposed brick walls and tasteful floral arrangements makes the mansion feel inviting without being overstimulating. It’s the kind of home most people would look at and think, “Yes, I’d live here”. This isn’t Apple’s NYC headquarters, but it is where they’ve chosen to unveil their biggest home product in six years: Apple HomeView. Apple HomeView is available to pre-order today, with prices starting from $449. Apple The launch marks Apple’s debut into smart display, designed to be a compact, efficient and personal device that makes your home frictionless, allowing you to focus on the things that matter most. Whether you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, constantly bookmarking recipes to test out on friends or live hours away from loved ones, the HomeView was designed with you in mind.



The tech giant announced the new product in the early hours of Wednesday morning (AEST), alongside updates to existing devices, the Homepod mini 2 and Apple TV 4K. Editor's pick Opinion

Phones I’d pay $3500 for an iPhone. So should you David Swan Technology editor HomeView is available for Australians to pre-order today, with prices starting from $449 for the standalone HomeView device and $543.95 for the wall-mounted models. It will be available to buy from November 13. Arguably late to the game given the launch comes nine years after competitor Amazon first introduced the Amazon Echo Show, Apple have taken the technology further by allowing full integration with your other Apple products. The personal context provided by your iPhone is key to setting these new smart home products apart from competitors Amazon and Google. For this reason, HomeView is best suited to people who already rely heavily on Apple devices, like the iPhone or iPad, as well as anyone who found the original Homepod’s Siri capability lagging and lacking.



Here’s everything you need to know about the Apple HomeView. What is Apple HomeView? HomeView is the new Apple smart home screen product, developed with three main considerations: how we enjoy entertaining, connecting with loved ones and managing the smart home. It’s essentially an extension of your iPhone or iPad, allowing you to keep those devices away while you’re spending time at home. It features a seven-inch liquid retina display; 12-megapixel centre stage camera, which tracks you as you’re on a call; and four-microphone array system, ensuring crisp and clear audio, while reducing background noise. Larger than an iPhone but smaller than an iPad, the HomeView will help you stay off your devices without becoming disconnected. Apple



The Apple HomeView comes in starlight, rose pink, space gray and silver. Apple Larger than an iPhone but smaller than an iPad, it was designed to be compact enough to blend into your home, but big enough to be used from across the room. The display is attached to a domed aluminum base by a stainless-steel hinge that’s adjustable for tabletops of different heights and comes in four different colours: starlight, rose pink, space gray and silver. Editor's pick Social media Most of us put off making this simple lifestyle choice but it changed Mel’s life There’s also three purpose-built mounts, which are priced depending on the type and are an additional cost on top of $449 for the HomeView: Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector ($94.95), Power Mount AC Wired ($124.95) and Power Mount PoE Wired ($199.95). To set up a profile, you need to connect your personal device, such as an iPhone or iPad, along with your Apple account. To be able to use the HomeView, your personal device needs to be in the house with you, be connected to the same Wi-Fi and recently unlocked.



When you stand in front of the HomeView screen, it recognises your face and when you swipe up, will automatically take you to your profile, which is fully customisable, in classic Apple style, with various display faces. Capable of supporting six different profiles, the idea is that everyone in the home can enjoy a uniquely personal HomeView experience. What makes HomeView different? Apple is positioning HomeView as singular in the market thanks to how it adapts to each user and essentially functions as an extension of your personal Apple device. Through a combination of facial recognition technology and Siri AI (powered by their AI and machine learning system, Apple Intelligence), the HomeView can leverage your iPhone for personal context understanding. For example, once you’ve unlocked the device, you can ask it to play the song a friend texted you earlier that day; check, update and add appointments; set reminders and continue tasks started on your phone – or vice versa.



Home cooks will find it particularly helpful. The HomeView has a designated cooking display that makes following recipes incredibly easy. Once you’ve found a recipe online, it will grab the relevant details and clearly show the ingredients list and instructions while you cook, integrating other features like the clock to help you manage your time. The days of unlocking your phone every time you need to check an ingredient are gone with Apple HomeView. Apple How is your data protected on HomeView? The Apple HomeView runs on the A18 chip with secure exclaves, which is the security technology the company developed to provide added privacy. With these exclaves, they partition off a secure compartment where the device processes all the data used for recognition and communication. Apple, OS and apps aren’t able to access the camera or microphone data captured by the device. Similarly, like all Apple products, it uses end-to-end encryption, meaning Apple can’t access any of your data.



When you’re using the HomeView, to access your personal content, the device needs to recognise your face and voice. If you leave it open on your profile and someone you live with tries to read your text messages, for instance, they won’t be able to because the HomeView will see they aren’t you. (Additionally, it will send a notification to your phone to verify if you’re the person trying to access the information.) If someone else has their profile open, you’ll still be able to use the HomeView for tasks like cooking, playing music or asking general questions, but you won’t be able to access personal content. Are there parental controls? Yes. The person who sets up the HomeView has control over what is displayed and can put in place restrictions on apps like Safari and elements like explicit language in music. For children under 13, the settings on their personal device will be honoured on the HomeView. If there are certain things restricted on their iPad, for example, those same settings will carry over to their HomeView profile.



What other announcements did Apple make? The company also announced the updated Apple Homepod mini 2 and Apple TV 4K. Apple Homepod mini 2 now comes with Siri AI, to enhance music discovery and allow for convenient use that leverages your iPhone information (so you can add events to your calendar or set reminders that will automatically sync with your phone). It has a new feature called Sound Glow, where the lights on top of the Homepod glow to match the colours of the album art that you’re listening to, and comes in three additional colours: blue, green and pink. The Apple HomePod mini 2 comes in three additional colours, including pink. Apple



The Homepod mini 2 will cost $229. It’s available to pre-order now, you can buy it from October 30. Meanwhile, Apple TV now comes in a 4K upgrade, along with Siri AI for your living room entertainment. You can ask for recommendations, and it will display results, while also letting you talk to Siri hands-free from your iPhone. The Apple TV 4K will also be able to pair with up to four compatible HomePod speakers for surround sound at home. And the new Siri remote can now play a sound when lost or be located using Apple’s Find My. Apple TV 4K costs $449, is available for pre-order now and will be available to purchase from November 13. The writer travelled to New York City as a guest of Apple. Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball Daniel Brettig October 13, 2026 — 11:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia has taken a 1-0 series lead over South Africa after Josh Hazlewood’s six wickets powered them to a 214-run victory over the Proteas in Durban. Here’s how the Australian team rated individually across the five days in Durban. Matt Renshaw - 10 Played one of the best Test innings by an Australian in the past decade with 190 in the first innings, and followed up with a percussive 82 in the second as the tourists built their lead. He was just as delighted by claiming the wicket of Temba Bavuma with his off spin. Whether he stays in the middle or moves back to opening, he has made a spot his own this week. Matt Renshaw’s 190 runs in the first innings set Australia up for victory. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe



Josh Hazlewood - 9 It’s a big call for someone with as many Test wickets as he has, but Hazlewood has never bowled better than during this game. Relentlessly accurate at good pace, he utilised new ball seam, bounce and also reverse swing at times to confound almost every Proteas batsman. His one-two punch with the second new ball sealed the game, and figures of 6-49 were a new personal high mark. Josh Hazlewood stood out with six wickets in South Africa’s second innings. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Pat Cummins - 9 An outstanding game with the ball and the captaincy. Over his time in the job, Cummins has become gradually more inventive, perhaps starting with the 2023 ODI World Cup in India. Here he used all his tricks to achieve a win on a pitch that required patience, even using six spinners in the second innings and being rewarded with two key wickets for Renshaw. As a paceman, he has seldom bowled faster, strong evidence of his refreshment by a year of lighter duties after a back injury.



Mitchell Starc - 7 A sturdy match if not quite as eye-catching as those for Hazlewood and Cummins, Starc’s major contribution was to get rid of Proteas batting ace Aiden Markram in both innings. His big right boot also created the footmarks that allowed Nathan Lyon and Renshaw to prosper. Mitchell Starc claimed the crucial wicket of Aiden Markram in both innings. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Nathan Lyon - 7 Outstanding batting contribution to the game-winning lower-order partnership with Renshaw, and bowled better than his two-wicket haul suggested. Spoke of all the hard work and discipline he had acquired to try to extend his career, and it paid off in unexpected ways this week.



Steve Smith - 6 Made a pair of starts and also had to reckon with a blow to the helmet that compelled him to be assessed for concussion. But it will be Smith’s incredible catching that lingers in the memory, particularly two anticipatory takes to catch chances from reverse sweeps off Lyon. As the bowler put it, Smith’s skills are freakish, further underlined by his day five snaffle of Kyle Verreynne . Loading Nic Maddinson - 6 Was given an enormously tough task to open the batting in his first red ball game in over a year, and a 33-ball duck was difficult to watch. But he hooked his first ball of the second innings powerfully to the boundary, and with a rapid-fire 48 gave the second innings a sprint start. Will get another opportunity in the second Test.



Alex Carey - 6 Tidy behind the stumps as ever, and a couple of starts with the bat. Claimed a wonderful legside catch to end a stubborn stand between Wiaan Mulder and Markram on day five. Carey will want to make another big score soon, and his best chance to do that will be by playing assertively. Needs more runs: Australia’s No.3 Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Marnus Labuschagne - 5



Two identical scores, 37 off 58 balls, demonstrated two things. Labuschagne is hitting the ball very well, and looking to score, which is exactly what Australia want from him. But he is also in his head about going from starts to big scores. It’s been over three years now since his previous Test century. Somehow Labuschagne needs to find a way to calm his mind and lock in like Renshaw. Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket The pitchforks were out, but Bailey and Test selectors can now breathe easy Beau Webster - 5 Wasn’t needed much with the ball and got a second-ball duck on day one. But contributed handily in the second innings and remains a useful utility option for the touring side. Webster is open about his place being up for debate every game, and his current tenure may hinge on the availability of Cameron Green to bowl. Travis Head - 3



A pair of low scores and has looked somewhat out of sorts, struggling to find his timing and spooning an unconvincing front edge to mid-on in the second innings. Still believes his best value to the side is by opening the batting, and had plenty of spiky things to say pre-game about those past player critics who think otherwise. World.content:

Steady rain wreaked havoc with the Everest barrier draw broadcast at Sydney’s Luna Park on Tuesday night, but trainer David Hayes believes the wet weather was no worry for Ka Ying Rising, for now, and that a wide gate was no problem. All eyes were on the draw for the defending champion and solid $1.40 favourite, who gained gate 11 of 12 for the $20 million Everest (1200m) on Saturday at Randwick. Loading Hayes said he wasn’t worried about the wide alley for the on-pace Hong Kong superstar, who will shoot for a 22nd consecutive win on Saturday. “He’ll come across and if the tempo is too fast for him, he’ll sit second or third. If it’s not fast enough, he’ll lead,” Hayes said of the world’s highest-rated horse.



“I’d be more worried about being boxed in in one, two or three and he had a slow jump. I think he will be out of trouble and the Randwick 1200, it’s wonderful. You’ve got a nice, long run to get across. It’s not chaotic like Sha Tin. At Sha Tin, you’ve only got 200 metres, and he still makes it easy to get across. “I’d be more worried about a heavy 10 than barrier 11.” Zac Purton on board Ka Ying Rising. Getty Images How Ka Ying Rising handles a potentially heavy track is the only question mark for the six-year-old, who has broken the Sha Tin track record four times since winning his first overseas assignment last year in the Everest. “Luckily it’s Tuesday. If it was Friday, I’d be a bit worried,” he said of the rain, which forced interviews inside after the draw was projected onto the Sydney Harbour Bridge.



“But the forecast says it won’t be.” Still, Hayes was confident Ka Ying Rising would handle a slow track, despite racing and winning on it just once in Hong Kong. “I’ve seen him on wet ground. One day he won on a genuine yielding track, but his time was of a fast track. And the other races were yielding to slow [times],” he said. “Then when I bought him, he was on a slow to heavy track. I was a bit worried I was buying a wet tracker. And I’ve seen him trial many times in the slush, on the dirt track, and he’s been very good.” As for Ka Ying Rising finishing runner-up to Everest rival Ninja in a trial on a soft 7 at Randwick on October 6, he said: “I think the other day, the combination of long grass and being out in the middle of the track, looking around, and probably, stewards’ room, not really trying that hard.



“The heavy would worry me, though. I’d be really worried going for a race if it was heavy. If it’s dead, I’m sure he’ll handle dead. And I’m pretty comfortable on slow, and I really don’t know on heavy. Aussie heavy is different to Hong Kong heavy.” Main rival Tempted, runner-up last year, drew gate one and was into $4.50. “Having just watched the 7.30 report on gun violence in the Philippines, I was reminded of an offer made to me years ago by a Filipino,” says Paul Fergus of Croydon. “I escorted a group of Colombo Plan educational broadcasting trainees from Canberra to Melbourne. Saying farewell in Melbourne, he said: ‘Paul, when you visit our lovely country, don’t buy a gun, borrow one of mine’.”

“To round off a night out in the early 1960s, my cousin suggested we have something to eat at the Chelsea Restaurant (C8),” offers Barry Wooldridge of Harden. “She assured me the pancakes on the menu were reasonably priced. We ordered and discovered they were not the solid circle of cooked batter that we called pancakes but wafer-thin and listed as ‘crepes’. They were not liberally smeared with butter and jam but were floating in alcohol. Before we had a chance to eat them the waiter set them on fire. Very strange and, yes, expensive.”

“‘Versing’ (C8) not appropriate?” questions Helen Lewin of Tumbi Umbi. “Well, of course some football is actually poetry in motion. Others, not so much.”

As is often the case, Jim Dewar of Davistown made his point in … erm … verse.

A worldly-wise sage from Djibouti

Once said, ‘Poetry offers such beauty’

Aye, no one’s averse

To the use of a verse

Except when it pops up in footy.

“If you stepped outside and were ‘shevelled’ (C8), could you also be ‘gruntled’ and ready to face the day?” asks John Richardson of Raymond Terrace.

World.title: Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct Matthew Lee October 14, 2026 — 3:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday (US time) after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she’ll “vigorously defend” herself. Trump’s administration said earlier on Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as US President Donald Trump listens at the White House in March 2025. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr. The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing on Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well”.



Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. “Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.” White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior US official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week. In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.



Guilfoyle addressed the allegations directly in a post on X, saying, “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.” “I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.” View post on X In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services – public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination – that had not been paid. The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations”.



After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” But after another report appeared later, Rubio – speaking on Thursday before leaving Athens – berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. Related Article Trump's White House Trump picks Fox News expert for next White House press secretary “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. A second US official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general (IG) was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.



The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament on Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary. Related Article Updated

US politics Federal agents raid home of Democratic congresswoman targeted by Trump Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens, as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law. The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Representative Robert Garcia, Democrat for California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.



Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $US100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behaviour appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece. World.title: Renshaw had the game of his life at five. Cummins says he could open next Test
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Renshaw had the game of his life at five. Cummins says he could open next Test Daniel Brettig October 14, 2026 — 1:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Durban: Pat Cummins has hinted that Matt Renshaw may be on the move back up the order following his match-winning turn at number five in Durban, as the victorious tourists stressed their desire for a flexible batting line-up. With 190, 82 and a pair of wickets in South Africa's fourth innings, Renshaw was the outstanding contributor to one of Australia's finest contemporary wins overseas against the team that upset them in last year's World Test Championship final at Lord's. Matt Renshaw and Pat Cummins on day five in Durban. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Cummins, who lauded Renshaw's batting as a blueprint for the rest of the top six, suggested it was possible that the left-hander could move back up the top for the second Test in Gqeberha from Sunday, with Travis Head and the recalled Nic Maddinson also capable of shuffling around. Head, who vigorously defended his role as an opener before the Test, had another quiet match with the bat, and has tailed off in performance since the first three Ashes Tests.



“We’re always big on how the order functions as a whole,” Cummins said. “Seeing the way that he played spin in the one-day series led me to the thought [that] he would look pretty good at number five. “Give us a few days, we’ll look at the conditions of the next Test and whether that’s still the case. I mean, it’s got to be pretty compelling to move him from there. But we’ve seen Travis Head down at number five as well, [he] can do a job. Related Article Test cricket Australia claim series opener with 214-run win over Proteas; Waugh says Marnus needs to do more “We’re always working out the six batters or seven plus Kez [Alex Carey]. How’s that going to function as a whole? So if anything, I still think he can be a great opener, and now he’s got another string to his bow.” Cummins talked through how he came to decide that Renshaw should move down to number five this week, in consultation with tour selectors Andrew McDonald and George Bailey.



“So particularly between me and Ron, and you know, George as a selector as well, we kind of nut out what we think is going to be the best batting order,” he said. “We’re pretty certain that, yeah, we like Marnus at three, Smithy at four, and then the six and seven felt pretty locked up. “So I think bringing Maddo [Maddinson] in, we really like the idea of bringing that flexibility. That unlocks a lot – Trav back to number five, Renners down at number five, even Maddo himself at number five. We haven’t had that option the last few years where we feel like we’ve got plenty of options at the top. You know we’re very big on that flexibility. “I know you’re sick of us talking about it, but why not next week have different openers with the conditions somewhat different, or swapping out the batting orders between innings? I think having the structure that we do now with a few guys that can open, that’s really unlocked it.” Loading Maddinson worked his way into the game after a 33-ball duck on day one, cracking 48 from 38 balls in the second innings then being one of six spinners called upon by Cummins as the victory was completed by a yawning 214-run margin.



“It was good to see him get a bit of time out there in the middle in the second innings. I mean, open the batting day one as a Test batter, that’s as hard a test as you’re going to get really. So, yeah, we didn’t read into that too far,” Cummins said. “He was great around the group. Bowled a few handy overs at the end, but yeah ... kudos again to the selectors of whenever you’re presented with a problem, it’s how do they go about solving it. I think George and Ronnie [McDonald] and Dods [Tony Dodemaide] keep finding ways to solve them.” Back in touch: Nic Maddinson cracked 48 in Australia’s second innings in Durban. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Cummins also spoke about Steve Smith's recovery from a potential concussion to take a fifth sharp catch for the match at slip. Had he entered concussion protocols, Smith may have been ruled out of the next Test and potentially the whole series. “Yeah, he just manufactured a couple of wickets, he’s just so good to have in the cordon there,” Cummins said of Smith. “So it was good news this morning when he woke up and told Marnus to get out of his way. He was going to go back there.



Related Article Australian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball “I think he just took a couple [of] hours just to make sure he was kind of okay, and then woke up this morning, passed all his tests, was feeling really good, and obviously desperate to get back out there. So that’s great, a huge relief. “It’s always nice having him out there – feels like anything that gets nicked behind, he’s going to make sure he grabs it.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Apple’s latest launch will help you stay off your phone at home
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsHome tech Apple’s latest launch will help you stay off your phone at home Courtney Thompson October 14, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. On an unassuming street in Tribeca sits the six-storey loft that Apple calls home in New York City. A ceiling of skylights, exposed brick walls and tasteful floral arrangements makes the mansion feel inviting without being overstimulating. It’s the kind of home most people would look at and think, “Yes, I’d live here”. This isn’t Apple’s NYC headquarters, but it is where they’ve chosen to unveil their biggest home product in six years: Apple HomeView. Apple HomeView is available to pre-order today, with prices starting from $449. Apple The launch marks Apple’s debut into smart display, designed to be a compact, efficient and personal device that makes your home frictionless, allowing you to focus on the things that matter most. Whether you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, constantly bookmarking recipes to test out on friends or live hours away from loved ones, the HomeView was designed with you in mind.



The tech giant announced the new product in the early hours of Wednesday morning (AEST), alongside updates to existing devices, the Homepod mini 2 and Apple TV 4K. Editor's pick Opinion

Phones I’d pay $3500 for an iPhone. So should you David Swan Technology editor HomeView is available for Australians to pre-order today, with prices starting from $449 for the standalone HomeView device and $543.95 for the wall-mounted models. It will be available to buy from November 13. Arguably late to the game given the launch comes nine years after competitor Amazon first introduced the Amazon Echo Show, Apple have taken the technology further by allowing full integration with your other Apple products. The personal context provided by your iPhone is key to setting these new smart home products apart from competitors Amazon and Google. For this reason, HomeView is best suited to people who already rely heavily on Apple devices, like the iPhone or iPad, as well as anyone who found the original Homepod’s Siri capability lagging and lacking.



Here’s everything you need to know about the Apple HomeView. What is Apple HomeView? HomeView is the new Apple smart home screen product, developed with three main considerations: how we enjoy entertaining, connecting with loved ones and managing the smart home. It’s essentially an extension of your iPhone or iPad, allowing you to keep those devices away while you’re spending time at home. It features a seven-inch liquid retina display; 12-megapixel centre stage camera, which tracks you as you’re on a call; and four-microphone array system, ensuring crisp and clear audio, while reducing background noise. Larger than an iPhone but smaller than an iPad, the HomeView will help you stay off your devices without becoming disconnected. Apple



The Apple HomeView comes in starlight, rose pink, space gray and silver. Apple Larger than an iPhone but smaller than an iPad, it was designed to be compact enough to blend into your home, but big enough to be used from across the room. The display is attached to a domed aluminum base by a stainless-steel hinge that’s adjustable for tabletops of different heights and comes in four different colours: starlight, rose pink, space gray and silver. Editor's pick Social media Most of us put off making this simple lifestyle choice but it changed Mel’s life There’s also three purpose-built mounts, which are priced depending on the type and are an additional cost on top of $449 for the HomeView: Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector ($94.95), Power Mount AC Wired ($124.95) and Power Mount PoE Wired ($199.95). To set up a profile, you need to connect your personal device, such as an iPhone or iPad, along with your Apple account. To be able to use the HomeView, your personal device needs to be in the house with you, be connected to the same Wi-Fi and recently unlocked.



When you stand in front of the HomeView screen, it recognises your face and when you swipe up, will automatically take you to your profile, which is fully customisable, in classic Apple style, with various display faces. Capable of supporting six different profiles, the idea is that everyone in the home can enjoy a uniquely personal HomeView experience. What makes HomeView different? Apple is positioning HomeView as singular in the market thanks to how it adapts to each user and essentially functions as an extension of your personal Apple device. Through a combination of facial recognition technology and Siri AI (powered by their AI and machine learning system, Apple Intelligence), the HomeView can leverage your iPhone for personal context understanding. For example, once you’ve unlocked the device, you can ask it to play the song a friend texted you earlier that day; check, update and add appointments; set reminders and continue tasks started on your phone – or vice versa.



Home cooks will find it particularly helpful. The HomeView has a designated cooking display that makes following recipes incredibly easy. Once you’ve found a recipe online, it will grab the relevant details and clearly show the ingredients list and instructions while you cook, integrating other features like the clock to help you manage your time. The days of unlocking your phone every time you need to check an ingredient are gone with Apple HomeView. Apple How is your data protected on HomeView? The Apple HomeView runs on the A18 chip with secure exclaves, which is the security technology the company developed to provide added privacy. With these exclaves, they partition off a secure compartment where the device processes all the data used for recognition and communication. Apple, OS and apps aren’t able to access the camera or microphone data captured by the device. Similarly, like all Apple products, it uses end-to-end encryption, meaning Apple can’t access any of your data.



When you’re using the HomeView, to access your personal content, the device needs to recognise your face and voice. If you leave it open on your profile and someone you live with tries to read your text messages, for instance, they won’t be able to because the HomeView will see they aren’t you. (Additionally, it will send a notification to your phone to verify if you’re the person trying to access the information.) If someone else has their profile open, you’ll still be able to use the HomeView for tasks like cooking, playing music or asking general questions, but you won’t be able to access personal content. Are there parental controls? Yes. The person who sets up the HomeView has control over what is displayed and can put in place restrictions on apps like Safari and elements like explicit language in music. For children under 13, the settings on their personal device will be honoured on the HomeView. If there are certain things restricted on their iPad, for example, those same settings will carry over to their HomeView profile.



What other announcements did Apple make? The company also announced the updated Apple Homepod mini 2 and Apple TV 4K. Apple Homepod mini 2 now comes with Siri AI, to enhance music discovery and allow for convenient use that leverages your iPhone information (so you can add events to your calendar or set reminders that will automatically sync with your phone). It has a new feature called Sound Glow, where the lights on top of the Homepod glow to match the colours of the album art that you’re listening to, and comes in three additional colours: blue, green and pink. The Apple HomePod mini 2 comes in three additional colours, including pink. Apple



The Homepod mini 2 will cost $229. It’s available to pre-order now, you can buy it from October 30. Meanwhile, Apple TV now comes in a 4K upgrade, along with Siri AI for your living room entertainment. You can ask for recommendations, and it will display results, while also letting you talk to Siri hands-free from your iPhone. The Apple TV 4K will also be able to pair with up to four compatible HomePod speakers for surround sound at home. And the new Siri remote can now play a sound when lost or be located using Apple’s Find My. Apple TV 4K costs $449, is available for pre-order now and will be available to purchase from November 13. The writer travelled to New York City as a guest of Apple. Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball Daniel Brettig October 13, 2026 — 11:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australia has taken a 1-0 series lead over South Africa after Josh Hazlewood’s six wickets powered them to a 214-run victory over the Proteas in Durban. Here’s how the Australian team rated individually across the five days in Durban. Matt Renshaw - 10 Played one of the best Test innings by an Australian in the past decade with 190 in the first innings, and followed up with a percussive 82 in the second as the tourists built their lead. He was just as delighted by claiming the wicket of Temba Bavuma with his off spin. Whether he stays in the middle or moves back to opening, he has made a spot his own this week. Matt Renshaw’s 190 runs in the first innings set Australia up for victory. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe



Josh Hazlewood - 9 It’s a big call for someone with as many Test wickets as he has, but Hazlewood has never bowled better than during this game. Relentlessly accurate at good pace, he utilised new ball seam, bounce and also reverse swing at times to confound almost every Proteas batsman. His one-two punch with the second new ball sealed the game, and figures of 6-49 were a new personal high mark. Josh Hazlewood stood out with six wickets in South Africa’s second innings. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Pat Cummins - 9 An outstanding game with the ball and the captaincy. Over his time in the job, Cummins has become gradually more inventive, perhaps starting with the 2023 ODI World Cup in India. Here he used all his tricks to achieve a win on a pitch that required patience, even using six spinners in the second innings and being rewarded with two key wickets for Renshaw. As a paceman, he has seldom bowled faster, strong evidence of his refreshment by a year of lighter duties after a back injury.



Mitchell Starc - 7 A sturdy match if not quite as eye-catching as those for Hazlewood and Cummins, Starc’s major contribution was to get rid of Proteas batting ace Aiden Markram in both innings. His big right boot also created the footmarks that allowed Nathan Lyon and Renshaw to prosper. Mitchell Starc claimed the crucial wicket of Aiden Markram in both innings. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Nathan Lyon - 7 Outstanding batting contribution to the game-winning lower-order partnership with Renshaw, and bowled better than his two-wicket haul suggested. Spoke of all the hard work and discipline he had acquired to try to extend his career, and it paid off in unexpected ways this week.



Steve Smith - 6 Made a pair of starts and also had to reckon with a blow to the helmet that compelled him to be assessed for concussion. But it will be Smith’s incredible catching that lingers in the memory, particularly two anticipatory takes to catch chances from reverse sweeps off Lyon. As the bowler put it, Smith’s skills are freakish, further underlined by his day five snaffle of Kyle Verreynne . Loading Nic Maddinson - 6 Was given an enormously tough task to open the batting in his first red ball game in over a year, and a 33-ball duck was difficult to watch. But he hooked his first ball of the second innings powerfully to the boundary, and with a rapid-fire 48 gave the second innings a sprint start. Will get another opportunity in the second Test.



Alex Carey - 6 Tidy behind the stumps as ever, and a couple of starts with the bat. Claimed a wonderful legside catch to end a stubborn stand between Wiaan Mulder and Markram on day five. Carey will want to make another big score soon, and his best chance to do that will be by playing assertively. Needs more runs: Australia’s No.3 Marnus Labuschagne. Getty Images Marnus Labuschagne - 5



Two identical scores, 37 off 58 balls, demonstrated two things. Labuschagne is hitting the ball very well, and looking to score, which is exactly what Australia want from him. But he is also in his head about going from starts to big scores. It’s been over three years now since his previous Test century. Somehow Labuschagne needs to find a way to calm his mind and lock in like Renshaw. Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket The pitchforks were out, but Bailey and Test selectors can now breathe easy Beau Webster - 5 Wasn’t needed much with the ball and got a second-ball duck on day one. But contributed handily in the second innings and remains a useful utility option for the touring side. Webster is open about his place being up for debate every game, and his current tenure may hinge on the availability of Cameron Green to bowl. Travis Head - 3



A pair of low scores and has looked somewhat out of sorts, struggling to find his timing and spooning an unconvincing front edge to mid-on in the second innings. Still believes his best value to the side is by opening the batting, and had plenty of spiky things to say pre-game about those past player critics who think otherwise. World.title: Hayes unfazed about wide draw for Ka Ying Rising but keeping an eye on the skies
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Hayes unfazed about wide draw for Ka Ying Rising but keeping an eye on the skies Craig Kerry October 13, 2026 — 9:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Steady rain wreaked havoc with the Everest barrier draw broadcast at Sydney’s Luna Park on Tuesday night, but trainer David Hayes believes the wet weather was no worry for Ka Ying Rising, for now, and that a wide gate was no problem. All eyes were on the draw for the defending champion and solid $1.40 favourite, who gained gate 11 of 12 for the $20 million Everest (1200m) on Saturday at Randwick. Loading Hayes said he wasn’t worried about the wide alley for the on-pace Hong Kong superstar, who will shoot for a 22nd consecutive win on Saturday. “He’ll come across and if the tempo is too fast for him, he’ll sit second or third. If it’s not fast enough, he’ll lead,” Hayes said of the world’s highest-rated horse.



“I’d be more worried about being boxed in in one, two or three and he had a slow jump. I think he will be out of trouble and the Randwick 1200, it’s wonderful. You’ve got a nice, long run to get across. It’s not chaotic like Sha Tin. At Sha Tin, you’ve only got 200 metres, and he still makes it easy to get across. “I’d be more worried about a heavy 10 than barrier 11.” Zac Purton on board Ka Ying Rising. Getty Images How Ka Ying Rising handles a potentially heavy track is the only question mark for the six-year-old, who has broken the Sha Tin track record four times since winning his first overseas assignment last year in the Everest. “Luckily it’s Tuesday. If it was Friday, I’d be a bit worried,” he said of the rain, which forced interviews inside after the draw was projected onto the Sydney Harbour Bridge.



“But the forecast says it won’t be.” Still, Hayes was confident Ka Ying Rising would handle a slow track, despite racing and winning on it just once in Hong Kong. “I’ve seen him on wet ground. One day he won on a genuine yielding track, but his time was of a fast track. And the other races were yielding to slow [times],” he said. “Then when I bought him, he was on a slow to heavy track. I was a bit worried I was buying a wet tracker. And I’ve seen him trial many times in the slush, on the dirt track, and he’s been very good.” As for Ka Ying Rising finishing runner-up to Everest rival Ninja in a trial on a soft 7 at Randwick on October 6, he said: “I think the other day, the combination of long grass and being out in the middle of the track, looking around, and probably, stewards’ room, not really trying that hard.



“The heavy would worry me, though. I’d be really worried going for a race if it was heavy. If it’s dead, I’m sure he’ll handle dead. And I’m pretty comfortable on slow, and I really don’t know on heavy. Aussie heavy is different to Hong Kong heavy.” Main rival Tempted, runner-up last year, drew gate one and was into $4.50.
