“Having just watched the 7.30 report on gun violence in the Philippines, I was reminded of an offer made to me years ago by a Filipino,” says Paul Fergus of Croydon. “I escorted a group of Colombo Plan educational broadcasting trainees from Canberra to Melbourne. Saying farewell in Melbourne, he said: ‘Paul, when you visit our lovely country, don’t buy a gun, borrow one of mine’.”

“To round off a night out in the early 1960s, my cousin suggested we have something to eat at the Chelsea Restaurant (C8),” offers Barry Wooldridge of Harden. “She assured me the pancakes on the menu were reasonably priced. We ordered and discovered they were not the solid circle of cooked batter that we called pancakes but wafer-thin and listed as ‘crepes’. They were not liberally smeared with butter and jam but were floating in alcohol. Before we had a chance to eat them the waiter set them on fire. Very strange and, yes, expensive.”

“‘Versing’ (C8) not appropriate?” questions Helen Lewin of Tumbi Umbi. “Well, of course some football is actually poetry in motion. Others, not so much.”

As is often the case, Jim Dewar of Davistown made his point in … erm … verse.

A worldly-wise sage from Djibouti

Once said, ‘Poetry offers such beauty’

Aye, no one’s averse

To the use of a verse

Except when it pops up in footy.

“If you stepped outside and were ‘shevelled’ (C8), could you also be ‘gruntled’ and ready to face the day?” asks John Richardson of Raymond Terrace.

World.title: National's claim foreign aid increased by 26% 'incorrect', Winston Peters says
World.content:
Claims by the National party that foreign aid money had increased by 26 percent since 2021 are "incorrect", according to a spokesperson for the foreign minister, saying the "much more modest" increase was around 10 percent.

They said the lower 10 percent figure was the right one because it's adjusted for inflation, but National is sticking by the un-adjusted higher number.

The National Party announced last week it wanted to redirect foreign aid money into funding $604 million for new medicines and wider access to those already funded, if it led the next government.

"We will largely pay for it by reducing foreign aid and associated administration costs by 10 percent, while fully protecting aid to the Pacific."

The ACT party had also since come out saying it would also cut foreign aid to 2017 levels, excluding support for Ukraine, saving around $238m a year.

National's health spokesperson Simeon Brown told RNZ at the time the foreign aid budget had increased by 26 percent since 2021.

Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters, who is also the New Zealand First leader, said it was "desperate" from National, and that ACT's policy was "training wheel stuff", leaving New Zealand with no influence.

Speaking to Morning Report last week, Peters also said some of the aid programmes were not worth millions of dollars.

"They're going to finance a hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of millions pharmaceutical programme on the basis of this - this is a fantastic lie. None of these projects could finance any one of those drugs."

RNZ asked National what exactly would be cut, whether humanitarian causes would be affected, and regions like South East Asia - which National leader Christopher Luxon had a great focus on.

A National Party spokesperson said the party would require the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) to determine how the savings were achieved, targeting non-essential aid first while protecting pacific funding.

The spokesperson also reiterated the statement that foreign aid funding had increased by around 26 percent since 2021 "while families are having to tighten their own household budgets".

National's health spokesperson Simeon Brown. Calvin Samuel/RNZ

RNZ then asked MFAT for more information, a request that was then referred to the minister of foreign affairs' office.

A spokesperson responded saying New Zealand "simply cannot protect its security and economic interests in the order shattering time we live in by rolling back our international spending".

"If we don't pull our weight internationally, we will be judged harshly by partners, and our voice will be weak."

The spokesperson also stated the recent increases in the International Development Cooperation (IDC) budget were "much more modest than the incorrect claim made of a 26 percent increase".

In inflation adjusted terms, the annual IDC budget had risen from $1.009 billion in Budget 2020 to $1.111b in Budget 2026 - "an increase of $102 million, or 10.1 percent".

The spokesperson added that as a proportion of the overall government spend, the IDC budget had "not increased at all since 2021".

"The IDC budget for 2020/21 was 0.72 percent of the actual core Crown expenses for that year (i.e., for every $100 the Government spent on core Crown expenses, 72 cents was budgeted for IDC).

"The IDC budget for 2026/27 is also 0.72 percent of the forecast core Crown expenses for this year."

The spokesperson for Peters indicated that two-thirds of New Zealand's aid spending in the last financial year was focused on the Pacific, which meant an overall 10 percent cut in the aid budget - while ring-fencing Pacific funding - would require a "30 percent cut in every aid dollar New Zealand spends outside of the Pacific".

Outside of the Pacific, the region that got the most aid spending was Asia, receiving around 17 percent in 2025/26 (or 51 percent of non-Pacific aid funding), the spokesperson explained, which supported New Zealand's foreign policy reset - prioritising lifting relationships with South East Asian partners.

"New Zealand's recent lift in its relationships with South East Asian partners would be put a risk by cutting our aid to the region, with consequent impacts on our country's security, prosperity, and reputation."

Finally, the spokesperson indicated humanitarian crises were "also big draws" from non-Pacific aid funding. For example, over the last three financial years, New Zealand had provided an average of $14.5m a year to the Israel-Hamas conflict humanitarian response and $12.9m a year to Ukraine.

"This humanitarian budget would also need to be radically cut if New Zealand's non-Pacific IDC budget were cut by 30 percent."

The spokesperson said other parties needed to be "upfront" about how much they proposed to cut in these areas.

When asked about the comments suggesting its figure was "incorrect", a National Party spokesperson reiterated to RNZ that foreign aid funding had increased by around 26 percent since 2021, "from $777m to $982m a year over 2024 to 2027".

World.title: Erica Stanford hits out at union president after Teaching Council sex offender report
World.content:
The Education Minister has hit out at the president of the country's largest education union, questioning whether she should remain in the role because of her previous involvement with the Teaching Council.

Erica Stanford said a "rotten culture" inside the Teaching Council allowed sex offender teacher Timothy Fisher to continue teaching despite multiple warning signs.

On Tuesday, barrister Katherine Anderson KC released a scathing report finding the council should have struck Fisher off a decade before he was convicted of a litany of indecency and sex offences against children, most of them under 12-years-old.

Stanford said unions had too much influence over the council through elected positions, creating conflicts between their role representing teachers and the council's responsibility as a regulator.

"I have got rid of the ability for the elected members to be on the governing body. I have got 100 percent ministerial appointed people who have skills in child protection, regulatory systems, disciplinary systems, finance and risk and governance as well as great principles," she said.

"That is going to be key to shift that rotten culture out of the Teaching Council which frankly was infected by the unions."

NZEI Te Riu Roa president Ripeka Lessels. Supplied / NZEI

Stanford singled out NZEI Te Riu Roa president Ripeka Lessels, a former deputy chair and long-serving council member, saying she was involved in shaping the culture.

"I'm not sure her position is tenable as head of the teaching union any more," she said.

NZEI and the Post Primary Teachers' Association (PPTA) were still calling for the return of an independent Teaching Council, "and I suggest they should reconsider their position after [Tuesday's] pretty appalling report".

In a statement, NZEI did not directly address Stanford's criticism of Lessels.

The union said the report exposed failures in the system and supported strengthening child-safety processes, but argued removing elected teacher representatives from the council risked " further politicisation of the education system by the government of the day".

Current Teaching Council chair Patrick Walsh. Supplied / Sacred Heart College

It also noted current Teaching Council chair Patrick Walsh, who was appointed by Stanford, was on the Teaching Council's disciplinary tribunal and governing council during the period covered by the report.

"The safety and well-being of our tamariki are paramount, and we support calls to strengthen processes at the Teaching Council," NZEI said.

"Upholding child safety and the mana of the teaching profession are mutually reinforcing, not binary objectives. Ensuring the teaching profession has an independent and elected voice on the governance of the Teaching Council is an important way of ensuring teachers have a say in the effective strengthening of ways to achieve both objectives."

World.title: 'Constipated bureaucratic beast': Shane Jones says Otago fast-track mine going too slow
World.content:
New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones says the proposed Bendigo-Ophir gold mine has taken too long to advance through the fast-track approvals process, blaming legislation that has taken on the form of a "constipated bureaucratic beast".

On a visit to the mine site near Cromwell on Tuesday, he reinforced his support for the industry, taking aim at "woke, brittle, anti-mining mythology" as a group of local protesters rallied at the gate.

Jones told a crowd of staff, supporters and other local election candidates that he had previously visited the site about two years ago.

"I wasn't to know that mythology, falsehoods and misinformation would mar what is a legitimate process i.e. securing the necessary consents so that our country can grow," he said.

Protesters outside the Bendigo-Ophir mine site in the Dunstan Mountains on Tuesday. RNZ / Katie Todd

Australian-based Santana Minerals claimed the mine would deliver billions of dollars in revenue and employ hundreds of people.

The company's fast-track application, lodged nearly a year earlier, had been beset by processing pauses, requests for hundreds of pages of technical evidence, unresolved legal and Treaty hurdles, and pushback from conservation groups.

There had also been fierce opposition from some locals with concerns about potential impacts on the environment, native species, waterways and existing industries.

Chief executive Damian Spring said the company was committed to taking good care of the place its people called home.

"To date, we've put in $100 million behind our belief. We're ready to keep going. We're now less than 50 days from the panel's expected draft decision. There's a great deal [of] work behind us and hopefully much more ahead," he said.

Shane Jones at Santana Minerals' Exploration Base near Cromwell on Tuesday. RNZ / Katie Todd

Jones' visit was criticised by opposition groups opposed to the mine, who labelled it inappropriate and accused Jones of putting pressure on the fast-track panel.

Nine locals gathered to share their feelings in person at the mine gate, equipped with placards and loudhailers.

Chris Naylor, from Clyde, said he was particularly concerned about any risk of the tailings dam failing near the Clutha River, "poisoning everyone basically from Cromwell right down to Balclutha".

"It's privatising the profit and socialising the costs ... Shane Jones is just prepared to poison the environment for short-term political gain. It's just appalling," he said.

Deb Robb said the country did not need more gold, particularly in a climate crisis, and Jones should stay clear of the consenting process.

"He shouldn't be pushing this when it's sitting before the panel now. Completely inappropriate," she said.

A spokesperson for Sustainable Tarras said Jones' visit had sent a clear message to the local community.

"He drove straight past some of the locals most impacted by the mine, to be schmoozed by the Australian mining company he champions, members of Santana's online support group and other attendees at the private event."

Protesters outside the Bendigo-Ophir mine site in the Dunstan Mountains on Tuesday. RNZ / Katie Todd

Jones rejected any notion of undue pressure on the fast-track panel, saying his visit was to affirm his ongoing commitment to expand the mineral sector.

However, while paying a visit to a historic rabbiter's hut on the mine site, Jones joked "if I don't get the right decision out of this fast-track, that's their new residence".

Jones said when campaigning on fast-track improvements in 2023, he expected approvals to move "a lot quicker" than they actually had.

Politicians surrendering control of the process to the Environmental Protection Authority was "probably a mistake", Jones said.

Later, at a public event in Cromwell, Jones' pro-mining rhetoric continued with a commitment that New Zealand First would never tolerate the weakening of mining "in order to suit people's beliefs as they seek to worship at the feet of the climate change idols".

Before a packed room of about 150 people, Jones fielded questions on fishing, carbon credits, fast-track housing and AI.

World.title: Social housing development offers residents ability to use electric cars
World.content:
Residents of a new social housing development in Auckland's Glen Eden will be able to book and drive two electric cars as part of a trial to reduce their transport costs.

Visionwest has built 24 apartments on land near the local baptist church that founded the organisation, and people who are on the Ministry of Social Development's housing register move in next month.

Chief executive Lisa Woolley said it wanted to help provide affordable housing and the subsidised rent included the use of two electric cars.

"Running a car is expensive, it's especially expensive right now ... and so what we've provided through partnership with others are two bookable EV cars."

She said the apartments were close to both bus and train stations.

"Our hope is that in time the tenants won't even need to own a car. We're excited about that, it's about making a sustainable transport option for the whanau that live there," Wolley said.

"Once we get whanau in we'll be able to share with them how they can use those cars, we're really keen to see them well used."

There were more than 1100 people on the wait list for public housing in West Auckland and more than 19,000 waiting across the country.

Visionwest's outreach team worked alongside many people struggling to find stable housing and afford basic living costs.

"There a lots of varied reasons why people are in housing distress ... we need more houses that are for social and affordable housing to make sure that people can access affordable housing with the right support," Woolley said.

Visionwest chief executive Lisa Woolley says more affordable housing is needed. Supplied

Visionwest housed more than 1000 households and last year helped 441 families move into permanent housing.

The 24 apartments were among 800 tenancies it managed, including 200 town houses it owned.

The apartments were the fist stage of its Village of Hope - Te Kāinga o te Tūmanako, which officially opened on Tuesday.

The development was supported by the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport with financing from the Community Housing Funding Agency and Visionwest's own funding.

Woolley said the residents would have access to wraparound support and be in a community that included kaumatua and older residents, people with disabilities, families and single adults.

Visionwest helped to provide housing, food support, financial mentoring, youth, counselling and home healthcare.

"Community housing providers play an important role in providing and increasing the supply of social and affordable housing. Alongside this provision, the wrap around support is equally important to ensure whanau can get the support they need as they look at their goals for their future and the future of their children," said Woolley.

Eight ground-floor apartments were designed for accessible living and reserved for kaumatua and older residents, and those with disabilities.

Woolley said when people had secure housing, they started to thrive.

World.title: Kingmaker in waiting? Opportunity's Qiulae Wong makes her mark in debate
World.content:
Analysis - Winston Peters has spent three decades perfecting the art of being kingmaker. But last night, there were signs of a changing of the guard - with Opportunity's Qiulae Wong making a compelling claim to the title.

It was on 12 October 1996 that New Zealand went to the polls for its first MMP election, finally breaking the stranglehold of the two big parties and granting Peters the balance of power.

So, it was fitting that, 30 years and one day later, the minor parties had the debate stage and spotlight all to themselves. And boy, did they make the most of it.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406736353112

Each participant brought enthusiasm in spades to TVNZ's Multi-Party Debate, testing their differences and trading barbs.

In the aftermath, ACT leader David Seymour held a can of Red Bull aloft, neatly capturing the extra energy injected since their last, almost-cordial confab at Stuff's Kingmakers debate.

The contenders had plenty to be energised about. The 1News-Verian poll, released an hour before the showdown, put the parties' combined support above 40 percent - an extraordinary slice of the electorate.

At the last election, the minor parties won just 31 percent of the vote. The election before that, 18 percent. And before that, a measly 15 percent.

No longer are these just fringe outsiders. They are pivotal parties, some of whom will wield considerable influence over the next government.

And according to the latest poll, the biggest bargaining chip could well belong to the newest player. Opportunity has surged to 8 percent, handing it the balance of power.

From the debate's outset, its leader Qiulae Wong made clear her willingness to work with just about anybody on stage - even if the feeling was less reciprocal.

At various points, she was criticised or dismissed outright by every other participant. But the political neophyte largely held her own, appearing unfazed by the badgering and laughing off the insults.

The sharpest conflicts were with ideological opposite Winston Peters and her most alike, the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick.

Winston Peters (L) and Qiulae Wong at the debate. TVNZ / Harley Peters

Peters invoked his decades of experience, even pointing out he'd met former Singapore PM Lee Kuan Yew, "unlike some people around here".

The NZ First leader drew a deliberate contrast with Wong, describing her as having been around for only "five minutes".

But Wong did not let the comments slide. She repeatedly challenged Peters, most forcefully over his comments on unity and diversity, which she labelled "really dangerous rhetoric".

Nor did she retreat from her refusal to serve in a government with Peters as foreign minister, describing his remarks directed at Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan as "clearly racist".

One of the most instructive exchanges was with Swarbrick, when the exceptional moderator Tova O'Brien asked both leaders to explain what separated the Greens and Opportunity.

"The Green Party want to change the government," Swarbrick shot back, before rattling off the "massive attacks" she said the coalition government had inflicted over the past three years.

Wong had a ready rejoinder too: "Imagine how many of those most egregious things … the Greens could have stopped if they were willing to work with National."

That conveniently ignored that National was equally unprepared to work with the Greens. But it drove home a distinct difference - one party, prepared to act as a handbrake on "extreme ideas", the other preferring to be an accelerator for its own.

Both leaders made their case clearly, and both have reason to be satisfied. Indeed, few of the participants will be particularly upset with how the night unfolded.

David Seymour stood alone on several issues. TVNZ / Harley Peters

Seymour was especially effective at carving out his own ground in a crowded field, repeatedly distinguishing ACT from its potential partners and opponents.

On several issues, he stood alone - the only leader prepared to back drug-testing beneficiaries, and the only one willing to defend the supermarkets.

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Rawiri Waititi also delivered a more assured performance than in the first showdown, speaking directly to his party's supporters.

His priorities are different too. While the other parties are battling over their share of the party vote, Te Pāti Māori is concentrating on winning electorate seats.

Waititi even suggested that strategy had done the Greens a favour: "You're welcome, Chlöe."

Ultimately though, the stakes were highest for Opportunity - dependent on clearing that five percent threshold.

World.title: As it happened: 13 October on the Election 2026 campaign trail
World.content:
ACT's David Seymour, Te Pāti Māori's Rawiri Waititi, New Zealand First's Winston Peters, Opportunity's Qiulae Wong and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick were canvassed on their views across a range of topics - from the government's books and cost of living to health and transport.

The leaders once again outlined which other parties they would be willing (or not) to work with, whether they thought GST should be removed from food, and if there were too many people in the country's prisons.

World.title: 'Humiliating' - former PM Helen Clark slams NZ abstention on UN pandemic vote
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Helen Clark has slammed New Zealand's abstention on a vote on global pandemic preparedness at the United Nations, describing it as "humiliating".

New Zealand was among five countries that did not vote for a UN declaration designed to strengthen national, regional and international co-operation in the event of a future pandemic.

The United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response, while New Zealand and Paraguay abstained.

The other 153 member states of the UN voted for the declaration, which called for "stronger national, regional and international cooperation, guided by science, equity and respect for human rights, and it welcomes last year's landmark adoption of the World Health Organization (WHO) Pandemic Agreement".

In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) said "New Zealand supports the aim of strengthening global health systems and improving pandemic preparedness and response."

But it said: "New Zealand does not support language welcoming the adoption of the Pandemic Agreement…It is very important to New Zealand that its sovereign decision making on health is protected."

The UN said the declaration was "political and non-binding".

Helen Clark - a former UN official - called the vote "humiliating for NZ" in a social media post.

Embedded content removed for printing https://x.com/HelenClarkNZ/status/2109748226123591956

"How low can NZ go?... This results from [New Zealand First]'s courting of the anti-vax vote," she said.

"As New Zealand noted at the time of the adoption of the Pandemic Agreement by the World Health Assembly [2024], any future decision on whether or not to sign and ratify the Pandemic Agreement will be informed by a full National Interest Test under domestic procedures," MFAT said.

The International Health Regulations (IHR) define countries' rights and obligations in handling public health events and emergencies that have the potential to cross borders, a statement on the Ministry of Health website said.

New Zealand was a signatory and had been since its establishment.

But earlier this year, New Zealand told the WHO Director-General it was rejecting the amendments.

Political reaction

In a statement on social media, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said his party "ensured the National Interest Test was included in the coalition agreement to keep our sovereign decision making with New Zealand, not Geneva".

"We believe it is essential to New Zealand that its sovereign decision making on health is protected," Peters said.

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins called the vote "an embarrassment to New Zealand".

"Frankly, I am astounded that New Zealand has shown such cowardice in an important vote before the UN," he said.

It was another example of Christopher Luxon "letting Winston Peters embrace conspiracy theories as New Zealand government positions", Hipkins said.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon initially tried to skirt questions about the vote, saying: "It wasn't a Cabinet decision, you'll need to direct further questions to the foreign minister."

But he then appeared to disagree with Hipkins that it was an "important vote".

"There is literally, every day, a number of declarations that go through the UN - of major and minor significance and importance. Important ones come through a Cabinet decision-making process," Luxon said.

"But in this case, this is one that is up to the Minister of Foreign Affairs to make a call on."

National MP Matt Doocey said National ministers supported voting in favour while formally recording their reservations. However, a Cabinet decision was not required, and Winston Peters made his decision as Foreign Affairs Minister.

World.title: 'Knee jerk response' - Coastguard air volunteers grounded over safety rule changes
World.content:
An air patrol volunteer for Coastguard says he has major safety concerns for boaties in the upper North Island after two teams were grounded.

The volunteer pilots in Auckland and Northland have been immediately benched, due to a change in safety standards which now requires pilots to have commercial licenses.

Coastguard Auckland Air Patrol president Andrew Lamb told Checkpoint the decision came as a total shock.

"We had been having some discussions and then on Friday morning, I got a phone call saying that the board had stood us down for taskings or flight training on the Saturday," he said.

Regulation changes by the Rescue Coordination Centre New Zealand (RCCNZ) had implications for maritime rescue and aviation assets, Lamb said.

"Where we had been flying under one regulation, we no longer would qualify for that and we wouldn't meet the new standards because of being a volunteer organisation effectively," he said.

Lamb said it had not been well thought out as to how search and rescue support gaps would be filled.

"Is Defence Force going to be able to fill that gap? I don't think so," he said.

"We are a search vessel, so we guide the boats… onto the distressed vessel, or it might be a person in water. So we get there a lot quicker. We travel at over 140 knots. So we get there a lot faster than a boat would."

There had been no details shared with grounded volunteers as to how the gap would be filled, Lamb said.

"[From] Ohakea to get an Air Force defense crew up to Auckland and Haraki Gulf… my understanding is it would take about four hours whereas we could probably get there in an hour to an hour and a half. So less than half the time and an awful lot cheaper as well," he said.

"RCCNZ won't task Coastguard in any of these searches because we don't meet their requirements. So there's just a big gap and I my concern is no one has actually thought about this gap. We've made a knee jerk response to something and we haven't backfilled the solution."

Coastguard said the decision was not a reflection on its air patrol volunteers but because Maritime New Zealand's Rescue Coordination Centre introduced new standards for search and rescue operations last year.

World.title: Australia defeats South Africa by 214 runs on day five in Durban
World.content:
Australia has taken a 1-0 lead in the three-Test series against South Africa after a dominant 214-run victory on day five at Kingsmead.

The Proteas lost their last four wickets for just five runs to be bowled out for 206, with Josh Hazlewood finishing with career-best figures of 6-49.

Matt Renshaw was named player-of-the-match for his knocks of 190 and 82, as well as his two second-innings wickets.

His spot in the team is now assured for the foreseeable future, but with Cameron Green still to return from injury, questions will be asked about where Renshaw is best suited in the line-up and he said after the match it was "pretty nice" to settle in the middle order.

"It's a bit different to opening the batting, but happy to do whatever the team needs me to do," he said during the post-match presentation.

Renshaw's batting set up the victory but his part-time off-spin became key to winning the game in the fourth innings after a dogged 69-run partnership between Aiden Markram (75 off 237) and Wiaan Mulder (29 off 110).

It finally came to an end after 34 overs when Mulder got a feather on a Hazlewood delivery down the leg side, where wicketkeeper Alex Carey completed a phenomenal one-handed grab.

Loading Instagram content

Four balls later, Renshaw nicked off Kyle Verreynne for a duck to give Australia momentum heading into lunch.

Markram, the hero of South Africa's run chase in last year's World Test Championship final victory over Australia, continued his resistance alongside Marco Jansen (35) before Hazlewood clean bowled him with the second new ball.

Simon Harmer (0) gloved one through to Alex Carey later in the over and Markram's vigil finally ended when Australia successfully reviewed an appeal for caught behind, with DRS showing a faint inside edge.

When Anrich Nortje (4) lobbed Hazlewood to the leg side, South Africa had lost 4-5 in three overs and the match was over.

Look back on all the day five action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in our ScoreCentre.

World.title: How NRL's Super League bid could revive a fallen giant
World.content:
As talks over the NRL's proposed investment in Super League near the pointy end of negotiations, Trent Robinson says a partnership between the two competitions could help reinvigorate the sport in France.

After guiding the Sydney Roosters to the fourth NRL premiership victory of his tenure earlier this month, Robinson would have every right to be sat somewhere in the south of France with his feet up sipping a glass of red.

But instead he finds himself offering his services to the French national team, where he supports head coach Laurent Frayssinous as director of rugby, in preparation for Friday's World Cup opener against Samoa.

On the other side of the world, club owners in England and the Super League's two French sides — Catalans Dragons and Toulouse Olympique — are weighing up an offer that would lead to the NRL providing an investment into the code's only other professional competition.

NRL's Super League investment offer Britain's Super League has revealed it has received an investment offer from the NRL, taking Australian involvement in British rugby league's premier tournament a significant step closer.

Some British clubs are reluctant to cede power to the NRL but Robinson is a firm believer in how Australia can help revive France as an international force.

"I think the NRL will have a world vision of rugby league, and I know they see the value of French rugby league and the importance of it," the Roosters coach told AAP.

"I think it would continue the progression of having a place at the table."

France was one of the sport's leading powers in the 1950s and 1960s but their stock has fallen considerably.

The presence of two French clubs in Super League, from which the majority of the national team is drawn, has so far failed to translate into international success.

France was supposed to host this year's World Cup until the government pulled the pin, citing the expense of hosting rugby union's World Cup in 2023 and the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Ranked 11th in the world, France are seen as $21 outsiders by bookmakers for their meeting with a Samoan team laden with NRL talent at Western Sydney Stadium.

Mitchell Pearce, who has retired in France after playing for Catalans, said: "There's some great French talent and they'll be enjoying the opportunity (to play in the World Cup).

Samoa plans World Cup tilt With the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup officially launched, Samoa are looking to repeat their fairytale run to the 2022 final.

"I think it'd be great for the NRL to expand and open up French rugby league and help the development pathways."

France's struggles to field a strong international side, they were hammered 62-4 by Samoa four years ago, can surely be attributed to the fact their clubs are operating in the most cash-rich market in any rugby code.

France's top rugby union competition, the Top14, has a salary cap of roughly $18 million, the NRL's is around $12 million, while the Super League's is approaching $4 million.

"There's a respect that is growing in France for rugby league from when I first went 24 years ago," Robinson said.

"It's because we've got a great sport and because of the Catalans and Toulouse.

"It's a fair mountain to climb, the Top 14, and trying to catch up with that.

"But it (league) does have respect and the NRL would add to that because there's an enormous amount of respect for it in rugby union circles."

AAP

World.title: Michael Jordan Last Dance jersey sells for record $20m
World.content:
The jersey Michael Jordan wore during Game 2 of the 1998 NBA Finals, featured in the Last Dance documentary, has sold for a record $US14 million ($20 million).

Hunt Auctions announced yesterday that the game-worn, autographed Chicago Bulls jersey was purchased by Miami real estate investor Ron Firman in a private sale.

It is the highest price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia, and according to the auction house, the newly sold Jordan jersey ranks as the second-largest sale in history among game-worn sports jerseys.

The New York Yankees jersey worn by Babe Ruth in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series — during which Ruth called his shot ahead of a home run — went for $US24.12 million in 2024.

Jordan and the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in six games to win the 1998 championship, the sixth and final title of his career in Chicago.

Game 2, played on June 5, 1998, in Salt Lake City, saw Chicago even the series 1-1 in large part due to a dominant performance from its superstar guard.

Jordan put up 37 points, five rebounds, and three assists in a 93-88 victory. He would go on to collect his sixth and final Finals MVP award, two more than anyone else in NBA history, nine days later.

The wildly popular Last Dance documentary, released in 2020, was centred around that 1997-98 Bulls season.

"The record-setting price achieved for the related Michael Jordan jersey is yet another corroborative result as to the significance of Jordan within the industry and popular culture. This remarkable garment bore witness to one of Jordan's most hallowed NBA Finals appearances as part of his 'Last Dance' season to complete his illustrious career," David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions, said in a statement.

"While Michael Jordan's importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established, it has now escalated to an elite asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art."

The previous record for a basketball memorabilia item was $US12.26 million for the home jersey worn by Jordan in Game 3 of the 1998 Finals, which was sold via auction in September.

Reuters

World.title: European Tour gives LIV golfers ultimatum and shuts door on playing both
World.content:
The European Tour has delivered an ultimatum to players contemplating the new version of LIV Golf, saying anyone who joins will not be allowed to remain a tour member.

"Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, chief executive of the European Tour, said in a statement yesterday first reported by the BBC.

The tour previously let LIV players keep their European membership as long as they paid fines for playing LIV events that conflicted with the tour.

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Australian golfers Cameron Smith, Lucas Herbert, Elvius Smylie and Marc Leishman all played in the LIV league in 2026.

It extended an olive branch earlier this year to nine players, allowing them to play LIV events without sanctions provided they settled all previous fines and agreed to add European Tour events to their 2026 schedules.

Kinnings delivered a much stronger message — us or them — as LIV tries to emerge from bankruptcy after Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund cut off financial support.

LIV has up to $300 million from BC Partners as it leans into a 10-tournament season focusing on team competition and players owning equity in LIV 2.0. Players have until October 25 to decide whether to stick with LIV, which could determine whether the beleaguered circuit can move forward out of bankruptcy.

The European Tour, however, is requiring anyone seeking to join to disclose where they intend to play in 2027. The tour said it would terminate membership if the disclosures prove false.

"As we have said for many years, we have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by," Kinnings said. "Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour."

Players must be European Tour members to compete in the Ryder Cup next September, adding pressure to the likes of Tyrrell Hatton of England, Tom McKibbin of Northern Ireland, Adrian Meronk of Poland and Thomas Detry of Belgium.

A lawyer for Jon Rahm said last week in a bankruptcy hearing for LIV that the former number one wanted to terminate his LIV contract. The question for Rahm, a two-time major champion, is how he works his way back to the PGA Tour.

Sergio Garcia also asked to end his LIV contract, and David Puig of Spain has indicated he is ready to take on a European Tour schedule.

The European Tour is negotiating a renewed alliance with the PGA Tour, which involves commercial opportunities and a path for the 10 leading players on the Race to Dubai to get PGA Tour cards.

Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra, who both previously played for LIV Golf, are a lock to earn PGA Tour cards this year off the European Tour points list. Bernd Wiesberger of Austria, another player who signed early with LIV, also has a chance at a tour card.

The plan of LIV 2.0 is to have such a streamlined schedule to allow players to compete elsewhere. But the PGA Tour bans LIV players for at least one year dating to their last LIV appearance, and now the European tour is demanding them to pick a tour.

AP

World.title: Smith monitored for concussion after hit to helmet while batting
World.content:
Australia will continue to test Steve Smith for a delayed concussion, after the vice-captain's blow to the head added further questions around the side for the second Test.

Smith did not take the field on day four in Durban, after being struck on the side of the helmet by a short ball from South African speedster Anrich Nortje while batting in the morning session.

The 37-year-old was assessed on the field and passed a test, appearing unfazed as he reached 27 in Australia's pursuit of quick runs.

Steve Smith copped a blow on the helmet early in his innings. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

However, Australia opted to keep him off the field in case there had been a concussion, and conduct further tests. As of stumps, Smith had not failed any.

He is expected to be tested again on Tuesday morning in Durban, and will continue to be assessed for as long as Australia sees fit.

Smith has previously battled concussions, most famously when he was struck in the head by Jofra Archer during the 2019 Ashes.

While the early signs are good, any concussion would leave Smith in serious doubt for Sunday's second Test in Gqeberha given the tiered-return protocols.

It would also add to the quandary around the make-up of Australia's side for that match.

Josh Inglis is back in South Africa after his fractured finger, batting in the nets wearing a splint on Monday and offering every sign he will be available for Sunday.

Cameron Green is also recovering from an abdominal strain, and not yet ruled out of the second Test.

Either of the pair would likely have batted at number five in this Test if fit, but Matt Renshaw's scores of 190 and 82 have made the case for him to stay there.

AAP

World.title: Blakey vows to 'win back trust' after Roos move as Blues add Whitfield
World.content:
Nick Blakey has apologised for his involvement in the Pullman Hotel scandal after sealing a move to North Melbourne.

The trade with Sydney for Blakey was North's first deal of the day, with the second coming in the form of Zane Duursma's trade to Melbourne.

However, the headliner was well and truly the move for Blakey, one of the biggest names involved in the trade period.

The Kangaroos parted ways with the No.6 pick in this year's draft as well as pick 47, its 2027 and 2028 second-round picks and a 2028 first-round pick while receiving pick 52 and Sydney's 2028 second-rounder in return alongside Blakey.

In his first public comments since being suspended by the Swans for his involvement in the Pullman Hotel scandal from August, Blakey apologised for his actions.

"I want to say that I'm sorry for the events that led up to my exit from Sydney," Blakey said in a North Melbourne statement.

"I know I have to win back the trust of the broader community, football and otherwise.

"Now I have the opportunity to move forward and I want to thank North Melbourne for helping me find a fresh start.

Carlton bolstered its list with the acquisition of two-time All-Australian halfback Lachie Whitfield from the Giants. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Brendon Thorne)

"I'm grateful I have landed at a place that has such deep connections to me and my family.

"There is so much potential in this group and I'm looking forward to getting to work to help take North Melbourne forward."

Kangaroos list manager Brady Rawlings said the club's board was "very supportive" of the move to acquire Blakey despite the police investigation hanging over his head.

Elsewhere in the trade period, Carlton was involved in a pair of moves, sending ruckman Flynn Riley to Collingwood for a future third-round pick while adding two-time All-Australian halfback Lachie Whitfield in a deal with the GWS Giants which saw a total of five draft picks exchanged.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from the penultimate day of the AFL trade period.

World.title: Cyclist who ditched Australia withdrawn from world champs over allegations
World.content:
British track cyclist Matthew Richardson, who defected from Australian cycling at the end of the Paris Games, has been withdrawn from this week's UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai

Richardson had been earlier named in the British squad for the championships, which run from October 14 to 18, before British Cycling confirmed he had been withdrawn.

"British Cycling can confirm that Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain Cycling Team squad for the upcoming 2026 Tissot UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai, China," a spokesperson said in a statement provided to Reuters.

The governing body did not give a reason for Richardson's withdrawal.

The Times reported that Richardson had been removed from the team amid an investigation into "alleged discriminatory posts and behaviour".

Reuters has not independently verified the allegations, and has contacted Rocket Sports, Richardson's management agency, for comment from the rider.

Richardson was injured in a crash during the World Series keirin event in Japan and was ruled out from making his highly anticipated England debut at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in July.

Richardson was born in Maidstone, England, and moved to Australia at the age of nine.

A week after the closing ceremony of the Paris Games — where Richardson won silver medals in the individual sprint and men's keirin and a bronze in the team sprint — he stunned Australia by announcing his defection.

In 2025, Richardson became the first rider to break nine seconds for the "flying 200m", setting a new time of 8.941 seconds.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Refusing to yield momentum, ruthless Australia is perfectly set for victory
World.content:
Momentum, most agree, is among the most elusive psychological phenomena in professional sport. How to obtain and maintain the positive kind? How exactly to halt and reverse its opposite?

For three and a half days of this Durban Test, since Matt Renshaw began calmly pulling Australia's first innings out of the fire and seizing the game's initiative, Australia has stubbornly maintained control. South Africa, haphazardly, has failed to regain it.

Renshaw's dream Test continues Matt Renshaw claims his maiden Test wicket to help Australia reduce South Africa to 4-102 at stumps on day four of the first Test in Durban.

Early on day four, Renshaw made a further mockery of the difficulties that have curtailed the progress of every other batter in this game — so far, none from either team has managed so much as a half-century — and belted 82 more precious runs in even time.

More absurdly still, as shadows covered the Kingsmead pitch late on day four, the burly Queenslander ripped one of his unheralded off-spinners out of the rough and removed Temba Bavuma, capping a horror game in which the Proteas skipper has been unable to buy a run and incapable of engineering the moments of inspiration his opposite number constantly pulls from his hat.

Could Bavuma have done much to drastically alter what has transpired here? Other than by contributing his usual runs, probably not.

He certainly can't grab the ball himself and rip through a middle-order batsman, as Pat Cummins did to Tristan Stubbs within sight of stumps.

Nor can Bavuma and his teammates always play out of their skins, above expectations, beyond their limitations, which has been the impossible task South Africa has pulled off, to the betterment of Test cricket, in the last two years.

That the home side enters the final day 319 runs in arrears with six wickets in hand is a testament to the chain of events a single player can set in motion, as Renshaw has in this game.

Only a few forced errors prevented Australia calling it a perfect day: looking less like a Test opener by the day, Travis Head fell cheaply again; thanks to a fast, frightful bouncer from the indefatigable Anrich Nortje, Steve Smith is being assessed under concussion protocols, which may imperil his selection for the second Test, although it did not stop him from using an iPad to assess the catching chances he missed out on as he sat in the pavilion.

Steve Smith copped a blow on the helmet early in his innings. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Basically everything else about Australia's gung-ho approach worked out. To set a target as imposing as 421, they rattled along at 4.65 runs an over in the first session and a spirit-sapping 6.36 in the second, each batsman more enthusiastic than the last to attack at all costs.

Nic Maddinson clubbed an entertaining 46 to establish the launching pad. Smith and Marnus Labuschagne wound back the clock with a typically hyperactive partnership, the latter reaffirming the sense he has turned the corner, towards big runs. Renshaw reprised his peak Matthew Hayden routine, toying with the South African bowlers. Even Beau Webster, previously out of sorts, made fluent runs too and could be permitted some frustration that the declaration halted his spree.

Cummins, in a contrasting cameo to his first innings vigil, hammered 32 from 12 deliveries, bombing Simon Harmer for a string of sixes that left South Africa dejected and dashed any remaining hope the off-spinner held of selection in the second Test.

The final effect of the Australian batting effort was something like a WCW tag team taking turns flying off the ropes with elbows extended.

All that now stands between Australia and certain victory is the solitary excellence of Aiden Markram, who always saves his best for Australia and finished the day undefeated on 45.

In the corresponding Test eight years ago, when the Cape Town fiasco was still on the horizon, Markram's epic century delayed Australia's victory in almost identical circumstances.

If the day was characterised by one team doing a bunch of things far better than its opponent, special mention must go to Josh Hazlewood for not just the most classically Hazlewoodian stat line — eight overs, three maidens, 2-20 — but for nipping out David Bedingham for 46, thus ending a 66-run second-wicket partnership with Markram that shaped as South Africa's last realistic chance of getting close.

Are Australians complacent about the unassuming New South Welshman and his mountains of wickets? Do we underestimate the problem it poses to batsmen when a 196cm giant releases a heavy ball from that kind of stratospheric trajectory, lifting length balls into their ribs? How much harder is that to handle when, at the other end, the skipper skids it through lower, attacking the off stump from a different angle?

Probably it is the closest thing in the present era to what batsmen encountered four decades ago when Malcolm Marshall and Joel Garner combined to devastating effect for the golden-era West Indies.

Another good thing South Africa has given Test cricket in recent years is the guarantee of a result: not a single encounter there in the past decade has ended in a draw. Long may it be so.

Tech.title: Google finally releases Gemini 4 Argon
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After months sitting on the sidelines of the frontier AI race, Google has finally launched its long-awaited Gemini 4 Argon model, claiming it can compete with the best the industry has to offer.

Google says Argon delivers “frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows,” while cutting down on hedging, repetition, and the cliches that continue to plague AI chatbots. The company claims Argon outperforms rival models like GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.5 across a range of benchmarks, including coding, cybersecurity, science, finance, and law.

Google says it’s already putting Argon to use internally, such as finding and patching cybersecurity vulnerabilities, halving the computing power needed to power YouTube’s comments section, and debugging the drone physics simulator for Alphabet’s drone delivery company Wing.

The model is rolling out today to Google’s higher-tier Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and AI mode in Search, as well to Ultra subscribers on its agentic development platform Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Argon will be available to Plus subscribers or free users.

Google is pricing Argon very competitively. The model is launching with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5 models. Even after those costs double at the end November — when the introductory period finishes — Argon will still be significantly cheaper than its frontier rivals on a per-token basis, though this doesn’t necessarily translate to lower costs in practice, as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks.

The launch fills in some of the blanks left behind from when Google first teased Argon a few weeks ago. In line with other recent frontier model releases, the public rollout follows a limited release to a select set of “trusted cyber defenders” to be tested for potential risks.

Argon is Google’s first major frontier release since Gemini 3 in late 2025. In the intervening months, impressive models from Anthropic and OpenAI have seen Google trail far behind its rivals. Seismic internal shakeups raised further doubts about the company’s ability — or desire — to reclaim its position and compete at the frontier of AI.

But Argon’s arrival suggests we can’t count Google out of the AI race just yet. Landing just a day after Meta announced its own frontier model, Muse Wonder Full, Argon is a reminder of how quickly the balance of power can shift in AI, and that the frontier is far from a two-horse race.

Tech.title: Buying Apple’s wall-mounted HomeView? The mount costs extra
Tech.content:
The HomeView smart home display announced by Apple today comes in two models that both cost $299: one with a speaker base, and the other being a self explanatory “Wall Mounted” version. If you want the latter, however, you’ll actually have to pay at least $59 more — the mounts required to actually affix the display to your wall are sold separately. Maybe calling it the “Mountless” version would have been more accurate?

Apple isn’t exactly shouting about that sneaky additional premium for wall-mounted HomeView customers. The details are mentioned in the small print at the bottom of the product announcement page:

HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (US), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (US), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (US).

It also becomes apparent when you go through the process of adding the HomeView to your basket on Apple’s webstore. You’re asked to choose from the available mount options (which doesn’t include the Power Mount PoE Wired yet) which each bump up that $299 price, or select “No mount” to proceed with no extra charge — but Apple clearly states on this option that the “HomeView (Wall Mounted) requires a mount and power solution to operate.”

Given you don’t get the funky iMac G4-style speaker base, it feels like Apple is charging the same price for half the product. Image: Apple / The Verge

Given it doesn’t ship with a power source, you can’t have the wall model HomeView leaning against something or laying on a flat surface to evade the extra cost. You also can’t buy the desktop model that doesn’t have any additional requirements and keep the speaker base aside because it can’t be converted into the wall version. They’re two distinct versions, and the wall option only comes in two colors. Presumably some third-party manufacturers will release more affordable wall mount options in time, but either way, folks who want to wall mount their HomeView will pay a premium over those who opt for the desktop model.

Tech.title: Apple’s HomeView display is now available to preorder
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is getting into smart displays with its new HomeView. It has a seven-inch squircle design, looking similar to a gargantuan Apple Watch mounted to a speaker base. The $299 HomeView is meant to be the centerpiece for Apple’s big push into the home, as it’s capable of controlling a host of smart home tech. Additionally, it can display recipes, show music playback controls, let you make FaceTime calls, and display a host of widgets.

The HomeView launches on Friday, November 13th, and it’ll likely be a popular holiday gift. You can preorder in in multiple colors, and you have the option at checkout to either include a speaker base (it includes a custom down-firing woofer and two passive radiators), or opt for a wall-mounted option that omits the base and its extra sound performance. They’re the same price.

The HomeView, like the Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini 2 that were announced today, goes big on Siri AI. When connected to an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, it supports natural-language voice interactions. Obviously, as a smart display with Thread and Matter connectivity it can control your smart home devices, but its AI capabilities let it surface info from your messages, emails, and more as well.

Tech.title: Here are all the new HomePod Mini 2 colors
Tech.content:
Apple’s HomePod Mini 2 is here, and we’ve gotten a close-up look at the second-gen smart speaker.

The HomePod Mini 2 comes with an upgraded S10 chip capable of powering Siri AI, though Apple says support for new AI features will roll out as part of a future update. It also offers a sound glow feature that matches its LED lights with the colors of a song’s album art and can work as your Mac’s default speaker.

Physically, the HomePod Mini 2 is almost identical to its predecessor, but the colors have changed. There’s now a pink model and a green model, and the blue has changed colors. There’s still black and white for those who want basics as well. I got to see them in Apple’s demo space, and the colors looked particularly striking when paired with iMac models that share the same color. One of the new features this year is the ability to use the Minis as the default speaker for a Mac.

The HomePod Mini 2 in blue.

The HomePod Mini 2 in pink.

Apple is launching the HomePod Mini 2 alongside a new HomeView smart display and a collection of smart home devices. Preorders for the $149 HomePod Mini open today, and the device will start shipping on October 30th.

Tech.title: Epic shifts to ‘AI-accelerated development’ for upcoming Disney game
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Epic Games plans to use AI to generate code and art for an unannounced Disney game, which is now delayed from its original March release window, according to a report from Bloomberg. The project’s developers have been given an “AI-first” mandate directing them to use tools like Anthropic’s Claude more to finish the game.

According to Bloomberg, one of the game’s directors said in a message to staff, “No more hand-written code.” Staff were also told that all of the game’s art will be “generated with full AI workflows.” In a statement given to Bloomberg, Epic Games spokesperson Jake Jones said the company is “embracing AI-accelerated development.”

Epic Games and Disney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The upcoming game is reportedly a shooter featuring characters from Marvel and Star Wars. It’s part of a multiyear collaboration between Epic and Disney, which also invested $1.5 billion in Epic in 2024. Epic already uses AI in Fortnite, which has previously featured Disney characters like an AI Darth Vader. But it sounds like Epic may be aiming to have AI do most of the heavy lifting on its new Disney game.

Tech.title: Apple’s HomePod Mini 2 is available to preorder
Tech.content: The speaker includes the S10 chip, which debuted in the Apple Watch Series 10, and it can power a host of features. It will support Siri AI after a future update, pairing you with a better, more helpful voice assistant. The speaker can be integrated into a four-speaker surround system with the new Apple TV 4K, and they can serve as speakers for a Mac computer (so long as it supports Wi-Fi 6E). Lastly, the top of the HomePod Mini 2 can arrange its LEDs to mimic the album artwork for the music you’re listening to.

Tech.title: DLSS 5 gets toned down for its Hogwarts Legacy debut next month
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When Nvidia originally showed off DLSS 5 earlier this year, the technology immediately got branded as gen AI for video games. To gamers, Nvidia had lost the plot. I personally couldn’t get over how faces were transformed using DLSS 5. The 15-year-old student from Hogwarts Legacy suddenly looked much older, and Grace from Resident Evil Requiem looked yassified.

Now more than six months later, DLSS 5 is about to debut properly in Hogwarts Legacy, and it looks like it has been seriously toned down. Nvidia published new comparison screenshots today, where the changes to faces are as subtle as they are in NBA 2K27. Teenagers no longer look like middle-aged men, and even the environmental changes look more subtle.

Nvidia’s DLSS 5 in Hogwarts Legacy in March.

Nvidia’s new Hogwarts Legacy DLSS 5 comparisons.

Nvidia has always maintained that developers have “detailed artistic control” over DLSS 5, and ultimately make the choice on how to implement the technology in their own games. DLSS 5 will now appear in Hogwarts Legacy on November 5th, and it’s also coming to Where Winds Meet late next month.

Nvidia is also improving the performance hit of DLSS 5 with an October update to the neural rendering system that should make it twice as fast on RTX 50-series GPUs and the upcoming RTX Spark laptops. “The DLSS 5 October update shrinks the footprint by 24 percent to roughly 118 million parameters while reducing 4K VRAM usage by 20 percent,” says Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes. This new DLSS 5 model will debut first in NBA 2K27 on October 16th and “will ship by default with future DLSS 5 games.”

Alongside the DLSS 5 updates, Nvidia has also shipped a new Nvidia app beta update that includes a faster performance mode for Frame Generation on RTX 40- and 50-series GPUs. The updated AI model uses a “faster and lighter algorithm to boost frame rates” for Frame Gen, Multi Frame Gen, and Dynamic Multi Frame Gen. Nvidia says it has “minor trade-offs in image quality,” and that performance mode for Frame Generation should now be up to 35 precent faster.

Tech.title: Satlyt, founded by a former Google and SpaceX product manager, raises $8M to run AI on satellites
Tech.content:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.

The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.

“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.

So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt, a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.

The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.

Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.

“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.

Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.

Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.

This week’s launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.

Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.

The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.

Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.

One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”

Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.

“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.

Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco. It all kicks off on Tuesday. Learn more here.

Tech.title: The 2026 Startup Battlefield Top 20: From organs to orbit and everything in between
Tech.content:

Every year, thousands of founders from around the world pitch us on what they believe the future should look like. This year’s Top 20 are building it from organs to orbit and everywhere in between.

Across this cohort, one theme kept emerging: Making the previously invisible measurable.

These founders are finding ways to understand signals we couldn’t previously capture, model systems too complex to predict, and turn the physical world into data that machines can actually act on. They’re measuring the biological clocks inside our bodies and growing miniature human organs in labs. They’re teaching robots to take on increasingly complex physical work and modeling the real world closely enough to predict what might happen next — even the behavior of wild animals. They’re extracting intelligence from scam calls and finding new ways to use the computing power already orbiting above our heads.

And then, of course, there’s the company trying to launch cargo into space with a giant hydrogen-powered cannon.

Subtle, this group is not.

What connects these 20 companies isn’t a single technology or industry. Tech.title: Spotify users on iOS 27 can now ask Siri to play music without having to say ‘on Spotify’
Tech.content:
In Brief

It’s now easier to use Spotify by talking to Siri on iPhones updated to iOS 27, Spotify said on Tuesday. Users will no longer need to specify “on Spotify” when they’re asking Siri to play music or other content using the streaming service’s apps.

Instead, users can just say whatever it is they want to hear, and Spotify will play the content, whether that’s a specific track, album, podcast, audiobook, or a broader query, like “play workout music,” or a request for one of Spotify’s features, like “play my DJ.”

Siri’s voice control can also be used to do things like request personalized recommendations, resume podcasts, search your library, or even create a Prompted Playlist with AI.

Spotify says removing the extra voice command will make hands-free listening feel more natural, as users can just focus on what they want to hear, not how to phrase the request properly to get their preferred music app to respond.

This feature works because Siri can now learn your music app preference. If you consistently use Spotify, it will route your audio requests to that app automatically.

The new feature is available globally for users with an iPhone 15 Pro or later, outside the EU, if Apple Intelligence is enabled in Settings.

Tech.title: Bumble agrees to a $1.3B acquisition deal as online dating faces a reset
Tech.content:
Bumble is getting a new owner. The dating app announced Tuesday that it has agreed to a $1.3 billion acquisition deal with Ithaca Holdings, marking a major shift for a company that once looked like one of the biggest success stories in online dating.

The deal would take the company private after years of declining subscriber numbers, falling revenue, and mounting pressure to rethink the online dating experience. The move may give Bumble a chance to work on its next chapter away from the pressure of public markets.

Founded in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble made a name for itself for its unique approach where only women made the first move. That helped it stand out in a crowded dating market, and the company eventually went public in 2021 at a valuation of roughly $14 billion.

Since then, however, the dating app landscape has changed considerably. Bumble has faced declining paying users, weaker revenue, and growing dissatisfaction with the familiar swipe-based model. The company recently reported second-quarter 2026 revenue of $211 million, down 15.2% year over year, while its paying user base fell 16.4% to approximately 3.2 million.

The acquisition follows a review of strategic options by an independent committee of Bumble’s board, which recommended the transaction after consulting outside legal and financial advisers. Wolfe Herd did not participate in the board’s discussions or vote on the deal, according to the press release.

“In Ithaca, we have found a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future,” Wolfe Herd said in a statement.

She also confirmed that she plans to stay actively involved in the business, working alongside Ithaca’s Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, and the Bumble team.

Going private might give Bumble more flexibility to experiment with new features and make changes without having to answer to public-market investors every quarter. The company has been exploring AI-driven features and putting more energy into helping people connect offline, reflecting a broader shift in how younger users approach dating.

One example is Plans, announced in July, which focuses on bringing people together through real-world activities. Wolfe Herd also recently revealed that the company is developing a new way for users to interact that could eventually replace the swipe-based model.
