Tech.title: SpaceXSI bundles X Premium, Grok, and Cursor into one subscription
Tech.content:
In Brief

In a bid to attract more subscribers, the company now known as SpaceX Super Intelligence is bundling all its subscriptions, including X Premium, Grok, and Cursor, into one plan called simply “The X Subscription.”

The idea is that the combined offering could potentially attract more subscribers than any single subscription, given the competitive paid AI subscription market, where SpaceXSI faces rivals like OpenAI, Anthropic, and others.

With The X Subscription, users can gain access to Grok for AI-powered chat, with support for voice, images, video, and the API. Grok’s agentic AI Bot is also available, as is Cursor for AI coding and the paid features that come with an X Premium subscription, like the blue verified checkmark, creator tools, and fewer ads.

There are five plans available on the new subscription: free, Plus ($8/month), Premium ($30/month), Super ($100/month), and Ultra ($200/month), with AI usage caps increasing as you move up through the tiers. The free plan will only offer limited chat and agent usage, and Premium or higher is required to access the latest Grok models.

There’s another draw for existing X Premium+ subscribers: The comparable plan on the new X subscription costs the same or less, the company noted.

Existing users can either switch from their subscription settings on X to upgrade to the new bundle, or maintain their current plan. The option to upgrade will roll out gradually, so interested customers will need to keep an eye on their billing settings for the offer to upgrade.

Tech.title: Apple refreshes its HomePod mini with a new chip and $149 price tag
Tech.content:
Apple’s new HomeView device was the center of the show at its smart home event on Tuesday, but the company also refreshed its HomePod mini smart speaker with a new chip and Siri AI integration, the latter of which will be available through a future update.

The $149 update is $50 more expensive than the original version launched over six years ago in 2020. The new HomePod mini has an S10 chip that helps improve optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance.

With the new HomePod mini, users can control their smart home devices through voice commands. Plus, the speaker can listen for sounds like a smoke alarm and send a notification to users’ phones — a feature that Alexa devices have offered for years.

Apple said that with Siri AI, users will be able to have multi-turn conversations, but it didn’t provide a date for when the new assistant will be available to HomePod mini 2 buyers.

The company also said the new speaker works better with its other devices. For instance, users could form a four-speaker home entertainment system paired with the new Apple TV 4K. Plus, the HomePod mini 2 speakers can be the default speaker for Mac for video calls or music playback instead of built-in speakers.

The device has another new feature, as well: a visual canvas called “Sound Glow,” which uses the color scheme of the album art to turn the top of the HomePod mini into a visual canvas that will glow and pulse in sync with the music. Users can also pick soundscapes like rain or ocean waves to start animations.

The new speaker comes in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight colorways and will be available starting October 30. Consumers can preorder starting today.

Tech.title: Apple’s new smart home lineup includes a smart lock, thermostat, and video doorbells
Tech.content:
Apple is getting serious about the smart home space. The company on Tuesday showed off its new Apple Home Collection, which includes a new smart deadbolt lock, video doorbell, thermostat, temperature sensor, and a range of security cameras.

The new devices are designed to work with HomeView, the company’s new smart home hub which can be used to control connected accessories and interact with Apple’s software.

This new range of smart home accessories could help Apple compete better with Amazon Ring and Google Nest, two established players in connected home security. The products will become available in December.

Apple says the devices were built in partnership with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric — an interesting move for the company, which has long sought to build and support every smart home accessory itself.

The smart lock, priced at $349.95, stands out for its support for ultra-wideband (UWB), a wireless technology that enables more precise proximity detection than traditional Bluetooth. This could allow the lock to recognize when an authorized user approaches and automatically unlock the door, reducing the need to pull out a phone or reach for a physical key.

The $249.95 wired video doorbell, meanwhile, will let homeowners see who’s outside, monitor visitors, and receive notifications when someone approaches their property. When someone rings it, a chime will sound through Apple devices like HomeView, HomePod, and HomePod mini. Users will also be notified on their iPhone or iPad.

As for the temperature sensor, it can provide insight into conditions in individual rooms, helping users identify temperature differences between areas and make adjustments.

For security, Apple is also introducing indoor and outdoor cameras, as well as a floodlight camera ($399.95) that combines exterior lighting with video monitoring. The camera lineup includes features such as live viewing, motion detection, intelligent alerts, and video storage.

Tech.title: The ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Filmmakers Terrified Bystanders With Their Monster Sounds
Tech.content:
Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.

While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”

While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.

“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”

Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.

“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”

For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.

Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.

Tech.title: Apple Reboots Its Smart-Home Strategy With New Hardware and a ‘Home Collection’
Tech.content:
Apple has lagged in the smart home race, which Amazon and Google have dominated for a decade with Alexa and Google Assistant (now Gemini), respectively.

But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.

That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.

Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras.

Here's everything you need to know.

The Apple HomeView

The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.

It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.)

Tech.title: The Apple HomeView Is Like a Giant Apple Watch for the Home
Tech.content:
Courtesy of Apple

A Big Apple Watch

The first thing I thought of after seeing the Apple HomeView in action is that it looks like a blown-up Apple Watch. The 7-inch square screen has multiple “faces” you can swipe through, exactly like the smartwatch. You can even customize the face’s colors and add different complications for more glanceable information.

The faces can range from a clock, your favorite photos of friends, family, or pets (you can even use shared albums) to weather updates and, yes, Snoopy animations. Swipe up for the home screen, which is more like an iPhone or iPad, with apps neatly arranged alongside widgets. Except the HomeView doesn’t run iOS or iPadOS—it runs the generically named HomeView software.

It doesn’t have an App Store. Instead, Apple has a curated selection of apps, including FaceTime, Messages, and Safari. A handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps. If your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup. (There are no video streaming apps like YouTube, Netflix, or Disney+, but if those companies choose to make their apps available on the CarPlay framework, they will show up on the HomeView; for now, you'll have to consume videos by using the Safari browser.)

To get the most out of the HomeView, you need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer)—you can’t set it up with an iPad. Apple says you can still set it up with an older iPhone and access some of Siri AI's smarts (like broad world knowledge), but smarter app actions and personal context queries require an iPhone with Apple Intelligence.

Tech.title: Wikipedians Believed AI Would Come and Go. They Were Wrong
Tech.content:
Long before the storm of AI struck Wikipedia, the Wikimedia Foundation was making preparations. Wikipedians battened down the hatches and made confident-sounding predictions that it would break and wash over them. Large language models might even improve Wikipedia, it was said, automating more of the housekeeping—formatting, sources, citations, missing links—and so freeing up humans to do creative work. It was not so simple. In 2019, then-Wikimedia Foundation head Katherine Maher wrote an op-ed in The New York Times under the headline “Without Humans, A.I. Can Wreak Havoc.” “Too often,” she wrote, “artificial intelligence is presented as an all-powerful solution to our problems, a scalable replacement for people.” The issue confronting Wikipedia, retaining human control over machines, was the same one soon being faced everywhere.

Already in 2018 Google was training AI to write “Wikipedia-like articles,” and by October 2024, a Princeton University study found that about 5 percent of nearly 3,000 newly created articles on English Wikipedia in a single month (August 2024) contained a substantial amount of AI-generated content. There were signs. ChatGPT was fond of em dashes—parenthetical statements that look like this one—and curly quotation marks. Sometimes, residues from the prompts used to compose articles were left behind (“Here is your Wikipedia article,” they might say.)

At first, Wikipedians tried to shape and control AI, to make its output “acceptable and constructive,” or to fix or remove if it proved otherwise. Generic fluff like “praising a village for its fertile farmlands, livestock, and scenic countryside” and fake sources were weeded out. By March 2026, AI content was found to violate its core principles so often that writing with large language models was banned outright, and their role restricted to translation and minor proofreading.

A much-read essay titled “Death of Wikipedia” explained this defensive posture. It predicted a ripple effect: As contributors reduced their contributions in response to AI pervading the platform, there might be a temptation to replace their work with still more AI, creating a downward spiral. One viral X post lamented that artificial intelligence seemed to be changing things in the wrong direction: “I want AI to do my laundry and dishes so that I can do art and writing, not for AI to do my art and writing so that I can do my laundry and dishes.” The “Death of Wikipedia” warned against something similar: Rather than AI performing Wikipedia’s “housekeeping” roles, it might compose its articles instead, leaving humans relegated to formatting and cleanup. The result would trap editors in an endless curatorial project derived not from human priorities but from the frostbitten harvests of machines.

“The potential ‘whittling down’ each year of our pool of talented writers is the greatest threat to Wikipedia,” another Wikipedian wrote, “as we must increase the number of editors, especially expert editors, to be able to fix the sprawling hellscape of weak, inaccurate and incomplete articles that drag down the project.” A Wikipedia written and read by machines threatened to create a new, deracinated Wikipedia, stripped not only of its context, but of its animating passion. It would be artless, and soulless. When the Wikimedia Foundation says that the care and commitment of Wikipedians to “reliable encyclopedic knowledge is something AI cannot replace,” that is not the same as saying that it will not be replaced.

Once Google introduced AI Overviews in search, they quickly became as central to the experience as Wikipedia was until recently. (This also means Wikipedia still does play a crucial role as a source, only at one step removed.) Anyone who uses AI agents knows that they give plausible, almost intuitive answers, which can pass a superficial review of their sourcing. They are also often wrong. If Wikipedia itself becomes corrupted by artificial intelligence, by what means will we prove when they are wrong?

Courtesy of W. W. Norton & Company Buy This Book At: Amazon

Bookshop.org

Books-A-Million If you buy something using links in our stories, we may earn a commission. This helps support our journalism. Learn more.

Implicit in the idea of a single, machine-edited encyclopedia to rule them all is that such a phenomenon should act as a final authority. Its appeal, to the kind of people who find it appealing, is that it will be coolly rational, a kind of digital King Solomon that can act as a disinterested arbiter. There is no reason to think such cold logic would not be cruel instead. Its aesthetic failings are a clue: “Slop” is a useful word for the product of artificial intelligence, which implies something unvariegated and monotonous, absent not only of nutritional value but also of the flavor that makes nutrition a pleasure.

There is also no reason to believe an AI encyclopedia, or any other encyclopedia, should be unifying. Whatever its shortcomings and eccentricities, Wikipedia is the closest thing to an “encyclopedia of everything” we have ever had. Once smartphones became widespread after the iPhone’s launch in 2007, the old speculations, however far-reaching, were realized: Wikipedia was costless, portable, immediate, and electric. Enormous and omnipresent, it really became an approximation of the “sum of all human knowledge.” But so what? What did access to this oracle mean for human flourishing? What good has Wikipedia done?

Tech.title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues
Tech.content:
Only one person agreed to be Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says.

Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk, which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed.

“Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.”

Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies.

Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film.

I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today.

ALEX GIBNEY: Good to see you, Zoë.

This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk, Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film?

Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character.

I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it.

Tech.title: The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Has Poured Millions Into Nevada Shell Companies
Tech.content:
The Spanish Springs shopping center in Sparks, Nevada, hosts many businesses, including a Spirit Halloween, a hearing aid supplier, and a Vietnamese restaurant. It’s also home to a consulting agency that’s received millions of dollars from one of the biggest pro-AI super PAC networks ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The problem is that the company—Lantern Production Consultants LLC—doesn’t seem to exist anywhere beyond a post office box in the Spanish Springs shopping complex.

Lantern Production Consultants has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, part of a network of pro-AI super PACs funded by the Leading the Future PAC, for a wide array of services, including polling, digital advertising, research, and strategy, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by WIRED. Backed by major AI investors, Leading the Future has taken a main role in supporting candidates who back what it calls “an AI innovation policy agenda.”

It is just one of four mysterious LLCs based out of Nevada that have received payments from super PACs in the Leading the Future PAC network, including Think Big and American Mission. The network, which is also based in Nevada, has raised over $140 million to influence political campaigns that align with AI-industry priorities in the midterms.

Summit Ridge Media Group LLC, which received around $13 million between December 2025 and September 2026 from American Mission, lists an address at a mail center in a Reno strip mall. Blue Horizon Compliance Consultants, which also appears in the filings, has its address listed as a Staples location in Reno. And Prusik Partners LLC’s listed address is at a strip mall in Henderson, Nevada, sharing a building with a chiropractor and a beauty salon.

Tech.title: How to Fix the iOS 27 Settings That Are Annoying You Right Now
Tech.content:
You can tone down Liquid Glass, shorten Siri AI’s memory and stop subtitles from automatically appearing in videos — here’s where to find each setting. Patrick Holland/CNET

iOS 27 is out, and most of what it brings is worth having. You get faster performance, more capable AI photo tools and a Siri that can actually act across apps rather than just answering questions.

But, unfortunately for many, it also brings is a set of defaults that not everyone’s going to want exactly as shipped. Liquid Glass cranked to full intensity. Automatic subtitles on videos. Siri AI saving and syncing conversations across every Apple device you own.

None of it is a reason to skip the update, but all of it is worth knowing where to find and adjust before it becomes a recurring irritation.

More from CNET



Some of those additions are useful, but a few can quickly get annoying. Siri now appears in more places and its app keeps conversations forever by default. Liquid Glass also remains a major part of the iPhone’s look, whether you love all that transparency or struggle to read through it.

Fortunately, you can change many of these settings, and we’ve outlined how to do so in this article.

Make Liquid Glass easier to read

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, giving menus, buttons, notifications and other interface elements a translucent appearance. Not everyone was a fan of the new design, and with iOS 27, you now get more control over exactly how transparent the interface looks.

Go to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. Drag the slider to the right to add more tint and opacity, making buttons and text easier to distinguish from whatever is behind them. Moving it left makes the interface more transparent.

If the most opaque setting still isn’t enough, go to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and turn on Reduce Transparency. This makes translucent backgrounds more solid across iOS, although it overrides the regular Liquid Glass appearance controls.

More tint makes Liquid Glass easier to read. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Stop Siri from keeping your conversations forever

The new Siri AI works similarly t ChatGPT or Claude in iOS 27. It now comes complete with a dedicated app where you can revisit previous conversations. Those chats sync through iCloud so you can start a conversation on your iPhone and continue it on another Apple device, such as your Mac.

By default, iOS 27 keeps those conversations forever, but there is a way to automatically get rid of older conversations if you don’t want them piling up.

If you don’t need a permanent archive of everything you ask Siri, go to Settings > Siri > Keep Conversations and choose 30 Days or 1 Year. Selecting either option permanently deletes conversations beyond that timeframe.

Siri keeps your conversations forever unless you choose a shorter limit. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

While you’re there, tap Opens To and select A New Conversation if you want the Siri app to open with a blank chat instead of showing your recent conversations every time.

Siri AI requires an iPhone 15 Pro or 15 Pro Max, iPhone Air or an iPhone 16 or later.

Turn off Write with Siri if you never use it

iOS 27 puts a new Write with Siri button above the keyboard in apps including Messages, Mail and Notes. You can ask Siri AI to draft something from scratch, proofread what you’ve written or rewrite it in a different tone.

The thing is, I’m not a big fan of the AI writing tools, so I don’t use them at all.

If you prefer writing without the extra AI prompt like I do, you can restrict Siri’s writing features by using Screen Time. Go to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions, turn on the restriction and then tap Siri > Writing Assistance > Don’t Allow.

Screen Time lets you completely disable Siri’s writing tools. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

This disables access to the writing tools across your iPhone, rather than simply hiding the keyboard button, so only do this if you don’t use Apple’s AI writing tools at all. You can return to the same menu and choose Allow if you want them back. Apple documents the restriction under its Apple Intelligence Screen Time controls.

Stop Siri from activating so easily

Introduced back in iOS 17, Siri can now wake up when you simply say “Siri” instead of “Hey Siri.” The one-word command is convenient, but it also makes accidental activations more likely whenever someone says Siri’s name in a conversation or a video they’re watching online.

Siri goes absolutely bonkers whenever I’m in work meetings about Apple features.

To disable the feature, go to Settings > Siri > Talk to Siri. Choose “Hey Siri” instead of “Siri.”

Requiring “Hey Siri” can help prevent accidental activations. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

You’ll still be able to bring up Siri with your voice, but the extra word makes it less likely to wake up when you aren’t talking to it directly.

This isn’t exclusive to iOS 27, but it’s been annoying me more recently, so thought I would throw it in here, especially with Siri AI being the prominent feature on this update.

Stop subtitles from automatically appearing in videos

iOS 27 now automatically shows subtitles on videos in Photos, Safari and other apps that use Apple’s video player. I don’t mind captions when I need them, but they can take up too much of the video and distract me from whatever I’m watching.

They don’t appear randomly though. By default, iOS can turn them on when the video is in another language, when your iPhone is muted or when you skip back.

Whenever subtitles appear in Apple’s video player, you can tap the video to show the playback controls, tap the More Controls button, select Subtitles and choose Off.

You can disable subtitles per video. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

If iOS keeps turning them on because it thinks the video is in another language, go to Settings > Accessibility > Subtitles & Captioning. Under Automatic Subtitles, turn off When Languages Don’t Match.

The same menu also has switches for Show When Muted and Show on Skip Back, so you can disable those behaviors individually without turning off every automatic subtitle feature.

You can also disable each automatic subtitle trigger individually. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Some apps and websites use their own video players, so you may need to find a separate CC or subtitles button instead.

For more on iOS 27, check out this article on the features it brings to your iPhone and how Siri AI helped one of my colleagues avoid eating diarrhea lettuce.

Tech.title: Want Your New iPhone Duo Fast? Lock in Your Details Now
Tech.content:
If you’re eager to get your hands on the highly anticipated iPhone Duo, the first foldable iPhone, here’s how to get a head start on ordering. Apple has opened a staging page for preorders on apple.com, where you can get ready to place a preorder for the viral phone.

Head over to Apple’s online storefront, and you’ll find that a new iPhone Duo configurator is now live. On that page, save your preferred phone color, storage, mobile carrier and payment method. Saving these details in advance ensures you can complete your purchase immediately when preorders open at 5 a.m. PT on Friday.

Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, one of its first new products under the helm of new CEO John Ternus, during its Surprise and Shine event in Cupertino, California, on Friday. It’s the first foldable from Apple, although merely the latest in a wave of new bendy phones to hit the market.

The iPhone Duo opens to reveal a 7.6-inch display and folds down to a pocketable passport size. The shifting shape supports split-screen multitasking and Apple Pencil, and brings a host of new features and animations to Apple iOS 27.

Pricing starts at $1,999 for the 512GB model and tops out at $3,199 for the 2TB version — before carrier subsidies — making the iPhone Duo the most expensive iPhone ever released. Price aside, observers expect demand among early adopters to be high, so prepping your order now is a smart idea.

Not quite sure that the new iPhone Duo is the right phone for you? I’m also on the fence. Check out CNET’s coverage leading up to the launch of the new foldable and iOS 27, as well as the more conventionally shaped iPhone 18 Pro, so you can make an informed decision.

Tech.title: Microsoft President Says AI Has Fewer Regulations Than Milk. So Now What?
Tech.content:
The next time you pick up a carton of milk, consider this: It has likely passed through more safety inspections than the AI system writing your emails, screening your job application or negotiating with your bank. That, according to Microsoft President Brad Smith, is the problem.

In an interview with ITV last week, Smith said that AI is less regulated than milk and washing machines. He proposed that governments adopt established production safety practices and that AI companies build “kill switches,” a kind of emergency brake that would allow operators to shut down a system that begins behaving in an unsafe or unintended way.

Smith’s comments come amid growing public concern that voluntary industry commitments to safety — a form of toothless self-regulation — are not enough to manage systems that can influence decisions, handle sensitive data and, in the wrong hands, enable cyberattacks. Recent cases of so-called “rogue AI agents” escaping their environments, such as the summer’s infamous Hugging Face hack and attempted breaches of Australian and US government websites, have drawn scrutiny to AI’s alleged “existential risk” and sparked calls for a pause.

More from CNET

On Saturday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed Smith’s sentiments in a lengthy X post, saying that the biggest companies lack a “mechanistic understanding” of the tools they deploy. Nadella also argued for slower development, incident reporting and independent review.

“We must build contained systems whose behavior we can observe, limits we can test and actions we can always contain,” Nadella wrote.

Microsoft’s statements come less than two weeks after top AI executives, including Nadella, met with President Donald Trump, who announced his proposal to rename AI as “super intelligence.“

Several Silicon Valley leaders — including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk — signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, pledging to establish internal committees to oversee development and to work with independent auditors. (Though Microsoft doesn’t appear to have signed Trump’s voluntary accord, Nadella notably uses the term “super intelligence” in his recent X post.)

Smith’s and Nadella’s comments place Microsoft closer to Anthropic’s camp of “caution,” which calls for stronger AI oversight. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s Altman said that we should all just “accept some bad things happening” for the benefit of AI, whereas Zuckerberg and Huang continue to double down on their rejection of an industry-wide, coordinated slowdown in AI development.

Wherever they stand on the regulation debate, AI leaders all stand to benefit in some way from engaging in the discussion on safety guardrails. For example, Microsoft recently released Microsoft Execution Containers, an enterprise security feature that protects devices by restricting the files and programs AI models can access and providing a built-in kill switch to instantly shut them down if needed.

A Microsoft representative declined to make any further comment.

The “rogue AI” narrative and Trump’s “super intelligence” rebrand serve as implicit marketing for the biggest AI companies — making them wealthier and more powerful. Cheng Xin/Getty Images

The ‘rogue AI’ narrative and Big Tech regulation

Despite increasingly public safety threats, it’s unlikely that the Trump administration will back regulation across the entire AI industry. The president has declared AI safety concerns a hoax, even as insiders report that more nuanced debates are unfolding behind closed doors. Last month, Trump posted on Truth Social that the only guardrail the AI industry needs is a “strong and smart president.”

In December 2025, Trump issued an executive order designed to prevent states from passing “cumbersome legislation” regulating AI model development, passing the buck to his own administration. The president continues to post online about maintaining a low-regulation environment for the biggest AI companies.

Many prominent AI critics argue that the entire regulatory framework is flawed from the start because it lets AI companies define the security threats and respond on their own terms. Distributed AI Research Institute founder Timnit Gebru has argued that the “rogue AI” narrative surrounding incidents like Hugging Face and access to government websites shifts attention away from basic corporate failures.

“This is not models going rogue,” Gebru told Democracy Now during an interview on Oct. 1. “This is gross incompetence and negligence by a particular company.”

Gebru said that people need to understand that these fallible machines don’t act autonomously with their own agency. “We need to hold corporations liable for unleashing these kinds of error-prone models into the world,” she said.

According to Gebru, the focus on so-called runaway AI and the push for voluntary self-regulation are ways for the industry to avoid accountability under existing law. Rather than face liability for unsafe security practices occurring now, AI companies redirect the conversation to an unprecedented danger likely to occur in the future.

The real danger is regulatory capture, where AI companies shape the rules that are supposed to constrain them. In this way, the public is asked to trust the morality of the very companies that build and profit from AI.

Tech.title: Meta Launches Muse Wonder AI Models to Play Catch-Up With Rivals
Tech.content:
Tech giant Meta debuted its new Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full premium AI models on Monday, continuing a push toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently called the “AI frontier,” where the heavy hitters in the artificial intelligence space have dominated.

The models build upon the Muse Spark AI model, launched earlier this year. Meta calls the new paid tiers its “most capable models to date,” reporting the models can perform personal and professional agentic tasks ranging from handling insurance claims to helping renters understand a lease agreement to building entire working apps.

Playing catch-up

Meta says its new models, the fruits of billions of dollars invested over the last year, leapfrog the competition. But it’s playing catch-up with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google in the AI race.

More from CNET

“Meta is making up for lost time with lots of new AI tools,” Katelyn Chedraoui, CNET’s expert reporter on artificial intelligence, told me. “But this new frontier model comes amid serious safety concerns in the AI industry. Safeguards will be essential to any new launch.”

Many researchers and experts are advocating for external evaluation and regulation of the technology, with some AI executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, making high-profile calls to slow AI development. Meanwhile, Zuckerberg has been vocal in his belief that labs can and should self-police to stave off the worst effects of AI.

“I’m much closer to the belief that AI is a technology that can be engineered with normal guardrails and built responsibly than the anthropomorphic vision of AI, which is that it is just going to go do its own thing,” Zuckerberg told Financial Times in an interview this week.

Meta recently announced the Muse Charm AI hardware, which looks like a keychain or pendant. Meta/CNET

Muse Wonder and Wonder Full

Muse Wonder is the “state-of-the-art” premium-tier AI model from Meta. It is available first to coders who pay for access to the Meta Model API, via the Power Plan at $20 per month or the Maximum Plan at $100 per month. However, Meta’s announcement says it “will soon power experiences in Muse” with more flexible per-million-token pricing.

Meta says Muse Wonder builds on the core capabilities of its Muse Spark AI model with more advanced features, greater processing power and improved capability in law, finance and health applications. Meta gives the example of Muse parsing a leasing agreement or handling an insurance claim. (To be clear, do not rely on AI for healthcare or mental health.) Muse Wonder’s new “frontier coding performance” will also enable the agent to assist in building games and apps.

Muse Wonder introduces two new features: Active Memory and Active Focus.

The first, Active Memory, enables the model to remember and carry information across conversations. Storing potentially sensitive data immediately sets my privacy-conscious Spidey Sense on edge. That said, Meta says it has trained its Muse Wonder model to avoid sharing private information without permission and has hardened it against cyberattacks. The company even says that “developers and security teams can use models like Muse Wonder to find flaws in their own code and strengthen their systems,” which — I gotta be honest — sounds to me like the peak tech hubris.

Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, has been vocal in his belief that labs can and should self-police to stave off the worst effects of AI. James Martin/CNET

The second new feature, Active Focus, keeps the AI agent working when it runs into technical dead ends. With Active Focus, Muse Wonder is said to be capable of alternative approaches, recovering from errors and asking the user for clarification. That should let the model handle more complex tasks than Spark and encounter fewer roadblocks, which we’ve seen firsthand in our testing.

But boasting that your AI model can more effectively circumnavigate what may be blocks put in place (perhaps for a reason) sounds eerily familiar. Recently, Anthropic revoked access to its AI models, Mythos 5 and Fable 5, after the US government imposed sweeping restrictions on who could use them.

Muse Wonder Full is said to be an even more powerful version of the premium Wonder model with all of the same new features, but with a shift in focus toward businesses and power users. Tech.title: Smartphone Shipments Just Hit a New Low. Thanks, RAMageddon
Tech.content:
If you’re holding on to your phone despite a wave of new, high-powered options, you’re not alone. Hitting the lowest mark since 2012, smartphone shipments worldwide continued a months-long skid, slumping 20% in the third quarter of 2026 due to the RAMageddon memory shortage, according to a new analysis by Counterpoint Research.

Counterpoint said that the cost of DRAM and NAND — the two main memory chips used in smartphones, computers and data centers — continues to rise, forcing manufacturers to raise phone prices, which are up 20% overall this year. Memory costs more because there’s less of it to go around, thanks to the massive AI infrastructure buildup and its voracious appetite for chips.

It was the second consecutive quarter to take “the full brunt of the memory crisis,” Shilpi Jain, a senior analyst at Counterpoint, said in a statement Monday.

More from CNET

Research firm Gartner has estimated that companies will spend $1.4 trillion on AI infrastructure this year and $2.6 trillion overall. More than 70% of global memory chip production will go toward AI investment, TrendForce said. Global fears about rising inflation for most products and services are also likely suppressing phone sales.

Some manufacturers fared all right during the third quarter, according to Counterpoint. Samsung’s market share was 23%, up from 19% in 2025, thanks in part to “robust initial demand” for the Galaxy Fold 8. Apple’s third-quarter market share was 22%, the first time the company has surpassed 20% in that three-month period. But both companies saw a year-over-year decline in shipments.

Things aren’t looking rosy for customers’ wallets, either. Earlier this month, Samsung hiked prices by $100 for its Galaxy S26 phones, and Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched last month with prices set $100 above the previous generation.

How are consumers responding?

The third quarter saw a number of notable smartphone introductions, including Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, the Google Pixel 11 and, in the period’s waning days, the iPhone 18 Pro line and Apple’s first foldable, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. Preorders for the iPhone Duo begin on Friday.

Shoppers will be cautious about buying the latest and greatest in smartphones because of higher prices, says TMT analyst Paolo Pescatore.

“New design features, including foldables, may generate excitement and appeal, but their steep price premiums remain hard to justify when most people want a device that delivers robust, reliable connectivity,” Pescatore told CNET via email. “For many, the question is straightforward: why replace a perfectly functioning smartphone that continues to meet their everyday needs?”

Counterpoint Research found in a recent survey that half of respondents — spanning the US, UK, India, China and Germany — would wait until holiday sales to buy a new phone. That number rises to 56% among Gen Z consumers. Counterpoint’s Jain said consumers are increasingly shopping for “refurbished devices and prioritizing higher-value devices.”

With sales down, phonemakers might resort to different strategies for customers, including refurbished handsets, repairs and trade-in schemes, Pescatore said. Cellphone carriers like T-Mobile, Verizon Wireless and AT&T could also use financing plans and bundled services as enticements.

As AI investment continues to devour memory supply, phone prices won’t be falling anytime soon. And with companies focusing more on premium devices, there could be fewer budget alternatives available for customers, Counterpoint Research said.

Tech.title: This Cheap Roller Is a Must for Dog and Cat Owners Battling Pet Hair
Tech.content:
Pets are family, but family can be messy. Managing pet hair from animals is a daily struggle for owners and during shedding season, things get especially dire. The same goes for cat owners with litter boxes: those tiny bits of clay end up in the darndest of places, including between the sheets. Ick.

No matter what I’ve tried, litter and pet hair end up on furniture or in your bed almost constantly. Vacuums work well for keeping floors free of pet hair, but they’re less effective in other parts of the home.

The inexpensive SandBar does things even the best pet hair vacuums can’t. John Carlsen/CNET

I recently spotted an inexpensive tool that promises to collect hair, sand, and pieces of litter. It doesn’t rely on a cord or battery and costs just $30. I took a chance and tested the SandBar, a dual-roll lint roller, to see if it can make it easier to keep stray hair and litter at bay. I also wanted to see how it would fare with other lint-roller-adjacent tasks like dusting and cleaning floors.

More from CNET

How SandBar Roller differs from other lint rollers

The SandBar Roller Starter Kit I tested included the roller head, an extendable handle and two preinstalled lint rolls. John Carlsen/CNET

The SandBar Roller’s appeal lies in its two large lint rollers instead of one. While the idea doesn’t seem like much of a departure from a typical large lint roller, I couldn’t find any other dual-roller designs intended for use between bedsheets like SandBar. By arranging the rollers this way, SandBar can clean the top and bottom sheets at the same time without getting stuck.

The Best Handheld Vacuums, Tested by CNET See at CNET

While SandBar markets its proprietary lint rolls as stronger than normal rolls, they’re not much different from the extra-large pet-hair version of the Scotch-Brite lint roller. Both are 8 inches wide, with an inner diameter of 1.5 inches. Much to SandBar’s credit, its six-pack of refill rolls is just $20, which is very competitive with other lint roll refills I found on Amazon, with the optional subscription price dropping to just $16 for each one-, two- or three-month delivery.

Testing the SandBar Roller

The extendable handle is very practical. John Carlsen/CNET

Ostensibly, this design targets coastal homes, where sand gets everywhere — hence the SandBar name. While I don’t live on the coast, I’ve experienced sand in my bed while traveling, or after day trips to the desert, and cat litter is a near-daily occurrence. With that in mind, I conducted a series of informal tests to see how the SandBar Roller holds up.

When I put the SandBar between the sheets, it moved fairly smoothly, at least until it snagged on some sheets that were too loose. It didn’t jam, but that means it works better for beds with the sheet firmly tucked at the foot — something I don’t do for various sleep-friendly reasons. Still, it worked well after tightening the sheets a bit, even snagging a few cat hairs and litter fragments. It’s a nice alternative to washing the sheets as frequently as I have to now.

I like the stickiness of the rolls, which is satisfyingly tacky without leaving residue or making used strips hard to pull off. John Carlsen/CNET

The SandBar removed cat fur from hard-to-reach places

Next, I wanted to see how it handled cleaning smart window shades and curtains, which often collect fur as my cat patrols windows a few times a day. It was a little more awkward, but taking the handle off proved effective, and the sticky roller collected a substantial amount of fur. I had to peel off multiple sheets because of the amount of fur, but it took only a few passes to clean the curtain. The SandBar Roller was very useful on furniture and pet beds, but I noticed that being too aggressive can occasionally dislodge a roll.

The SandBar Roller left a fairly clean surface when I dusted off a TV cabinet and soundbar. Still, I wouldn’t trade it out for the duster and handheld vacuum I usually use. Likewise, it did well on the linoleum floor and carpet near my cat’s litter box, but still, I prefer the cleaner result I get from vacuuming.

Should you buy the SandBar Roller?

The specialized design does its job well, but is probably too niche for people who aren’t pet parents or near vast swathes of sand. John Carlsen/CNET

At $30, the SandBar Roller is unlikely to break anyone’s budget, especially when you can find similarly large bed lint rollers for the same price. In that context alone, including the cost of refill rolls, it’s probably as good as any other option. Still, the dual-roll design’s ability to get between sheets is a compelling reason to consider the SandBar Roller over the competition. The design suits households that typically deal with a lot of sand and litter in the beds. I could even see myself taking it camping for quick dirt cleanup in a sleeping bag.

However, I wouldn’t recommend it for short-term beach house rentals because it cuts corners — new guests expect clean sheets when they arrive. That said, making a SandBar Roller available during a guest’s visit could improve their experience, as long as you leave instructions explaining what it’s for and how it works.

If you don’t need the second roll — and mainly deal with pet hair on furniture — the ChomChom Roller doesn’t need refill rolls, making it a much better option for $25. Likewise, a handheld vacuum can do the same job with a bit more flexibility around the house — though it’s not quiet enough to use when others are sleeping. While it’s nice to have so many options, it’s always worth going with what works best for your needs and situation.

Tech.title: Beats Teases Upcoming Pokemon Portable Pill Speaker: Gotta Hear ‘Em All
Tech.content:
Put a Pokemon character, especially Pikachu, on just about anything — including a $100 Polaroid camera — and fans will take notice. On Monday, Beats by Dre teased an upcoming collaboration where the colorful characters seem to be coming to decorate Beats Pill Bluetooth speakers.

Beats by Dre didn’t share a lot of information, but the caption “Time to catch something new” plays off the classic Pokemon tagline, “Gotta catch ’em all!” The 6-second video shows electrical charges in yellow and purple flashing over a shadowed Beats Pill speaker. It ends with a screen showing the Pokemon Poke Ball logo and the Beats by Dre “b” logo, with an X between them, teasing a product collaboration.

Time to catch something new. pic.twitter.com/Rt0IfTKENC — Beats by Dre (@beatsbydre) October 12, 2026

The inclusion of yellow sparks in the video seems to hint that the Beats speaker will be themed around the popular yellow Pokemon, Pikachu. Tech site 9to5Toys suggests that the purple flashes might mean another Beats speaker could be themed around a purple character, such as Mewtwo, Gengar or Ditto.

More from CNET

Beats’ teaser did not announce a release date for a Pokemon-themed Pill speaker, but Apple’s Welcome Home event, expected to focus on new smart home devices, is scheduled for Tuesday. Apple bought Beats by Dre for $3 billion back in 2014.

The speaker isn’t a brand-new revelation for those who stay up to date on all things Pokemon. Last week, a Pokemon fan who goes by BritBrattv posted a photo to Facebook showing a bright yellow Pikachu-themed Beats Pill speaker in what appears to be a Target shopping cart, though that photo hasn’t been confirmed as official.

And former Apple CEO Tim Cook shared a video on X in August showing Pikachu visiting Apple Park.

“Today’s agenda at Apple Park,” Cook wrote. “Introduce the @Pokemon team to John, talk gaming, and politely ask Pikachu to stay out of the pond. Two out of three were accomplished.” By “John,” he presumably means John Ternus, the new Apple CEO.

Representatives for Beats by Dre and Pokemon didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Beats Pill speaker, in non-Pokemon designs, is priced at $129 at Target and Amazon as of Monday. In a 2024 review, CNET executive reviews editor David Carnoy called the Pill “a very good compact Bluetooth speaker,” praising its sound quality and strong battery life.

Tech.title: Cyberattack Targets French Supermarket Refrigerators, Forcing Mass Food Disposal
Tech.content:
Hundreds of supermarkets in France were the subject of a coordinated hack early Monday morning that turned up the heat on fridges and freezers, causing food to spoil and, in some cases, fires to break out.

According to reports from AFP, three major grocery chains in the country — E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U — reported that hackers forced connected fridges and freezers at hundreds of stores to go into defrost mode for several hours, raising their temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). Paris authorities told the news agency that other grocery chains were also hit.

While it’s unclear who is responsible for the attacks or the exact exploit chain used, the hackers targeted software on two Danfoss system controllers. The company told the industry publication Cooling Post that the affected systems, AK-SM800 and AK-SC355, were running outdated firmware. “We are working with affected customers to implement appropriate mitigation measures, including firmware updates where available, stronger network protections and removing direct internet exposure where applicable,” Danfoss told Cooling Post.

More from CNET

On a web page for its AK-SM800 controllers, Danfoss says the company “takes security seriously” and that “new measures are being implemented” to improve security.

A representative for Danfoss didn’t immediately return a request for comment.

The incidents are alarming for several reasons. In addition to proving yet again that network-connected devices, especially older ones, can be targets of attack, the French supermarket attack highlights vulnerabilities in global food supplies that can be quickly and dangerously exploited.

Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Cooperative U, said in a post on X that an investigation into the attack is underway. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he posted (translated from French).

Je confirme qu’une cyberattaque touche depuis cette nuit les installations de production de froid de plusieurs magasins de notre réseau @CooperativeU.

Nos équipes sont pleinement mobilisées, en lien avec les frigoristes, pour rétablir la situation au plus vite. Une enquête devra… — Dominique Schelcher (@schelcher) October 12, 2026

The ‘internet of things’ is being attacked

The attack on a French supermarket underscores the growing risk of attacks on operational technology and cold-chain infrastructure. Though the fridges and freezer units weren’t consumer smart fridges with app controls and touch screens, the controllers were connected to the internet to remotely manage defrost cycles, temperatures and alarms across many stores.

Companies may have many reasons for using these kinds of OT devices. They can log temperatures to ensure they’re meeting food safety standards, deploy firmware updates to prevent security incidents like this one and get alerts if a fridge or freezer is malfunctioning. Some devices like this also monitor inventory or even update prices for digital shelf displays.

But just as appliances from companies such as Samsung can be affected by a hack or even software glitches — like a recent incident in Korea that bricked some smart fridges — these industrial devices rely on imperfect software and internet connections, which expose them to the outside world.

Older IT and operational systems that are incorporated into connected systems may be especially difficult to defend, said Nathaniel Jones, senior vice president of global threat intelligence at Darktrace. “A cyber incident no longer affects only data or business systems; it can manipulate physical equipment and cause real-world damage.”



That damage can scale quickly if those systems are spread across many locations, all of which are exposed to the internet. “If it is connected, it can be targeted,” Jones said in a statement to CNET via email.

If that’s not scary enough, these are the same types of vulnerabilities that can make utilities such as power grids, water suppliers and even nuclear power plants vulnerable to attack.
